title: Getting started: What it is
text: WolOS is an operating system for the PC you already own: the program that starts when you switch the computer on and that every other app runs on, the way Windows or macOS does on other computers. You get a desktop with a menu bar at the top and a Dock at the bottom, a Store for apps, System Settings for everything you can change, and your own files in your home folder. Nothing about it needs a terminal: every everyday task has a window, a button and a picture in this manual. You can try it before you decide. WolOS runs from a USB stick without touching the computer's disk, so you can see whether your Wi-Fi, screen and sound work, and then install it on its own or next to Windows.

title: Getting started: Why WolOS does it this way
text: You sat down to write, play, draw or talk to someone, not to look after a computer. So WolOS is built to stay out of the way: it starts quickly, it does not change a setting without asking you, and it keeps a second copy of itself for every update, so a bad update is undone by starting the computer again. The things that take a technical person an afternoon on other systems (codecs for music and video, the tools for games or programming) are one switch in the installer or one click in the Store.

title: Getting started: What you need
text: You need Why A 64-bit PC from roughly the last ten years WolOS starts through UEFI, which every such PC has. 16 GB of free disk space or more The installer refuses a smaller disk. More is better: your files go here too. A USB stick of 4 GB or more WolOS is copied onto it. Everything that was on the stick is erased. About half an hour Most of it is waiting while the stick is written and WolOS installs. Your Windows recovery key, if you keep Windows with BitLocker Windows may ask for it once after the install. Tip No spare PC? A virtual machine works too: give it the downloaded file instead of a stick. The Download page lists the settings that work.

title: Getting started: How
text: The way from the download to your own desktop has five steps. Each one links to the page that explains it in full. Download WolOS. Open the Download page and click the download button. You get one file whose name ends in .iso (an ISO), about 2 GB. The Download page also shows the file's checksum. Comparing it is optional; it proves the file arrived complete. On Windows, open PowerShell in your Downloads folder and run the one command of this page, then compare the long code it prints with the one on the Download page: Get-FileHash wolos-*.iso Write the stick. Use an image writer: balenaEtcher (Windows, macOS, Linux) or Rufus (Windows; choose DD Image mode when it asks). Choose the .iso file, choose the stick, and start. When the writer says it is done, the stick is ready. Careful The writer erases the whole stick. Copy anything you want to keep off it first, and check twice that you picked the stick and not another drive. Start the computer from the stick. Plug the stick in, switch the computer on and, right away, press the key that opens the boot menu: often F12, F11, F8 or Esc (the computer usually shows which for a second). Pick the entry with the stick's name; on some computers it starts with UEFI. You see the WolOS welcome page with two buttons. Try WolOS (1) runs the whole desktop from the stick and changes nothing on the computer. Install WolOS (2) starts the installer. While you try WolOS, the first icon in the Dock is Install WolOS, so you can start the installer from the desktop too. The trial account has no password, so there is no Lock Screen, and the Sharing rows that need an administrator are greyed out until you install. If the computer has Secure Boot switched on, it may show a blue screen before the welcome page. That screen comes from the computer, not from WolOS, and appears once; Secure Boot walks you through it. Install. Click Install WolOS and answer the installer's questions: language, time zone, which disk, whether to keep Windows, a password for the disk, your account. Every page says in plain words what will happen, and nothing on the disk changes until you click Install on the last page, a summary of every change. Installing WolOS shows every page, and Installing next to Windows has the extra steps for keeping Windows. Start WolOS. When the installer says WolOS Is Installed, click Restart and take the stick out when the screen goes dark. The computer starts WolOS. With one account it shows that account's lock screen: the time, your picture and Enter Password, with Sleep, Restart and Shut Down at the foot. Type your password and press Return. With several accounts it shows the login window: click your picture first. Your first day continues from there.

title: Getting started: A worked example
text: Alice has a three-year-old laptop with Windows on it and wants to try WolOS without losing Windows. She downloads the ISO on the laptop, writes it to a 16 GB stick with balenaEtcher and restarts with the stick in, pressing F12 until the boot menu appears. She picks the stick and clicks Try WolOS. In Control Center she joins her Wi-Fi, plays a video in the browser to hear the speakers, and closes the lid to check that the laptop sleeps and wakes. All of it works, so she restarts, clicks Install WolOS, chooses Install Alongside Windows and gives WolOS half of the disk. Twenty minutes later the laptop starts WolOS; when she wants Windows she presses F12 while it starts and picks Windows in the computer's startup menu, as the installer's last screen said.

title: Getting started: If something goes wrong
text: What you see What it means and what to do The computer starts Windows as if the stick were not there The boot menu key was pressed too late, or the stick is not in the list. Restart and press the key several times as soon as the screen lights up. If the stick is not listed, write it again; some writers need their DD or "image" mode. The boot menu lists the stick twice Pick the entry that starts with UEFI. A blue screen says "Verification failed" That is the computer's Secure Boot check. Press Enter and follow Secure Boot, or switch Secure Boot off in the computer's settings for the first start. The welcome page never appears and the screen stays black Wait a minute: the first start from a slow stick takes longer. If it stays black, try another USB port, preferably one directly on the computer. The installer finds no disk Click Look Again after connecting the disk. Installing WolOS explains what the installer never offers. The virtual machine shows a black screen after the install Check its display settings against the Download page. Anything else after the install Recovery lists every way back, from undoing a setting to starting the previous version of WolOS.

title: Installing WolOS: What it is
text: Install WolOS is the installer on the live USB stick. It asks a few questions, explains each page in plain words (what will happen, what is kept), and ends with a summary of exactly what will change. Nothing on the computer is touched until you click Install on that summary. At the first menu you can also choose Try WolOS, which runs the desktop from memory and changes nothing. Think of the installer as a builder who walks through the house with you, writes down every wall that will move, and only starts when you sign the list.

title: Installing WolOS: Why
text: A wrong step in an install can destroy someone's files. So the installer does not act page by page. While you answer the questions it writes down a plan that names every partition it may touch, shows you that plan as the summary, and only then starts. If anything else on the disk changed in the meantime (another program, a disk plugged in), it stops instead of guessing.

title: Installing WolOS: How
text: Before you start. You need a computer that starts with UEFI, at least 16 GB of free disk space, and WolOS on a USB stick or attached to a virtual machine (Getting started). Plug a laptop into power. To keep Windows, read Installing next to Windows first. Every installer page is one card with the same frame: the installer's icon and the page's title at the top, where you are on the right (for example 2 of 7), a few sentences saying what the page decides and what comes next, the choices, and Back and Continue at the bottom. Back never loses what you entered on later pages. Start from the stick and choose Install WolOS. You see the welcome page: "Install it on this computer, or try it first. Trying changes nothing." Try WolOS (1) opens the desktop from the stick; you can start the installer from there later. Install WolOS (2) opens the installer. If the computer has Secure Boot on, it shows one blue screen before this page; see Secure Boot. Choose your language and keyboard. You see "Choose your language and the keyboard you type on." Click your language in the list (1); the country next to it decides the date format and the spelling. The Keyboard menu (2) follows the language; change it if the letters printed on your keys are a different layout. Type a few letters, including ones special to your language, in the Try it field (3, "Type here to try the keyboard") to check that the keys type what you expect, then click Continue (4). Both can be changed later in System Settings (Language & Region and Keyboard). Choose your time zone. You see "Your clock follows this place." Type a big city near you in Search for a city (1): the list (2) shrinks as you type. Click the city in your time zone, then Continue (3). The installer ticks a guess for you: the time zone the computer already knows, or else the biggest city of the language you chose (New York for English). Check it, because being online plays no part. Choose the disk. You see "Choose where WolOS goes." Each disk in the computer has one row with its name, its size and where the system finds it (for example 1 TB · /dev/nvme0n1 · NVMe); click the one WolOS should go on, then Continue. The stick you started from, CDs and read-only disks are never listed, and a disk under 16 GB is refused. If no disk shows, connect it and click Look Again. Choose a method. You see "Nothing changes until the last step." Click one of the four ways in the list (1); each row says in a few words what it does (Keeps what's there, Erases one partition, keeps the rest, Starts clean, For experts). Check the Swap menu (2), then Continue (3): Erase Disk uses the whole disk. The page names what is on it ("This disk has Windows on it. Erasing removes it."). Install Alongside shrinks your other system and puts WolOS next to it. A slider ("Drag to choose how much room each system gets.") splits the room. See Installing next to Windows. Replace a Partition erases one partition and keeps the rest of the disk. Manual is for people who know partitions: create, delete and resize them, give each a job (system, startup files, your files /home, swap, another folder), choose whether to erase it, and keep an existing /home. The Swap menu chooses where the computer puts things when its memory is full. Compressed memory (the default) packs them in memory and is right for almost everyone; a swap file on the disk is for computers with little memory that you want to put to sleep for a long time. Choose encryption. You see "Encryption keeps your files private if this computer is lost." Pick Security Chip, Password or Don't Encrypt in the list (1), explained in the table below, then Continue (2). With Security Chip the line under the list adds that your account password opens the disk when the chip can't. encryption works like BitLocker on Windows or FileVault on a Mac. Choose Secure Boot. You see "Secure Boot checks at every start that nobody changed WolOS while the computer was off." The switch Use Secure Boot (1), with One blue screen after the restart under it, is off unless you turn it on. The box below it (2), One blue screen after restart, says what the one-time blue key screen looks like and lists its five steps; scroll it and read them now, because the mouse does not work there. Next to Windows with BitLocker the page also says what Windows will ask. Click Continue (3). Secure Boot explains the choice. Create your account. You see "You use this to sign in." Type your Full name (1); the Account name (2) fills itself in from it (lowercase letters and digits, starting with a letter), and you can change it. Type a password of at least 8 characters in Password and again in Verify (3); the eye button shows what you typed. With Security Chip chosen, the line under them reminds you that this password also opens the disk when the chip can't. The Computer name (4) is how other devices on your network see this computer. Log in automatically (5) skips the login window at start; leave it off on a laptop you carry. Click Continue (6). This account is an administrator: it can install apps and change any setting. A name the system already uses is refused. Pick modules (optional). You see "Add sets of apps for what you do, or none. You can change this later." Each module has a row with a line on what it brings and a switch (1): Developer Tools, AI Assistants, Local AI, Creative Apps and, at the end of the list, Gaming. None is on unless you turn it on. The line under the list (2) says how much the ones you turned on download. Click Continue (3). System Settings > Modules has these and two more (Sessions and Console) at any time; see Modules. Add media formats (optional). You see "Play the music and video files most people have, in one click." The switch Add Media Formats (1) adds MP3, AAC, H.264, HEVC, AC3 and common fonts; the list (2) says what each is for, and the line under it that some are patented in some countries. It is off unless you turn it on, because some formats are patented in some countries and the choice is yours. Click Continue (3). See Music and video formats. Read the summary. You see "Nothing has changed yet. This is exactly what will happen." The list (1) has one line per change: the disk and partitions, what is erased and what is kept, encryption, swap, the computer's name, modules and anything added later. A coloured box (2) warns about what cannot be undone: "Back up anything you need first. These changes can't be undone." when partitions change, the systems that erasing removes when you chose Erase Disk, too little room for WolOS, and once more that the files will not be encrypted when you chose Don't Encrypt. Read it all; Back changes anything. Install (3) starts writing. Wait. You see "This takes a few minutes. Keep your computer plugged in." The bar (1) shows the step it is on and the time left; below it (2), short tips about WolOS change every few seconds. Nothing restarts until you click Restart. Restart. You see "Click Restart to start using WolOS. When the screen goes dark, remove the USB stick or detach the ISO." For an encrypted disk, your recovery key (1) is shown here, once, under "Write this key down and keep it safe." Write it down on paper, or put a second USB stick in and click Save to USB (2). Turn on I wrote the key down or saved it (3); Restart (4) stays grey until you do. A line above the key also says whether Secure Boot is on. Careful Keep the recovery key away from the computer, for example in your wallet or with your passwords. If the computer's security chip and your password both stop working, it is the only way to your files.

title: Installing WolOS: Encryption: password, security chip or none
text: Choice What it means Security Chip (only shown when the installer finds a TPM) The disk opens by itself on this computer. If the chip refuses (after a firmware or Secure Boot change), your account password opens the disk instead, and the next start is automatic again. Password The disk asks for a password at every start. It must be at least 8 characters. Don't Encrypt Anyone who takes the disk can read your files. The summary says so once more. The disk password is typed before any desktop exists, on a plain keyboard map. Use letters, digits and common symbols only: accented letters cannot be typed at that point, and the installer refuses a password it knows you could not type. Your keyboard layout is applied before that prompt, so the password you type at start is the one you chose. With the security chip, the account password you choose becomes the fallback, so it must be long enough and typable too. The recovery key is a long machine-made key and opens the disk if both the password and the chip fail. It is shown once. Keep it off the computer. If the installer cannot read it at the end, a page says so and Try Again reads it before you restart; Restart waits until you have acknowledged the key.

title: Installing WolOS: Installing without a network
text: The installer works offline. The modules and media formats you ticked cannot download then, so the summary says which are added "at first start with a network" instead of promising more. They install in the background as soon as the network comes up, on Wi-Fi too, and the first start never waits for them. A module that cannot be installed is given up after five tries and is offered again in Settings > Modules under Could Not Be Added.

title: Installing WolOS: What the installer will never do
text: Write to the medium it started from, a CD, or a read-only disk. Touch a partition the plan does not name. If the disk no longer matches the plan, it stops with "The disk changed since you chose it". Finish without checking that everything the computer needs to start WolOS is in place. Leave your passwords or your recovery key written on the disk: they are removed if an install stops, and the record of the install that stays on the computer never holds them.

title: Installing WolOS: After the install
text: The computer restarts into WolOS. With Secure Boot on, a blue key screen may come first (Secure Boot). Then the first start finishes setting up the drivers for your hardware (NVIDIA graphics drivers install online when an NVIDIA card is present) and any modules that were waiting for a network, and the login window appears. Your first day continues from there. A layout made with Manual that does not use the system's own file system keeps one copy of the system instead of two, so an update cannot be undone by restarting; the installer says so on the summary.

title: Installing WolOS: A worked example
text: Alice puts the stick in an old laptop, starts it from the startup menu and clicks through the installer: language, the whole disk, a password for the disk, her name and a password for the account, no extra modules. She reads the summary, clicks Install and has a coffee. When it says WolOS is installed, she restarts, removes the stick and signs in to her new desktop.

title: Installing WolOS: If something goes wrong
text: What you see What it means and what to do The disk list is empty ("No disk found") The installer shows only disks it may write to. Connect the disk, then click Look Again; it checks again after you plug one in or free space. "WolOS needs at least 16 GB" Make more room or choose another disk. "This disk uses an older layout. Only Erase Disk can use it." The disk is divided the old way (from before UEFI). Use Erase Disk, or keep the other system and convert the disk with its own tools first. "Windows didn't shut down fully" Windows is hibernated or stopped by Fast Startup, so shrinking it could damage its files. Turn off Fast Startup in Windows, shut down fully, and start the installer again. "BitLocker protects Windows here" The installer cannot shrink a BitLocker partition. Turn BitLocker off in Windows, then try again. macOS partition Make room with Disk Utility in macOS, then start the installer again. "The disk changed since you chose it" Something else touched the disk after you chose it. Go back and choose it again. "Use at least 8 characters" / "Passwords don't match" The disk or account password is too short, or the two typings differ. "That name is already used on this computer" The account name belongs to the system. Choose another. The Failed page (below) The page names the step that failed ("The disk couldn't be prepared", "The system files couldn't be copied", "The disk couldn't be encrypted", "The startup files couldn't be installed", "Your settings couldn't be saved") and what to try. Details shows the end of the install log. When the installer refuses to go on, the page says why and that nothing on the disk was changed. "WolOS is installed, but its recovery key could not be read" The install worked. Click Try Again; Restart stays off until the key is shown. Still stuck? Click Details on the Failed page and take a photo of what it shows, then report it on GitHub. See also Recovery.

title: Installing next to Windows or Linux: What it is
text: Install Alongside puts WolOS on the same disk as Windows or another Linux. It makes the other system's partition smaller (you drag a slider to split the room), adds WolOS's partitions in the freed space, and leaves every file of the other system where it was. At start you choose which system to run. It is like moving a bookshelf to make room for a second one: nothing on the first shelf is thrown away, it just stands a little closer together.

title: Installing next to Windows or Linux: Why
text: Sharing a disk is risky when a tool guesses. WolOS reads the disk first (which systems are on it, whether Windows is hibernated or uses BitLocker), shows exactly what changes in the summary, and refuses the cases where shrinking could damage files. The plan names the partitions it may touch; if anything else moves, the install stops.

title: Installing next to Windows or Linux: How
Installing next to Windows or Linux: Before you start
text: Back up what matters. As with any change to a disk, back up first. The installer says so on the Alongside page. Shut Windows down fully. A Windows that is hibernated or was shut down with Fast Startup is refused, so its files cannot be damaged. In Windows turn off Fast Startup, choose Shut down (not Restart), then start the stick. Know your BitLocker state. The installer cannot shrink a BitLocker-protected partition ("BitLocker protects Windows here"). Turn BitLocker off in Windows for that partition, then try again. If Windows keeps BitLocker on and Secure Boot changes, Windows asks once for its recovery key (see below). macOS is not shrunk by the installer. Make room with Disk Utility in macOS, then start the installer again.

title: Installing next to Windows or Linux: In the installer
text: Choose the disk, then Install Alongside. You see "Nothing changes until the last step." on the method page, with Install Alongside Windows at the top, then "Drag to choose how much room each system gets." The page names each system found on the disk. Drag the slider to split the room. The other system only gets smaller; its files stay. If a partition cannot be shrunk, the page says why in one sentence (see the table below). Continue through encryption, Secure Boot, account and modules as in Installing WolOS. If Windows uses BitLocker and its computer trusts only Windows at start, you see "Change One Startup Setting First" with the steps, and the warning that Windows will ask once for its recovery key. Read the summary. You see "Nothing has changed yet. This is exactly what will happen." It lists what is kept, what is shrunk and what is created. If Windows stays with BitLocker and Secure Boot is on, it also tells you about the BitLocker recovery key. Click Install, wait, and read the last page. You see how to start the other system, for example "To start Windows, open your computer's startup menu while it starts, often with F12, F9 or Esc."

title: Installing next to Windows or Linux: Replacing one partition instead
text: Replace a Partition on the method page erases one partition you choose and gives it to WolOS; every other partition and its files stay. Use it when you already made room, or to replace an old Linux. If the disk already holds an earlier WolOS, you can install again over it: the old WolOS's startup files are cleared first and the rest of the disk stays.

title: Installing next to Windows or Linux: Choosing a system at start
text: When another system stays on the disk, WolOS's boot menu waits a moment so you can choose. When WolOS gets its own startup partition next to Windows', the WolOS menu lists WolOS only, because it cannot reach the other partition. Start Windows from your computer's startup menu, which you open while the computer starts, often with F12, F9 or Esc. The installer's last page says the same, with the other system's name. Another system's boot manager can start WolOS too. Most find it on their own. How to add WolOS to one that does not is in the Reference.

title: Installing next to Windows or Linux: The clock
text: WolOS keeps the clock in local time when Windows stays, as Windows does, so neither system shows the wrong time after the other has run.

title: Installing next to Windows or Linux: Secure Boot and BitLocker
text: Secure Boot changes can make Windows ask once for its BitLocker recovery key. When Windows stays with BitLocker on, the Secure Boot page and the Summary tell you before it happens: Have the key ready; it is saved at account.microsoft.com/devices/recoverykey. To avoid the prompt on a computer in Setup Mode, restore the factory Secure Boot keys in the startup settings first; WolOS then uses a one-time key screen instead. On a computer whose Secure Boot trusts only Windows, suspend BitLocker in Windows before you change the startup setting. Or leave Secure Boot off in the installer; Windows' keys are then untouched. You can turn it on later (Secure Boot).

title: Installing next to Windows or Linux: A worked example
text: Alice has Windows on a 600 GB disk and wants to try WolOS without losing it. In Windows she turns off Fast Startup and shuts down fully. She starts the stick, chooses Install Alongside Windows, drags the slider until WolOS has 215 GB and reads the summary: Windows shrinks from 600 GB to 392 GB and keeps every file. After the restart she presses F12 to choose a system. Windows opens as before, and WolOS opens when she picks it.

title: Installing next to Windows or Linux: If something goes wrong
text: What you see What to do "This disk is empty, so there's nothing to install alongside" Use Erase Disk. A disk with an older kind of layout (not GPT, the layout every recent computer uses) can only be erased too. "Windows didn't shut down fully" Turn off Fast Startup in Windows, shut down fully, try again. "BitLocker protects Windows here" Turn BitLocker off in Windows, then try again. "{partition} can't get that small" Choose a larger size for that partition (give WolOS less). "There isn't enough room for that" Delete or shrink a partition first, or give WolOS less. "Another system starts from that partition, so it can't be erased" (Manual) Do not erase Windows' startup partition: keep it as it is, or add a new startup partition of 1 GB for WolOS. After the install Windows is not in the menu Start it from the firmware's startup menu (F12, F9 or Esc). Windows asks for a BitLocker recovery key Enter it from account.microsoft.com/devices/recoverykey. It asks once. WolOS does not appear at all Open the firmware's startup menu and pick the WolOS entry; see Recovery.

title: Your first day: What it is
text: The first start after the install, and the few things worth doing in the first ten minutes. When WolOS starts with several accounts it shows the login window: the time and the date at the top left, one round picture per account at the bottom right, and Sleep, Restart and Shut Down at the bottom left. You click yours, type your password, and the desktop appears. With one account it shows that account's lock screen instead: the time, your picture and name, and the Enter Password field with an arrow button, with Sleep, Restart and Shut Down at the bottom left; type your password and press Return or click the arrow. If WolOS was installed for you without an account (for example by a shop, a school or the person who looks after the computer), a short Setup Assistant opens instead and asks a few questions, one card each: on some computers first one step for Secure Boot, then language, Wi-Fi, your account and a look, five cards in all (each says where you are, for example 2 of 5).

title: Your first day: Why WolOS does it this way
text: A new computer should not greet you with a list of chores. So WolOS asks only what it cannot guess (who you are and how you sign in), takes good defaults for the rest, and does any downloading in the background. Everything the first day touches can be changed later in System Settings, and every change you make there can be undone.

title: Your first day: How
Your first day: Sign in
text: Click your account (1), when there is more than one. A password field opens under the picture; Back returns to the list of accounts. With one account the password field is already there. Type your password and press Return, or click the arrow at the end of the field. The eye button in the field shows what you typed. While Caps Lock is on, a line under the field says so. Or leave the computer for later: Sleep, Restart and Shut Down (2), at the bottom left, work without signing in. After three wrong passwords the login window shows the password hint of that account under the field, as "Hint: …", if one was set. It never shows the password. Tip From WolOS 0.13, each person's first sign-in also opens a short setup of their own, for privacy, looks and the keyboard. See Your first sign-in. Tip If you turned on Log in automatically in the installer, the computer goes straight to the desktop and you never see this window at start. It still locks when you step away; see Lock Screen and login window.

title: Your first day: The Setup Assistant (only on a computer without an account)
text: The assistant opens on a welcome screen, then shows one card at a time over the wallpaper, each with the WolOS door and its title at the top and where you are on the right (1 of 5 to 5 of 5). Continue (or Return) goes to the next card, Back (or Escape) to the one before. Welcome. You see "Welcome to WolOS" and "Let’s get you set up." on the left, and the White Rabbit at a golden door on the right. Click Continue. Finish Secure Boot Setup (some computers only). You see "This computer hasn’t accepted its WolOS key yet. At the next restart a blue screen asks once." The five steps (1), under the WolOS door, say what that screen asks, and the password it wants is shown large (2): boot. Read them, then Continue (3). You can also start this later from System Settings > Privacy & Security. Language & Region. You see "WolOS uses this language and keyboard. You can change them later." Click your language and country in the list (1), check the Keyboard menu (2), then Continue (3). Wi-Fi. You see "Choose a network to get online. You can skip this and join later." Click your network (1); a lock means it asks for a password, which you type in the field that opens. Not Now (2) skips this card, and a computer on a network cable skips it by itself. Continue (3) joins. While it joins you see "Joining “…”…". If the password is wrong you see "“…” didn’t accept that password. Check it and try again." Create Your Account. You see "You’ll use this name and password to sign in." Your picture shows a question mark until you type your name; pick its colour in the row of dots under it (1). Type your Full name; the Account name fills itself in from it. Type a Password of at least 8 characters twice, and if you like a Hint that is shown after three wrong passwords (2). The line under the fields reminds you: "This account is the administrator: it can install apps and change any setting." Continue (3) stays grey until every field that is needed is filled in. Appearance. You see "Choose a look. You can change it any time in System Settings." Each choice is a small picture of a window in that look. The top row (1) is Light, Dark or Auto (light by day, dark from the evening). The second row (2) is the colour family: Wonderland, Ocean or Slate. Click Continue (3). You're All Set. You see "Your account is ready." Click Get Started; the screen fades into your desktop.

title: Your first day: The first ten minutes
text: You see your desktop: the menu bar along the top, the Dock along the bottom, and nothing else asking for your attention. The desktop explains every part of it. These six things are worth doing now: Get online, if the computer is not online already. Click the Control Center icon near the right end of the menu bar, click Wi-Fi and pick your network. See Control Center. Look for updates. Open System Settings (the gear icon in the Dock, or Super+,) and click Software Update. If a new version is listed, click to install it; it is prepared next to the running system and takes effect at the next restart. See Updates. Choose your look. System Settings > Appearance: Light, Dark or Auto, and an accent colour. See Looks and themes. Get your apps. Open the Store (the shopping bag in the Dock) and click Get next to an app. See The Store. Check the clock and the name. A computer installed for you without a plan can start on UTC time and be called wolos, so the clock in the menu bar may be hours off. Choose your city in System Settings > General > Date & Time, and, if you like, a name of your own in General > Sharing (Computer name). Learn three keys. Super+Space opens Search, which finds apps, files and settings as you type. Super+Tab switches between open apps. Shift+Super+/ shows every keyboard shortcut on one sheet. Super is the key with the Windows logo. Tip If you ticked modules or media formats in the installer while the computer was offline, they install by themselves in the background as soon as it is online. You can keep working; System Settings > Modules shows their progress.

title: Your first day: A worked example
text: Dinah's new computer came from a shop with WolOS on it and no account. She switches it on and the Setup Assistant greets her. She picks English (United Kingdom), and the keyboard follows. She chooses her home network, types the Wi-Fi password, and sees the next card a moment later. She types "Dinah Liddell"; the account name becomes dinahliddell. She picks the orange colour for her picture, a password, and "the cat" as a hint. She chooses Auto and Ocean, clicks Get Started, and lands on her desktop. In System Settings > Software Update she finds the computer is up to date. In the Store she gets a web browser she knows and a music app. Ten minutes, and nothing to type but her name, a password and the Wi-Fi password.

title: Your first day: If something goes wrong
text: What you see What it means and what to do "Incorrect password" Check Caps Lock and the keyboard layout, then type again. After three tries the hint shows, if the account has one. "Your password can’t be checked right now. Try again, or restart." The password check did not answer. Wait a moment and try again; if it keeps saying this, click Restart. "Passwords don’t match." The two passwords on the account card differ. Type both again. "Use at least 8 characters." The password is too short. "Use lowercase letters and digits, starting with a letter." The account name has a capital, a space or another character. "The hint can’t be the password." Choose a hint that reminds you of the password without being it. "That account name can’t be used. Press Back and choose another one." The system uses that name for itself. Go back and change the account name. "Your account couldn’t be created just now. Press Continue to try again." Something stopped the account from being made. Press Continue again. "No networks found" Move closer to the Wi-Fi and click Look Again, or choose Not Now and join later from Control Center. "“…” didn’t answer. Try again, or choose Not Now and join later." The network did not respond in time. Try again, or skip and join later. The desktop shows, but there is no internet Click the Control Center icon and turn on Wi-Fi, or check the network cable. See Control Center. A blue screen at the next restart That is the one-time Secure Boot key screen. Follow the steps from the card, or Secure Boot. The password is boot.

title: Your first sign-in: What it is
text: From WolOS 0.13, setting up comes in two parts. The installer and the Setup Assistant keep what belongs to the whole computer: the disk, the first administrator account, the network and Secure Boot. What belongs to one person comes at that person's first sign-in. A short setup opens in your own session, before the desktop, with one card per question and the page count at the upper right (1 of 6 to 6 of 6): Privacy: Send error reports, whether WolOS sends a short report when something breaks, without your files, and Location Services, whether apps that ask may learn roughly where you are. Error reports belong to the whole computer: an administrator turns them on or off and types their password once; any other account sees the answer, On or Off. Your Look: Light, Dark or Auto, a row of accent colour dots, and the picture for your desktop: Day, Dusk or Night. Online Accounts: the accounts already on the computer for you, and Open Mail. Mail asks for your address and password; Calendar then uses the same account. Keyboard & Typing: the Keyboard menu (the keys follow it at once) and a Try it field. Under Other scripts, a way to type Chinese, Japanese or Korean: Open Modules adds the input methods, or the row says they are installed. Assistants: Allow assistants and scripts. When it is on, AI helpers and scripts may help you with WolOS, and they ask before every change. When it is off, nothing they send reaches the system. The manual's helper on this website asks before it downloads anything. You're All Set: Get Started opens the desktop. Every page has a good default, so Continue without touching anything is fine. Each page saves its own choice when you press Continue, so a choice made before Later stays.

title: Your first sign-in: Why WolOS does it this way
text: A computer is often shared. The person who installs it should not have to choose the wallpaper, the privacy answers and the keyboard for everyone else. So the computer's own questions come once, at the install, and each person answers their own questions the first time they sign in, in their own session. Someone who gets an account a year later sees the same setup as the first person.

title: Your first sign-in: How it works
text: Sign in for the first time with your account. The setup opens before the desktop. The menu bar and the Dock appear when it ends. Answer each page and press Continue, or press Back to change an earlier answer. Return is Continue and Escape is Back. Or press Later. The desktop appears, and the setup asks again at your next sign-in. After the third Later it stops asking. Then System Settings > General shows Finish Setting Up, which opens it again, and every choice it holds is also a row in System Settings (see the table below). Finish with Get Started on You're All Set. The setup never opens again for this account. Every account added later, by you or by an administrator, gets the same setup at its own first sign-in. An account that already signed in before WolOS 0.13 is not asked. The live system from the USB stick never shows it.

title: Your first sign-in: Where these choices are in System Settings
text: Choice Where Error reports System Settings > Privacy & Security (Privacy) Light, Dark or Auto, and the accent colour System Settings > Appearance (Looks and themes) The wallpaper, also Dynamic and your own photo System Settings > Wallpaper (Wallpapers) Keyboard layout System Settings > Keyboard (The keyboard) Assistants and scripts System Settings > Privacy & Security, then Assistants & Automation The setup keeps a note of its own in your home folder: ~/.local/state/wolos/setup-done once you finish, and ~/.local/state/wolos/setup-later with the number of times you pressed Later.

title: Your first sign-in: A worked example
text: Alice installs WolOS on the family computer and makes her own account. Later she adds an account for her brother Bill in System Settings > Users & Groups. When Bill signs in for the first time, his own setup opens. On Privacy he sees Send error reports with Off beside it: Alice decides that one. He presses Later because he is in a hurry, and his desktop appears. At his next sign-in the setup opens again. He picks Dark and the green dot on Your Look, keeps the other pages as they are and presses Get Started. Alice's choices are not touched, and Bill never sees hers.

title: Your first sign-in: If something goes wrong
text: What you see What to do The setup does not open at your first sign-in Your account signed in before WolOS 0.13, or the setup was finished once. Make the same choices in System Settings, as the table above shows. You pressed Later three times and want the setup back Open System Settings > General and click Finish Setting Up. Privacy asks for your password after you change error reports Error reports are a choice for the whole computer. Type your own password; an administrator's account can change them. Press Later to leave them as they are. The setup closed in the middle (a crash, a power cut) Sign in again: it opens again, with what you saved so far already chosen. Another person's look appears in your session Looks belong to each account. Choose yours in System Settings > Appearance; it changes only your account.

title: The desktop: What it is
text: The desktop is everything you see once you are signed in. It has two bars and the space between them: the menu bar along the top, with the menus of the app in front on the left and the status of the computer on the right; the Dock along the bottom, with your apps, your Downloads and the Trash; the wallpaper in between, where your windows open.

title: The desktop: Why WolOS does it this way
text: One bar for "what can this app do" and one for "which app do I want" is a layout millions of people already know, so there is nothing to learn before you can work. The bars stay thin and quiet: no ads, no news, no badges that want your attention. Everything else (settings, notifications, quick switches) is one click away and out of sight until you ask for it.

title: The desktop: How
The desktop: The menu bar
text: From left to right, the numbers match the picture above. The WolOS menu (the WolOS mark at the far left). It holds About This Computer, System Settings… and App Store…, then Sleep, Restart… and Shut Down…, then Lock Screen and Log Out…. Sleep acts at once. Restart, Shut Down and Log Out ask first: for Shut Down you see "Are you sure you want to shut down your computer now?" with a countdown of 60 seconds. Cancel or Escape keeps you working. Doing nothing goes ahead when the countdown ends, so a computer left alone still turns off. While you try WolOS from the USB stick, the menu has no Lock Screen: the trial account has no password, so nothing could unlock it. The app in front. Its name in bold, then its own menus (for example Window). With no window in front, this part is empty. A plain click on a menu opens it; Ctrl+F2 moves the keyboard into the menu bar, Escape gives it back. Status icons: the network (Wi-Fi or cable) and the sound volume. A battery appears on a laptop, and a moon while Focus is on. Click one for its details. Search (the magnifying glass, or Super+Space). See Find anything with Search below. Control Center (the four small squares): Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, Focus, brightness, sound, music and quick switches. See Control Center. The date and time. Click it to open Notification Center, the list of notifications you have not cleared yet. What the menu bar shows can be changed in System Settings > Desktop & Dock (the date, the battery percentage) and System Settings > Control Center (which icons it shows).

title: The desktop: The Dock
text: Your apps. The Dock starts with Files, Apps, the Browser, Mail, Music, Photos, Calendar, Notes, Terminal, the App Store and System Settings. Click an icon to open the app. A small dot under an icon means the app is running; clicking it then brings its window to the front instead of opening a second one. Apps opens Search as a list of every app on the computer. Downloads. Click it to see your latest downloads stacked; click one to open it, or Open in Files for the whole folder. The Trash. Files you delete wait here until you empty it. Click it to open the Trash in Files, where you can put a file back. The Dock grows icons under the pointer and can hide itself until the pointer reaches the bottom edge. Both are switches in System Settings > Desktop & Dock; see The Dock.

title: The desktop: Windows
text: Every window has three round buttons at the top right. From left to right they minimize it (hide it to the Dock; click the app's icon to get it back), maximize it (make it fill the screen, click again to return) and close it, which is the rightmost. Drag a window by its title bar to move it, and by any edge to resize it. Closing the last window of an app usually quits it, and its dot leaves the Dock: the dot shows open windows. An app that keeps working without a window shows no dot. Super+Q quits the app in front.

title: The desktop: Switch between apps
text: Hold Super and press Tab: the switcher shows every running app in a row. Keep holding Super and press Tab again to move along the row; let go to bring the highlighted app to the front.

title: The desktop: Four desktops
text: WolOS gives you four desktops (also called spaces), each with its own windows: one for work, one for chat, one for a game. Ctrl+Alt+Left and Ctrl+Alt+Right move between them, and Ctrl+Alt+1 to 4 jump straight to one. Ctrl+Up opens the Overview: every window of the current desktop side by side and the four desktops in a row above them. Click a window to go to it, or a desktop to switch.

title: The desktop: Find anything with Search
text: Press Super+Space (or click the magnifying glass) and start typing. Search opens at once: it stays ready in the background from the moment you sign in, so the first letters you type land in its field. Search finds apps, files and folders in your home folder, and System Settings pages, as you type. Words can come in any order: "time date" finds Date & Time. The arrow keys move through the results, and Return opens the highlighted one, which is the first result until you move. Each result says what it is on the right: Application, Folder, PDF Document, Image, Text and so on. Search also does things. Type "sleep", "restart", "shut down", "log out", "lock", "screenshot" or "record" and the action is the first result: Return does it. Restart, Shut Down and Log Out still ask first. Search also works as a calculator: type 12*7 and the answer is the first result. When nothing matches you see "No results for “…”" and an offer to search the web for the words in your browser.

title: The desktop: When an app stops answering
text: Press Alt+Super+Esc. Force Quit Applications lists the open apps: "If an app doesn’t respond for a while, choose it and click Force Quit." Choose the app and click Force Quit. Work you had not saved in that app is lost, so give it a minute first.

title: The desktop: Every shortcut on one sheet
text: Press Shift+Super+/ (Super+?) and a sheet lists every keyboard shortcut, grouped: Search, Overview, Apps, App commands, Screenshots, Accessibility and System, plus Tiling while tiling is on and Custom shortcuts once you made one. A group with no keys is left out. The symbols are the ones printed on some keyboards: ⌘ is Super, ⌥ is Alt, ⌃ is Ctrl and ⇧ is Shift. The keyboard explains how to change a shortcut.

title: The desktop: The keys worth knowing first
text: Keys What they do Super+Space Search Super+Tab Switch between apps Super+, Open System Settings Super+Q Quit the app in front Super+W Close the window or tab in front Super+C, Super+V, Super+X Copy, paste, cut in every app, the terminal included Super+Z, Shift+Super+Z Undo, redo Shift+Super+V The last things you copied (Clipboard history) Shift+Super+3, 4, 5 A screenshot of the screen, of an area, or the screenshot toolbar (Screenshots) Ctrl+Up Overview Ctrl+Alt+Left, Right The desktop to the left or right Ctrl+Super+Q Lock the screen Ctrl+Super+F Full screen on and off Alt+Super+Esc Force Quit Applications Shift+Super+/ Every shortcut on one sheet Super with a letter always goes to the app in front, the way Command does on a Mac, so the same keys copy and paste in a browser, a document and a terminal. Ctrl keeps the meaning each app gives it.

title: The desktop: A worked example
text: Alice is writing a letter and needs a number from a PDF. She presses Super+Space, types "inv", and Search shows "Invoice March.pdf"; Return opens it. She selects the number, presses Super+C, then Super+Tab to go back to the letter, and Super+V to paste. Later a video call starts in the browser, so she presses Ctrl+Alt+Right to move to her second desktop, where only the browser is open. When the call ends, Ctrl+Alt+Left brings her back to the letter exactly as she left it.

title: The desktop: If something goes wrong
text: What you see What to do The Dock is gone It may be set to hide: move the pointer to the bottom edge and wait. To keep it visible, turn off Automatically hide and show the Dock in System Settings > Desktop & Dock. The menu bar shows no app name No window is in front. Click a window, or an app in the Dock. An app does not respond Wait a minute, then Alt+Super+Esc > choose it > Force Quit. A shortcut does nothing It may have been changed. System Settings > Keyboard > Keyboard Shortcuts > Restore Defaults brings back the keys on this page. Search does not find a file Search looks in your home folder and skips hidden folders. It refreshes its list of files when you open it, so close Search and open it again for a file saved a moment ago. Everything is too small or too big System Settings > Displays > Scale sets the size of everything on the screen.

title: Control Center: What it is
text: Control Center is the panel that opens from the icon with four small squares near the right end of the menu bar. It holds the switches you reach for many times a day, so you do not have to open System Settings for them: the network, Bluetooth, Do Not Disturb, Dark Mode, the brightness of the screen, the volume, the music that is playing, and a grid of tiles.

title: Control Center: Why WolOS does it this way
text: Small changes should take one click, like the light switches by the door. Everything in Control Center is also in System Settings with all its options; Control Center has only the part you change often. It opens at once and closes with Escape or a click anywhere else.

title: Control Center: How
Control Center: Open and close it
text: Click the Control Center icon in the menu bar. Press Escape or click the icon again to close it.

title: Control Center: What each part does
text: The numbers match the picture above. From the top: the four round switches, the Sound slider, Now Playing, the Display slider, then the tiles. Wi-Fi shows the network you are on. Click the round icon to turn Wi-Fi on or off (no password is asked); click the name for the list of networks. Bluetooth shows whether it is on. Click the icon to turn it on or off; click the name for your paired Bluetooth devices. Focus keeps notification banners quiet; click it to choose for how long. See below. Dark Mode switches the whole desktop and your apps between light and dark. See Dark Mode. Display: drag the slider to make the screen brighter or darker. It is there only when WolOS can set the screen's brightness (most laptop screens); in a virtual machine, or on a screen WolOS cannot dim, there is no Display slider and no Night Shift tile. The arrow at the end of the Display slider opens the Display page: Night Shift, Screen Mirroring and the keyboard light. Sound: drag the slider for the volume. The number above it is the volume in percent; 100% is the speaker's normal full level. The arrow at the end of the Sound slider opens the Sound page, where you choose the speakers, headphones and microphone. Now Playing shows the song or video that is playing, in any app, with buttons for back, play or pause, and next. The tiles, one switch each: Night Shift, the battery (with its charge), Stay Awake, Screenshot, Record (the screen as a video) and Screen Mirroring. Click a tile to switch it; a tile that is on is filled with the accent colour. On a computer with a radio, Airplane Mode is the first tile: it switches Wi-Fi, Bluetooth and mobile data off at once, the menu bar shows a plane, and switching it off brings back the radios that were on (see Network settings).

title: Control Center: Join a Wi-Fi network
text: Click the name next to Wi-Fi (1). The Networks page lists the network you are on (with Connected) and those nearby; a lock means it needs a password. Click a network. If it has a lock, you see "Join “…”" with a Password field. Type the password and click Join. For a network that hides its name, click Other Network…, type its Network name and password, and click Join. WolOS then asks for that network by its name, which a hidden network needs. The page lists up to 8 networks. When more are in range, a last row says how many, for example "5 More Networks…", and opens System Settings > Wi-Fi with all of them. Some networks at work or at a university ask for a user name or a certificate instead of one password. WolOS shows them in the list, and clicking one shows the line "This network asks for a user name or a certificate (Enterprise Wi-Fi). WolOS can’t join those yet." No password field opens, because a password alone could never join it. Wi-Fi Settings… at the bottom opens System Settings > Wi-Fi, where you can leave a network or forget it.

title: Control Center: Choose where sound plays
text: Click the arrow at the end of the Sound slider (8). The page lists Output (speakers, headphones, a TV) and Input (microphones), each with its own slider and mute button. Click a device to use it; the tick moves. Wireless headphones show the way their sound is sent (the codec) under their name.

title: Control Center: Brightness, Night Shift and a second screen
text: Click the arrow at the end of the Display slider (6). The page has Brightness, Keyboard Brightness (on laptops with a lit keyboard), Night Shift and Screen Mirroring. Screen Mirroring shows the same picture on a second screen or projector; with only one screen connected it says "No other display".

title: Control Center: Quiet for a while: Focus
text: Click Focus (3). Choose Do Not Disturb and how long: For 1 hour or Until tomorrow morning. While it is on, banners stay away and wait in Notification Center; a moon appears in the menu bar. Click Off to end it early. See Notifications.

title: Control Center: Pair a Bluetooth device
text: Click the name next to Bluetooth (2) for Devices: the devices you paired before, with Connected next to the one in use. Click one to connect it. To pair a new one, put it in pairing mode (see its manual) and open System Settings > Bluetooth. See Sharing and devices.

title: Control Center: Choose what Control Center shows
text: System Settings > Control Center. Always Shown lists Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, Focus, Dark Mode, Display and Sound. Under it, Show When You Want Them has a switch for each other part: Now Playing, Battery, Keyboard Brightness, Accessibility Shortcuts and the rest. Plugins can add tiles of their own. A plugin tile that runs something does so only after you allowed it; see Plugins.

title: Control Center: The same switches on the keyboard
text: Keys What they do Ctrl+Super+N Night Shift on or off Ctrl+Super+D Do Not Disturb on or off Ctrl+Super+I Stay Awake on or off Shift+Super+5 The screenshot toolbar, the same as the Screenshot tile The volume and brightness keys The same as the sliders; a sign in the middle of the screen shows the new level

title: Control Center: A worked example
text: Alice arrives at a café. She clicks Control Center, clicks Wi-Fi, picks "Café Hatter", types the password from the menu card and clicks Join. She plugs in her headphones, clicks the arrow at the end of the Sound slider and ticks them. Then she clicks Focus > Do Not Disturb > For 1 hour, so nothing interrupts her while she writes. When she leaves, the hour has passed and banners show again on their own.

title: Control Center: If something goes wrong
text: What you see What to do "No networks found" Wi-Fi is off or no network is in range. Click the Wi-Fi icon to turn it on, move closer, or use Other Network… for a hidden name. "“…” didn’t accept that password." Check the password, including capitals, and type it again. "Wi-Fi passwords have 8 to 63 characters. Check it and try again." The password you typed is too short or too long to be a Wi-Fi password. Check it against the router's label. "Couldn’t join “…”. Move closer to it and try again." The network did not answer, or gave the computer no address. Move closer, or restart the router, and try again. "WolOS can’t join those yet." The network is Enterprise Wi-Fi (a user name or a certificate). Use a cable, or another network for now. "Bluetooth is unavailable" This computer has no Bluetooth, or it is switched off in the computer's own settings. A small USB Bluetooth adapter adds it. "No paired devices" Nothing was paired yet. Put the device in pairing mode and open System Settings > Bluetooth. "No other display" on Screen Mirroring Only one screen is connected. Connect the second one, then try again. A slider moves but nothing changes The device does not let the computer change it (some external screens set their own brightness). Use the buttons on the device. No sound from the headphones Open the Sound page (8) and tick them under Output. See Sound. A tile you want is missing Turn it on in System Settings > Control Center.

title: System Settings: What it is
text: System Settings is the window where you change how WolOS looks, sounds and behaves: the Wi-Fi, the sound, the wallpaper, the Dock, your password, the updates and everything else. On the left is a sidebar of panes, one per subject, in groups. On the right is the pane you picked, made of rows: a switch, a slider, a menu, or an arrow that opens more.

title: System Settings: Why WolOS does it this way
text: A setting is only useful if you can find it, trust it and take it back. So System Settings has one search field that finds every row in every pane; every switch you see either does what it says or is not shown at all; a change that could not be saved puts the control back to what is really set and says so under it; and every change is written down, so System Settings > Restore can take it back later.

title: System Settings: How
System Settings: Open System Settings
text: Press Super+, (Super and comma), click the gear icon in the Dock, or choose System Settings… in the WolOS menu at the top left. The search field (1) at the top of the sidebar finds any setting; see below. The sidebar (2) lists the panes in groups: the network, then notifications and sound, then the desktop, then security and your account, then devices, then the rest. Click a pane to open it. Rows with an arrow (3) open a page of their own. General is made of such rows: About, Software Update, Storage, Login Items, Language & Region, Date & Time and Sharing. The back arrow at the top returns to General.

title: System Settings: Find any setting by typing
text: Click the search field and type a word, for example "volume", "dark" or "menu bar". As you type, the sidebar keeps only the panes that have a match (2), and the right side lists every matching row (3). Click a row, or press Return for the first one, to go straight to it. The round × at the end of the field clears it, and the full sidebar comes back. When nothing matches you see "No Results" and "No settings match. Try another word." A shorter word usually helps.

title: System Settings: Every pane
text: Pane What you change there More Wi-Fi Turn Wi-Fi on and off, see every network in range (Look Again looks once more), join one, join a hidden one with Other Network…, leave the network you are on with Disconnect, and forget a saved one. Control Center Bluetooth Turn Bluetooth on and off, pair headphones, mice, keyboards and phones (Add Device…), connect them, and forget the ones you no longer use. Control Center Network Airplane Mode; every connection with its state, address, router and DNS servers: the cable, Wi-Fi, and a VPN while it is connected, each under its own name, with IP settings for an address of its own. A connection that reaches no internet, or waits for a sign-in page, says so. Below them, the firewall that stops other computers connecting to programs on yours unless you started the connection (on by default), the VPN list with Add VPN, Proxy and DNS over TLS. Network settings Notifications Which apps may show banners, Focus and Do Not Disturb. Notifications Sound Speakers and headphones, the microphone, volume and balance, voice effects. Sound General About This Computer, Software Update, Storage, Login Items, Language & Region, Date & Time, Sharing, and the shell of new terminal windows. Updates, Sharing Appearance Light, Dark or Auto, the accent colour, themes, the wallpaper. Looks and themes, Dark Mode Accessibility Reduce motion and transparency, more contrast, zoom, a bigger pointer. Control Center Which switches and tiles Control Center and the menu bar show. Control Center Desktop & Dock The Dock's size, magnification and hiding, the date and battery in the menu bar, tiling windows. The Dock Displays Resolution, size of everything on screen, refresh rate, several screens, Night Shift. Night Shift Wallpaper The picture on the desktop. Wallpapers Effects & Looks Blur, transparency, rounded corners, shadows and animations. Looks and themes Widgets Cards on the desktop: clock, weather, calendar, music. Arranging widgets Battery or Energy Power modes, sleep, the lid, Memory Saver. Battery and sleep Lock Screen When the screen locks by itself. Lock Screen Privacy & Security What apps may use, the malware check, how the computer starts. Privacy Users & Groups Accounts on this computer, passwords, who is an administrator. Keyboard Key repeat, keyboard layouts, keyboard shortcuts. The keyboard Trackpad & Mouse Pointer speed, scrolling direction, tap to click. Printers Add a printer, choose the default. Scanners come with the Scanners module, which adds Document Scanner. Modules Hardware The devices in the computer and whether each works. Assistants & Automation What scripts and AI assistants may change, and what they did. Scripts that change settings Modules Add or remove sets of apps for development, creative work, games and more. Modules Restore Undo a recent change, or go back to an earlier state. Backups and undo

title: System Settings: How a change takes effect
text: Most changes take effect the moment you make them: there is no Save or Apply button. A few ask first, and say why: A change that affects everyone on the computer (a new account, a module, a printer) shows a sheet and asks for an administrator's password. A new screen resolution is saved only once the screen has really switched to it. If a change could not be saved, the switch, slider or menu goes back to what is really set, and a line under the section says what happened, for example "The shell couldn’t be changed. Try again in a moment."

title: System Settings: Take a change back
text: System Settings > Restore > Recent Changes lists what you changed, newest first, each with Undo. Undo puts that setting back as it was before. See Backups and undo.

title: System Settings: A worked example
text: Alice finds the volume of her laptop too low. She presses Super+, and types "louder" in the search field: the Sound pane stays in the sidebar, with the row Allow louder. She clicks it, turns the switch on, and the volume slider can now go past 100%. The next day she decides it was too much, opens System Settings > Restore > Recent Changes, and clicks Undo next to the change: the switch is off again.

title: System Settings: If something goes wrong
text: What you see What to do A switch flips back after you click it The change could not be saved, so the switch shows what is set. The line under the section says why. Try again. "No settings match. Try another word." Search found no pane or row. Try a shorter or more common word, like "sound" instead of "speakers". Displays says "Displays couldn’t be read" Click Try Again. If it keeps happening, restart the computer. Open System Settings from your desktop, not from a remote session. "That name is reserved by the system" when adding a user The system uses that account name itself. Pick another. Network says "Connected, but the internet can’t be reached through it." The cable or Wi-Fi works, but the internet behind it does not answer. Restart the router, or try another network. A notification says Sign In to This Network The network (a café, a hotel, a train) shows a sign-in page first. Open the notification to sign in; until then Network says "Connected. Sign in on the network’s page to use the internet." A setting you need is not where this page says Type its name in the search field: it finds rows wherever they are. You changed something and regret it System Settings > Restore > Recent Changes > Undo.

title: The Store: What it is
text: The App Store is where you get apps for WolOS. It shows apps picked for you in five shelves (Discover, Create, Work, Play and Develop), a search field that finds any app by name or by what it does, Kits that add a whole set of things in one step, Plugins that add to the desktop itself, and Updates. Its icon in the Dock is the shopping bag.

title: The Store: Why WolOS does it this way
text: The same app often exists in several places, packed in different ways, each with its own idea of an update. You should not have to know that. So the Store shows one entry per app, and its page says where it comes from and which version you get. Every app on the shelves was picked by people, and every install can be taken back: update it, keep a version that works for you, or roll back to the one before.

title: The Store: How
The Store: Find an app
text: Open the App Store from the Dock, or choose App Store… in the WolOS menu. Browse (2): Discover has the essentials and a featured app at the top; Create has drawing, photo, video and music apps; Work has office, mail and notes; Play has games; Develop has the tools for programming. Or search (1): click the search field at the top of the sidebar and type a name ("Firefox") or what you want to do ("photo").

title: The Store: Get an app
text: Click Get next to an app (3 or 4 on Discover, 2 in search results), or click the app to see its page first. Type your password if it asks. Most apps are installed for every account on the computer, which needs an administrator's password. The password counts for five minutes, so a second app right after does not ask again. Watch the ring. A ring next to the app fills as it downloads and installs; the button reads Installing…. When it is done the button reads Open, and the app is in Search and in Apps in the Dock.

title: The Store: An app's page
text: Click an app's name or icon to open its page. Get (1), Open once it is installed, or Update when a newer version is ready. Information (2) says how big the app is, who made it and where it comes from: System packages (WolOS's own collection, checked against its signature) or another collection that the page names. An app installed for every account also shows Installed for: All accounts; an app installed only for you has no such line. What It Can Do lists what the app may use, such as the camera or your files, when it says. The back arrow (3) returns to the shelf you came from. When the app is installed, its page also offers: Button What it does Update Installs the newer version. Keep This Version Stops updates for this app; the page says "It stays at this version." Click it again ("It updates again.") to let it update. Use it when a new version broke something you need. Roll Back Goes back to the version before the last update; the page says "Rolled back." Versions Lists the versions you can choose from. Remove Takes the app off the computer. Your own files made with it stay in your home folder.

title: The Store: Keep your apps up to date
text: Click Updates in the sidebar (1) and then Check (2): "See what is new for your apps." The Store lists every app with a newer version under Packages, and the button becomes Update All, which installs all of them at once. To update one app only, open its page and click Update there. Updates of WolOS itself are in System Settings > Software Update; see Updates.

title: The Store: Kits: a set in one click
text: A Kit adds several things you need for one job at once. Click Kits in the sidebar (1). Media Codecs plays and makes MP3, AAC, H.264, HEVC and AC3 files and adds common fonts; click Get (2), and the list (3) says what each part is for. "Nothing here is installed until you choose it." Once added, the button reads Added. See Music and video formats. Bigger sets of tools, for programming, creative work, games and AI, are modules in System Settings > Modules; see Modules.

title: The Store: Plugins
text: Plugins in the sidebar lists plugins: small additions to the desktop itself, such as a weather item in the menu bar, a timer in Control Center or a clock widget. Each says what it does and what it asks for, with Get, Turn On, Update or Remove. Every plugin on this page was checked and signed. See Plugins.

title: The Store: Apps from a file
text: A friend may send you an app as a single file. Double-click it: the Store opens its install sheet and says whether WolOS can check it: You see What it means "Verified" "Signed by a developer WolOS trusts, and unchanged since." Install it if you want it. "Not signed" "WolOS can’t check who made this app. Install it only if you trust where it came from." "Can’t be installed" "This file is damaged, was changed after it was signed, or comes from a developer WolOS doesn’t know." Delete the file.

title: The Store: Community packages
text: The Community tab at the bottom of the sidebar holds community packages: recipes anyone can publish. Nobody at WolOS reviews them, so they are kept apart: they never appear in Discover or in search, and the tab opens only after your password ("Community packages are not reviewed by WolOS. Enter your password to open them."). Each package shows what WolOS's check found before you decide. Most people never need this tab.

title: The Store: A worked example
text: Alice wants to edit her holiday photos. She opens the App Store, types "photo" in the search field and sees GIMP and darktable. She clicks GIMP to read its page: 155 MB, from System packages. She clicks Get, types her password, and watches the ring fill; the button changes to Open. A month later an update makes a filter she uses look different, so she opens GIMP's page and clicks Roll Back, then Keep This Version so it stays that way until she is ready.

title: The Store: If something goes wrong
text: What you see What to do "That did not finish. Nothing was changed." The install or update stopped part-way and was undone. Check that you are online (Control Center > Wi-Fi) and click Get again. The password sheet keeps asking Your account is not an administrator. Ask the person who looks after the computer, or get the app for your account only if its page offers that. An app you know is not found Try another word, or what it does instead of its name. Community packages never appear in search; they are on the Community tab. Get stays grey The app is being installed or updated already, or the Store is still loading ("Loading…"). Wait a moment. An app needs a restart to finish The page says so. Restart when it suits you; the app is kept. A Kit you expected is not there It does not apply to this computer. Modules are in System Settings > Modules. A plugin says it needs a newer WolOS Update WolOS in System Settings > Software Update, then try again.

title: Files and folders: What it is
text: Files is the app that shows what is on your computer: your documents, pictures, music, downloads and USB sticks. It is the first icon in the Dock. A file is one document, picture or song; a folder holds files and other folders, the way a drawer holds papers. Everything you keep lives in your home folder. It starts with these folders: Folder What goes in it Desktop Files you want close at hand. Screenshots are saved here. Documents Letters, spreadsheets, notes, anything you write. Downloads What your browser and other apps download. The Downloads icon in the Dock shows the newest. Music, Pictures, Videos Your songs, photos and films. Public Files you mean to share with other people on your network. Templates Documents you use as a starting point. Projects Folders for your own projects. Work Made when you add the Developer module: the place for your programming projects. Removing the module leaves it and its files.

title: Files and folders: Why WolOS does it this way
text: Your files belong to you, not to the system. That is why they live in one place that nothing else touches: updates replace the system and never your home folder, and going back to an earlier version of WolOS leaves your files exactly as they are. Deleting goes to the Trash first, because the most common way to lose a file is a click too many.

title: Files and folders: How
Files and folders: Find your way
text: Click Files in the Dock. The window opens on your home folder. The sidebar (1) has the places you go most: Home; Recent, the files you opened lately; Starred, files you marked with a star; Network, other computers and shared folders near you; and Trash. A USB stick or a second disk appears here too while it is plugged in. The path bar (2) shows where you are. Inside Documents it reads Home / Documents; click Home in it to go back up. Double-click a folder (3) to open it. The arrows at the top left go back and forward, like in a browser. The magnifying glass at the top left searches the folder you are in and the folders inside it. To find a file anywhere in your home folder, Search from the menu bar (Super+Space) is faster. The list button at the top right switches between big icons and a list with sizes and dates; the small arrow next to it sorts by name, size, type or date.

title: Files and folders: Open a file
text: Double-click it. Files opens it in the app made for that kind of file: a text file in Text Editor, a photo in Photos, a song in Music. To choose another app, right-click the file and pick Open With….

title: Files and folders: Copy, move, rename and delete
text: Right-click a file to see what you can do with it. To Do this Copy a file to another folder Right-click > Copy, open the other folder, then right-click an empty spot > Paste (or Super+C and Super+V). Copy to… does the same through a list of folders. Move it Cut and Paste (Super+X, Super+V), Move to…, or drag it onto a folder in the window or in the sidebar. Rename it Rename… (1) or F2. Type the new name and press Return. Keep the part after the last dot, the extension: it tells WolOS what kind of file it is. Make a new folder Right-click an empty spot in the window > New Folder…, type its name, press Return. Delete it Move to Trash (2) or the Delete key. The file waits in the Trash. Pack several files into one Select them, right-click > Compress…. You get one file that is easy to send. Send it by email Email… opens a new message with the file attached. See its size and dates Properties (Alt+Return). To select several files, hold Ctrl and click each one, or drag a box around them.

title: Files and folders: Get a file back from the Trash
text: Click Trash in the sidebar (or the Trash in the Dock). Right-click the file > Restore From Trash: it goes back to the folder it came from. Empty Trash at the top deletes everything in it for good. Careful Emptying the Trash cannot be undone.

title: Files and folders: Check a file for malware
text: Right-click a file you downloaded or were sent > Check for Malware (3). WolOS compares it, on this computer, with millions of signatures of known malware, and tells you what it found: You see What it means "Nothing Found" The check compared the file with the signatures and found no match. "Malware Found" The file matches known malware, and the message names it. Move it to the Trash and do not open it. "Check Not Finished" Nothing was found, but part of the file could not be checked. Treat it with care. "Signatures Are Off" The full check needs its signature set. Turn it on in System Settings > Privacy & Security; it downloads to this computer. Nothing was checked. Separately from this button, WolOS checks every program the first time it runs. If you open a new program and see "Not Checked Yet", wait a moment and open it again. See Privacy and permissions.

title: Files and folders: Hidden files
text: Names that start with a dot, such as .config, are hidden files: the settings of your apps. Files does not show them, so you cannot delete one by mistake. Press Ctrl+H to show them, and again to hide them.

title: Files and folders: USB sticks and other disks
text: Plug the stick in and it appears in the sidebar. Click it to see what is on it, and copy files to and from it like any folder. Before you pull it out, click the eject arrow next to its name and wait until it disappears from the sidebar; that makes sure everything has been written.

title: Files and folders: A worked example
text: Alice downloaded a recipe as pancakes.pdf and wants it with her other recipes. She clicks Downloads in the Dock, then Open in Files. She right-clicks pancakes.pdf > Move to…, chooses Documents > Recipes and clicks Select. In Recipes she right-clicks the file > Rename…, types Pancakes for Sunday.pdf and presses Return. Later she deletes an old recipe by mistake, opens the Trash, right-clicks it and chooses Restore From Trash: it is back in Recipes.

title: Files and folders: If something goes wrong
text: What you see What to do A file opens in the wrong app Right-click it > Open With…, choose the app, and turn on the option to always use it for this kind of file. "Your Disk Is Almost Full" Only a little space is left on the disk. Empty the Trash, then delete or move big files you do not need (the list view sorted by size helps). A file you deleted is not in the Trash The Trash was emptied, or the file was on a network folder, which has no Trash. A copy you made yourself is then the only way back; see Backups and undo. The USB stick does not appear Try another port. If it still does not appear, the stick may be broken or formatted for another kind of computer. "Not Checked Yet" when you open a program WolOS checks a program the first time it runs and opens it once the check is done. Try again in a moment. You cannot rename or delete a file It belongs to the system or to another account. Files you can change are in your home folder.

title: Updates: What it is
text: An update brings fixes, security repairs and new features. WolOS has two kinds: WolOS updates, for the system itself, in System Settings > General > Software Update; app updates, for the apps you got from the Store, in the Store's Updates page, and installed for you once a day if you allow it. WolOS keeps two copies of the system on the disk (two slots). An update is put into the copy you are not using, while you keep working. The next start uses the new copy, and the old one stays as the way back.
