One kind of computer is different: if you chose your own partitions in the installer and it said "This layout keeps one copy of WolOS, so updates can’t be undone.", there is only one copy. An update then changes the running system, no restore point is saved, and Software Update says so under the update: "This computer has one copy of WolOS, so there is no restore point; the update changes the running system."

title: Updates: Why WolOS does it this way
text: An update should never ruin your day. Because the new system is built next to the running one, a power cut or an error during the update leaves you exactly where you were. If the new system fails to start three times in a row, the computer starts the old copy by itself: there is no menu to find and nothing to type. Your files live outside both copies and never move. And before every update on a computer with two copies WolOS saves a restore point, so you can also go back on purpose.

title: Updates: How
Updates: Look for WolOS updates
text: Open System Settings > General > Software Update. (Software Update is a row on the General page.) Read the card at the top (1). It says whether WolOS is up to date or how many updates are ready, whether one of them fixes a security problem, and when WolOS last checked ("Last checked 3 h ago."). Under it, a line lists what the update contains. Click Check Now (2) to look right away. You see "Checking for updates…", then "WolOS is up to date" or the updates that are ready. Click Update Now (3) to install them. You see "Installing updates…" and "You can keep working while this runs." When it is done you see "Updates installed", and "Restart to finish updating." if the update changes the system itself. Restart when it suits you. Until then you keep using the current system, and nothing is lost.

title: Updates: Automatic updates
text: The switches under the buttons decide what happens without you. Switch Default What it does Automatic updates (4): "Keep WolOS and your apps current." On The main switch. It is on while either option below is on; turning it off turns both off. Download new updates (5): "In the background. You choose when to install." On WolOS looks for updates by itself, at most once every 20 hours, and downloads them. It never installs a WolOS update without you clicking Update Now. Install app updates (5): "Flathub apps, once a day." Off Updates the apps you got from the Store's app collection once a day, in the background, for your account. If a switch flips back after you click it, the change was not made (for example because the password sheet was cancelled); a line under the switches says why.

title: Updates: Update your apps
text: Open the App Store and click Updates in the sidebar, then Check. Every app with a newer version is listed, and Update All installs them all. To update one app only, click Update on its own page; there you can also Keep This Version (stop its updates) or Roll Back to the version before. See The Store.

title: Updates: What happens during a WolOS update
text: WolOS checks that the disk has room for a new copy. If it has not, nothing starts, and a line says how much space to free, for example "Update Now was not started: the system disk needs about 3 GB more free space for the update. Free some space in Settings > Storage, then try again. Nothing was changed." It builds the new system in a separate work copy, from the running one plus the update. You keep working. The system you use and your last restore point are not touched while it builds. Only when the new copy is complete and has passed its check does it take the place of the oldest copy. The system you are using now becomes the restore point "Before the last update". If anything fails on the way, WolOS throws the work copy away and tells you. The system you use and your restore points are exactly as they were. At the next start, the computer starts the new copy. If the new copy does not start properly three times in a row, the computer starts the old copy instead, by itself. One update runs at a time. If you click Update Now while another update is still being built (for example one started from the terminal), a line says "Another update is running. Wait for it to finish, then try again. Nothing was changed." Apps you install after an update was prepared but before you restart are kept in the new system.

title: Updates: When an update is cut off
text: If the power goes, or the computer is switched off, while an update is being built, nothing of that update is used. The next start is the system you had, with your restore point still there. Open Software Update and click Update Now again: the update starts from the beginning and finishes.

title: Updates: Go back to the system from before an update
text: System Settings > Restore lists the restore points under Restore Points: "Before the last update", the system as it was before the newest update, and the Current system marked "Running now". Click Start From This next to one; you see "Restart to use this restore point.", and the next start uses it. Your files are not touched, and the apps and programs you installed since that restore point are still installed after you go back. See Backups and undo.

title: Updates: Who has to say yes
text: Installing WolOS updates and going back to a restore point change the system for everyone, so they show a sheet and ask for an administrator's password. Nothing happens until you confirm.

title: Updates: A worked example
text: On Monday Alice sees a notification: updates are ready, one of them fixes a security problem. She opens System Settings > General > Software Update, clicks Update Now, and keeps writing while it installs. At lunch she restarts; the computer starts the new system and everything is where she left it. On Tuesday the printer stops working. She opens System Settings > Restore, clicks Start From This next to "Before the last update" and restarts: the system from Monday morning starts, with her files and the letter she wrote on Monday afternoon still there. When a fixed update arrives a few days later, she installs it.

title: Updates: If something goes wrong
text: What you see What to do "WolOS is up to date" but a friend already has the new version Click Check Now: WolOS looks by itself at most every 20 hours. The update stops with an error The work copy was thrown away and your system is unchanged. Check that you are online and click Update Now again. "Update Now was not started: the system disk needs about … GB more free space" The new copy would not fit. Empty the Trash, remove apps or files you no longer need (System Settings > General > Storage shows what takes room), then click Update Now again. "Another update is running." An update is already being built. Wait for it to finish; Software Update shows the result. The power went during an update Nothing of that update is used and your system is as it was. Click Update Now again. After a restart the computer shows the old version The new system did not start three times, so the old one started by itself. Nothing is lost. Try the update again later; if it keeps happening, report it. A switch under Automatic updates flips back The change was not made. Try again in a moment; if a password sheet appears, confirm it. Software Update cannot check while offline It keeps the last list it had. Connect to the internet and click Check Now. An app broke after its update Open its page in the Store and click Roll Back, then Keep This Version. The computer does not start at all See Recovery.

title: Backups and undo: What it is
text: Three ways back, for three kinds of mistakes: What went wrong The way back Where You changed a setting and regret it Undo the change System Settings > Restore > Recent Changes An update made something worse Start the system from before the update System Settings > Restore > Restore Points A file is lost, damaged or deleted A copy you made of your files A USB disk, another computer or a cloud folder WolOS keeps the first two for you without being asked. The third, copies of your own files, is yours to make: this page shows how, with nothing more than Files and a USB disk.

title: Backups and undo: Why WolOS does it this way
text: Most trouble with a computer comes from a change: a setting, an update, a deleted file. So WolOS writes down every change you make in System Settings and every change a script or assistant makes, each with Undo, and saves a restore point of the whole system before every update. Your files are kept apart from the system, so going back to an earlier system never takes your files with it. That also means a restore point cannot bring back a file you deleted: for that you need a copy somewhere else, ideally on a disk you keep away from the computer.

title: Backups and undo: How
Backups and undo: Undo a change to a setting
text: Open System Settings > Restore. Find the change under Recent Changes (1). Each line names what changed (Appearance, Wallpaper, Desktop & Dock, Desktop, windows and effects, Keyboard shortcuts, Displays, Sound…), who changed it (System Settings, Control Center, Terminal, or a script or an assistant by its name, as Script “backup”) and when ("Just now", "5 min ago", "Yesterday"). Click Undo (2) next to it. The setting goes back to what it was before that change. With nothing to undo you see "No changes to undo" and "Changes to settings show here, so you can take any of them back." Tip Changes made by a helper (a script or an AI assistant) are listed with its name, so you can see what it did and take back one change without touching the others.

title: Backups and undo: Go back to the system from before an update
text: Open System Settings > Restore and look under Restore Points (3). There is "Before the last update", the system as it was before the newest update, with its date and size, and the Current system, "Running now". Click Start From This (4) next to the one you want. You see "Restart to use this restore point." and the line changes to "Starts next time". Restart. The computer starts the system as it was then. Your files stay as they are, and so do the apps and programs you installed since: going back changes the system, not what you added to it. "A restore point is made before every update. Starting from one keeps your files and brings back the system as it was." The oldest restore points are removed first when the disk runs low; System Settings > General > Storage shows how many there are and how much room they take. If the computer does not start far enough to open System Settings, Recovery shows how to pick an earlier system while the computer starts.

title: Backups and undo: Keep copies of your files
text: You need a USB disk or stick with more room than the files you want to keep. An external disk you use only for copies is best. Plug the disk in. It appears in the sidebar of Files. Open your home folder in Files and select the folders you want to keep: usually Documents, Pictures, Music, Videos and Desktop (hold Ctrl and click each). Copy them: right-click > Copy to…, choose the disk, and click Select. Files shows the progress at the top of the window. Eject the disk with the arrow next to its name in the sidebar, wait until it disappears, then unplug it. Do it again regularly, for example every Friday. Name a folder on the disk by date (Copy 2026-11-03) each time, so an old copy is still there if a file was already damaged when you copied it. Careful A copy that stays plugged into the computer can be lost together with it (a spilled drink, a theft). Keep the disk somewhere else, and keep a second copy in a second place for files you cannot replace, such as photos. Tip If you like the terminal, a short script can make the copy for you every time in the same way; Scripts that change settings shows one that packs a folder into a single file.

title: Backups and undo: Get files back from a copy
text: Plug the disk in, open it in Files, find the file or folder, and copy it back into your home folder. If a file with the same name is there, Files asks whether to replace it or keep both.

title: Backups and undo: A worked example
text: Alice changes her wallpaper and the accent colour, then decides she liked the old look better. In System Settings > Restore she clicks Undo next to "Appearance" and next to "Wallpaper": both are back. A week later she spills tea on her laptop. Her photos survive, because every Friday she copies Pictures and Documents to a USB disk she keeps in a drawer. On her new laptop she installs WolOS, plugs in the disk and copies the folders back.

title: Backups and undo: If something goes wrong
text: What you see What to do "No changes to undo" No setting was changed since the list was last cleared, or the change was not made in System Settings (an app's own settings are kept by the app). Undo does nothing visible Some changes show only in a new window or after the app restarts. Open the pane again to check the setting. No restore points under Restore Points Restore points are made before updates; a new WolOS has none until its first update ("None yet" in General > Storage). The copy to the USB disk stops because the disk is full Use a bigger disk, or copy fewer folders at a time. A file is missing from the copy It was saved after the copy was made, or it was in a folder you did not select. Make copies more often.

title: Privacy and permissions: What it is
text: A permission is one thing an app may do on your computer: show you notifications, use your home folder, keep the computer awake, change the volume. WolOS asks you before an app, a plugin or a helper gets one, remembers your answer, and shows every answer in one place, System Settings > Privacy & Security, where you can take it back. This page covers that pane, the questions WolOS puts on your screen (the sheets), and the check for malware. The firewall switch is in System Settings > Network.

title: Privacy and permissions: Why WolOS does it this way
text: A permission you never see is not consent. So WolOS puts the question on your screen, names who is asking and what for, waits for you, and lets you change your mind later. Where WolOS can only record your wish and not enforce it (some older apps do not ask), the pane says so instead of showing a switch that promises more than it does. And WolOS sends nothing about you anywhere: the malware check runs on this computer, and error reports are off unless you turn them on.

title: Privacy and permissions: How
Privacy and permissions: See and change what apps may do
text: Open System Settings > Privacy & Security (Super+, then Privacy & Security in the sidebar). Read the groups. Each kind of permission has a group with one row per app that has it (1): Notifications ("Can show you notifications."), Remote Control ("Can type and click as if it were you."), Keep Awake ("Can keep this computer from sleeping while it works.") and so on. Turn a switch off (2) to take that permission away. Apps that asked for more have a group of their own (3), with one switch for each thing they asked for: your home folder, the network, the graphics card. Reset (4) gives the app back exactly what it asked for when it was installed. An app that was refused is listed too. When an app asks for something it has no permission for, WolOS refuses and tells it to send you here. From then on the app has a row under that permission with its switch off, so you can turn it on if you want to. Further down the pane: Part What it is Default Screen Recording Not a switch per app: an app asks each time it wants to share your screen, and you choose which screen or window. Only WolOS's own screenshot and recording tools take a picture without asking. Ask every time Disk encryption Whether your disk is encrypted, as chosen in the installer. As installed Malware Check Checks programs and files the first time they open; see below. On Send error reports "When a program or service fails, WolOS sends its name and the system version. No files or names." Turning it on or off asks for an administrator's password. Off Full Signature Database A larger check against millions of known malware signatures, downloaded to this computer. It uses about 1 GB of memory while it runs. Off Startup Security How this computer starts, and the Secure Boot step if one is waiting. See Startup Security.

title: Privacy and permissions: When WolOS asks you
text: When an app or a helper wants to change something for you, a sheet appears and names it. Nothing happens until you answer. Read the question (1): who asks, and exactly what they want to do. Deny (2) refuses. It is the button the keyboard starts on, so a stray Return never says yes. Always Allow (3) says yes now and from now on, for this helper and this kind of change only. You can take it back in System Settings > Assistants & Automation. Allow Once (4) says yes this time only. A sheet nobody answers closes by itself after a short while and refuses, so nothing changes while you are away. For changes that affect everyone on the computer, the sheet asks for an administrator's password instead, every time: When You are asked for An app is installed, removed or updated for everyone Your administrator password; the sheet names what will change. An account is added or changed, remote login or the firewall is changed, a restore point is chosen The administrator password, every time, even right after you typed it. A helper wants to change a setting Deny, Always Allow or Allow Once. A helper wants to add or remove a web app, add a module, save or restore your open windows, run a Doctor fix, or set a reminder It asks every time; a reminder shows its full text before you allow it.

title: Privacy and permissions: When an app is installed
text: An app from the Store's app collection says what it wants before it is installed, and you choose: Allow installs it with those permissions; Don't Allow installs nothing. Either way you can change each permission later in Privacy & Security.

title: Privacy and permissions: The malware check
text: The first time a program or a downloaded file opens, WolOS checks it on this computer against known malware. Nothing leaves the computer, and nothing appears when nothing is wrong. If the check finds something, you get one notification and a row in Privacy & Security with Move to Trash and Open Anyway…. Move to Trash moves the file to the Trash, where it cannot run. Open Anyway… opens it after one more question. Use it only for a file you trust completely. For a file you were sent, right-click it in Files > Check for Malware for the full check; see Files and folders. Careful No check finds every new piece of malware. Get apps from the Store, and be wary of programs from websites you do not know.

title: Privacy and permissions: Plugins and helpers
text: A plugin says on its Store page what it asks for ("Asks to: read data from the web"). A tile or a Dock item from a plugin that runs something does so only after you allowed it. A helper (a script or an AI assistant) can read without asking, but every change it wants goes through the sheet above. System Settings > Assistants & Automation lists each helper, what you always allow it, and what it did.

title: Privacy and permissions: Clipboard and history
text: Clipboard history keeps the last things you copied so you can paste them again; it never keeps one-time codes, and Clear empties it. System Settings > Restore lists the changes made to your settings and who made them.

title: Privacy and permissions: A worked example
text: Alice installs a recording app. Before it installs she sees what it wants: the microphone, her home folder and the network. She clicks Allow. Later she wonders why it needs the network, opens System Settings > Privacy & Security, finds the app's group and turns Use the network off. When an AI assistant she uses wants to switch her desktop to dark, a sheet asks first; she clicks Allow Once, because she wants to decide each time.

title: Privacy and permissions: If something goes wrong
text: What you see What to do An app stopped working after you turned a permission off Turn the switch back on, or click Reset in its group to give back what it asked for when it was installed. A helper keeps asking That is on purpose: every change asks. Choose Always Allow for that kind of change, or take it back later in System Settings > Assistants & Automation. A sheet appeared that you did not expect Click Deny. Then look in System Settings > Assistants & Automation for the helper that asked. "No WolOS session is showing" A helper asked for a change while nobody was signed in at the screen. Sign in and let it ask again. The malware check stopped a file you trust In Privacy & Security, click Open Anyway… next to it. A permission says it is not enforced WolOS records it, but that app does not ask before it acts. Remove the app if that matters to you.

title: This website and your privacy: What it is
text: This page is about the website you are reading, wolos.org, not about the operating system: what happens to your visit, what your browser keeps, and who can see it. For what apps may do on a WolOS computer, read Privacy and permissions. For the app and plugin store at hub.wolos.org, its Privacy Policy is on that site.

title: This website and your privacy: Why WolOS does it this way
text: A site about an operating system that asks you to trust it with your computer should be plain about what it does with a visit. So the site has no accounts, no cookies, no advertising, no analytics and no scripts from other companies, and there is nothing to accept before you read.

title: This website and your privacy: How
This website and your privacy: What leaves your device
text: Asking for a page. Like every website, wolos.org gets your network address, your browser's name and the page you asked for. The pages are served by Cloudflare, which keeps its own logs to run and protect the service. WolOS builds nothing from them. Network error reports. Cloudflare asks your browser to report failed connections to wolos.org to Cloudflare, for up to seven days at a time. You can switch this off in a browser that offers the setting. Downloads. The images and the packages come from cdn.wolos.org. That server writes down which file was asked for and how big it was, not who asked. The company that hosts it and Cloudflare in front of it see your network address, as with any download. Error reports from a WolOS computer are sent only if you turned them on in System Settings > Privacy & Security. They hold the kind of failure, the WolOS version, the kernel version and the name of the unit or program, and they go to cdn.wolos.org. No address is stored with a report, and one address can send only a limited number a day.

title: This website and your privacy: What your browser keeps
text: Your colour choice and your language, if you picked one, in the browser's local storage for this site. They never leave your device. The Docs helper, if you say yes to it: its files are stored in the browser's storage for this site, so the next visit does not download them again. Say no, or leave the page, and nothing is downloaded. Clearing the site's data in your browser removes all of it.

title: This website and your privacy: The Docs helper
text: It asks before it downloads. The helper is a small assistant that answers questions from this manual. Before you say yes, it shows its size (about 600 MB) and its licence. Nothing is downloaded until you do. It works on your device. The model runs in your browser. Your questions are not sent to WolOS or to anyone else. It looks at your device first. So that the page can tell you whether the helper will run, your browser is asked how much memory and which graphics it has. That answer stays on your device and is not sent anywhere. Its files come through wolos.org. The browser never talks to the download host for them, and each file is checked against its fingerprint before it is used.

title: This website and your privacy: Who to ask
text: Write to julia@wolos.org to ask what is kept about you, or to ask for something to be deleted. The person responsible is Júlia Klee, who runs WolOS.

title: This website and your privacy: Fix it
text: What you see What to do You do not want the helper's files on your computer Clear the site's data in your browser's settings, or turn the helper off in its panel. You want the colour or language choice forgotten Clear the site's data in your browser's settings. You want Cloudflare's network error reports off Turn off network error reporting in your browser's privacy settings, if it has the option.

title: Apps: What it is
text: An app is a program you use: the browser, Mail, Music, a game. WolOS comes with the apps most people need on the first day, all in the Dock: App What it is for Files Your documents, pictures, downloads and USB sticks. See Files and folders. Apps A list of every app on the computer, with search. Browser The web. Websites you use every day can become apps of their own; see Web apps. Mail Email from any provider. Music Your songs and albums. Photos Your pictures, sorted by date. Calendar Appointments and reminders. Notes Short notes and lists. Terminal Typing commands; see What a terminal is. App Store More apps; see The Store. System Settings Everything you can change; see System Settings. Text Editor, a calculator in Search and more are found with Search (Super+Space).

title: Apps: Why WolOS does it this way
text: The apps in the Dock are ones that do their job well and look like the rest of the desktop, so the first day needs no shopping. Anything else is one click away in the Store, and every app you add can be removed again just as easily.

title: Apps: How
text: To Do this Open an app Click it in the Dock, or press Super+Space, type the first letters of its name and press Return. See every app Click Apps in the Dock. Switch to another open app Super+Tab, or click its icon in the Dock (a dot under it means it is running). Quit an app Super+Q, or the app's menu in the menu bar > Quit. Close one window Super+W, or the rightmost round button of the window. Stop an app that does not respond Alt+Super+Esc > choose it > Force Quit. Add an app The App Store; see The Store. Remove an app Its page in the App Store > Remove. Your own files made with it stay. Open an app when you log in System Settings > General > Login Items: "Apps that open when you log in."

title: Apps: Each app's menus
text: While an app is in front, its name and menus are at the top left of the menu bar: for example File, Edit, View, Window. The same keys work in every app: Super+C copies, Super+V pastes, Super+Z undoes, Super+S saves, Super+F finds, Super+N opens a new window and Super+T a new tab.

title: Apps: A worked example
text: Alice wants Mail to open every morning when she logs in. She opens System Settings > General > Login Items, adds Mail, and the next day her inbox is waiting when she signs in. She tried a drawing app from the Store and did not like it; on its Store page she clicks Remove, and it is gone from Search and the Dock.

title: Apps: If something goes wrong
text: What you see What to do An app does not open Wait a few seconds: the first start of a big app takes longer. Then try again from Search. "Not Checked Yet" WolOS checks a new program the first time it runs. Open it again in a moment. An app does not respond Alt+Super+Esc > Force Quit. Unsaved work in it is lost. An app is missing from the Dock Open it from Search; the Dock shows it with a dot while it runs, after the other apps. To keep it there, right-click it in the Dock and choose Keep in Dock. An app opens by itself at login Remove it from System Settings > General > Login Items.

title: Web apps: What it is
text: A web app is a website with a launcher of its own. It opens in a window without tabs or an address bar, has its own name and icon in Apps and in Search, and can sit in the Dock like any installed app. Mail, a calendar, a chat or a project board stop being one tab among thirty. You make one with a single line typed in the terminal. If you have not used the Terminal before, The terminal shows you how in ten minutes; this page only needs the one line below.

title: Web apps: Why WolOS does it this way
text: The sites you keep open all day should look and switch like apps: each has its own window, Super+Tab finds it, and the Dock shows when it is open. A launcher is only a small file in your own account, so there is nothing to install and nothing to update. The address you type is checked before the launcher is written, so a web app can only ever open that address.

title: Web apps: How
Web apps: Make one
text: Open Terminal. Press Super+Space, type "te" and press Return. Type the line below and press Return. The name comes first, then the whole address starting with https://. wol webapp add Mail https://mail.example.com WolOS fetches the site's own icon. Without one, the launcher gets a plain web icon. Open it. Press Super+Space and type "Mail": the web app is listed as an Application. Click it to open it. To keep it in the Dock, drag its row from Search onto the Dock, or right-click the row and choose Keep in Dock. It sits after the other apps; right-click its Dock icon and choose Remove from Dock to take it off again. You see the site in a window of its own, with no tabs and no address bar. Two choices go after the address: Add What it does A picture file, an https:// address or the name of an icon Uses this icon instead of the site's own. --own-profile Gives the web app its own sign-ins, apart from your browser. Use it to be signed in to two accounts of the same site, or to keep a site's cookies to itself. Without --own-profile the web app shares sign-ins with the WolOS browser, so you are already signed in wherever you are signed in there.

title: Web apps: See and remove your web apps
text: Type the same line with list instead of add to show your web apps with their addresses, or with remove and a name to take one away. Removing deletes the launcher and the icon it fetched; a picture file of yours is left alone.

title: Web apps: Web apps that come with a plugin
text: A plugin can bring web apps of its own. They sit next to yours while the plugin is on and go away when you turn the plugin off (Plugins).

title: Web apps: Assistants
text: An assistant can add or remove a web app only through an approval sheet, and the sheet appears every time: there is no Always Allow for it.

title: Web apps: A worked example
text: Alice reads her mail in a browser tab that keeps getting lost among others. She opens Terminal, types the line with her mail provider's address and presses Return. She presses Super+Space, types "Mail", opens the web app and drags its row from Search onto the Dock. Next morning one click on the Dock opens her mail in a window of its own, and Super+Tab switches between the mail and her letter like between any two apps.

title: Web apps: If something goes wrong
text: What the Terminal says: It says What to do Type the full web address, starting with https://, without spaces or quotes. Copy the address from the browser's address bar, the whole of it. Give the web app a short name with letters or digits. Use a name of up to 64 characters with at least one letter or digit. A web app named "Mail" already exists. Choose another name, or remove the old one first. There is no web app named "Mail". List your web apps to see the exact names. Problem What to do The icon is a plain web icon The site offers none WolOS can fetch. Remove the web app and add it again with an icon after the address. You are signed out of the site in the web app A web app made with --own-profile has its own sign-in: sign in once inside it. A right-click on a row in Search shows no Keep in Dock The app is one of the Dock's own apps and is in the Dock already.

title: Clipboard history: What it is
text: A small panel that remembers the text you copied, so you can paste something from ten minutes ago without finding it again. Open it with Shift+Super+V. It lists your pinned snippets first, then the most recent copies, newest on top.

title: Clipboard history: Why
text: Copying replaces what you copied before, and the lost text is often the one you need next. A history fixes that, but a history also remembers things it should not. So the panel keeps little and forgets on purpose: it holds 25 recent copies, it never keeps a one-time sign-in code, and the recent list is gone when you log out. Only what you pin stays.

title: Clipboard history: How
text: Copy text as usual (Super+C, or Copy in any app). It shows up at the top of the list. Open the panel with Shift+Super+V. With nothing copied yet, you see "Copied text shows up here". Click a row. Its text goes back on the clipboard and the panel closes. Paste it with Super+V. Search by typing in the field: a row matches when it contains every word you type, in any order and any case. When nothing matches, you see "No matches". Pin a row with its pin button. Pinned rows stay at the top, survive Clear, and come back after a restart. Its tooltip then reads Unpin. You can pin up to 25. Remove a single row with its remove button, or press Clear to drop every recent copy at once. Pinned rows stay until you unpin them. What is not kept: One-time codes. Four to eight digits, maybe split by one space or dash, as banks and sign-in pages send them. They paste once and never enter the history. A notification that carries a code offers Copy Code; its tooltip says "Copies the code. Clipboard history skips it, and it is cleared after a minute." Very long text. A copy longer than 64 KB still pastes; it is just not listed. Blank text and an exact repeat of the newest entry. Where it lives: recent copies only in memory, until you log out or the desktop restarts. Pins in ~/.local/state/wolos/clipboard-pins.json, in your account only. Pinned text is plain text in that file, so pin snippets, not passwords.

title: Clipboard history: A worked example
text: Alice copies a street address from an email, then a phone number from a letter. Her friend asks for the address again. She presses Shift+Super+V, types "street" in the search field, clicks the address and pastes it with Super+V. The address she uses every week she pins, so it is always at the top.

title: Clipboard history: If something goes wrong
text: What you see What to do "Copied text shows up here" although you copied something The panel lists text only. A copied picture or file pastes as usual but is not listed. A code you copied is missing That is on purpose: one-time codes are never kept. Copy it again from where it came. Pin does nothing You already have 25 pins. Unpin one first. Yesterday's copies are gone Recent copies last one session. Pin what you want to keep.

title: Screenshots and markup: What it is
text: Four keys take a picture of the screen at once, and one more opens the capture toolbar, where you choose what to capture (the whole screen, a window, an area, or a recording) and where it goes. After a capture from the toolbar a thumbnail waits in the corner for a few seconds; its pen button opens Markup, where you draw on the picture before you save or copy it.

title: Screenshots and markup: Why
text: A screenshot is usually taken to show someone something, now. So the keys need no setup and no dialog, the picture lands where you will find it (the Desktop), and the common next step, circling the thing you mean, is one click away instead of another app. Only WolOS's own tools can copy the screen without asking; any other app has to ask each time (Privacy and permissions).

title: Screenshots and markup: How
Screenshots and markup: From the keyboard
text: Keys Does Shift+Super+3 (or Print) Saves a picture of the whole screen to the Desktop. Shift+Super+4 Lets you drag over an area, then saves a picture of it. Esc cancels. Ctrl+Shift+Super+3 Copies a picture of the whole screen, no file. Ctrl+Shift+Super+4 Copies a picture of the area you drag, no file. Shift+Super+5 Opens the capture toolbar. A saved picture is named "Screenshot" with the date and time, is also put on the clipboard, and a notification names the folder it went to (for example Screenshot saved to Desktop). A copy-only capture says Copied to clipboard.

title: Screenshots and markup: The capture toolbar
text: Open it with Shift+Super+5, or the Screenshot tile in Control Center. The Record tile opens it ready to record the whole screen. Pick a mode. From left to right: Capture Entire Screen, Capture Selected Window, Capture Selected Portion, Record Entire Screen, Record Selected Portion. Hover a button to see its name. Options sets where it goes (Save to: Desktop, Pictures or Clipboard) and a Timer (None, 5 or 10 seconds). Press Capture (or Return). The button reads Record in a recording mode. Esc or the close button leaves without capturing. Pictures saved to Pictures go to Pictures/Screenshots. Recordings go to the Desktop, or to Movies when you chose Pictures, and are named "Screen Recording" with the date and time. To stop a recording, start a recording again (the toolbar or the Record tile); a notification says where it was saved.

title: Screenshots and markup: Markup
text: After a capture from the toolbar, a thumbnail shows at the bottom right for five seconds. Click its pen button. Draw. Choose Red, Yellow or Blue and drag over the picture. Undo takes back the last stroke. Save writes a marked-up copy next to the original, named like the original with "(Markup)" added. The original is never changed. Copy puts the marked-up picture on the clipboard instead.

title: Screenshots and markup: A worked example
text: Alice wants to show a friend an error message. She presses Shift+Super+4, drags a box around the message and lets go: the picture is on her Desktop and on the clipboard. For a longer explanation she presses Shift+Super+5, picks the area mode, clicks Capture, then clicks the pen on the thumbnail and circles the right button in red. Copy puts the marked-up picture on the clipboard, ready to paste into the chat.

title: Screenshots and markup: If something goes wrong
text: What you see What to do Nothing happens after Shift+Super+4 It is waiting for you to drag over an area. Esc cancels. The toolbar is in the picture It never should be: it hides before the capture. If a Timer was set, the capture waits that long. No thumbnail after a capture The thumbnail follows captures from the toolbar that make a file. With Save to Clipboard there is no file, so no thumbnail; paste the picture instead. A recording does not stop Start a recording again from the toolbar or the Record tile: that ends the one running and saves it. The shortcuts do something else Check Settings > Keyboard > Keyboard Shortcuts, group Screenshots, where you can change them.

title: Notifications: What it is
text: A notification is a short message from an app or from WolOS: a new mail, a finished download, a low battery, an update that is ready. It appears for a few seconds as a banner at the top right of the screen, then waits in Notification Center until you clear it.

title: Notifications: Why WolOS does it this way
text: A message should reach you without stealing your attention. So banners are small, slide away on their own, and never cover the middle of the screen. Nothing is lost when you miss one: Notification Center keeps it. When you need quiet, one switch holds every banner back, and WolOS holds them by itself while a game or a film fills the screen. Only messages you must not miss, like a nearly empty battery, still show.

title: Notifications: How
Notifications: Banners
text: Click a banner to open what it is about (the mail, the download, the app). A button on a banner does something straight away; its label says what. Escape, or simply waiting, dismisses a banner. It stays in Notification Center.

title: Notifications: Notification Center
text: Click the date and time at the right end of the menu bar. Notification Center lists every notification you have not cleared, newest first. Click one to open it; Clear removes them. System Settings > Notifications > Notification Center > Show opens it too.

title: Notifications: Quiet: Do Not Disturb and Focus
text: Do Not Disturb keeps every banner off the screen. Notifications still arrive and wait in Notification Center. "Critical alerts, such as a low battery, still show." From Control Center: click Focus, then Do Not Disturb and how long: For 1 hour or Until tomorrow morning. From the keyboard: Ctrl+Super+D turns it on and off. From System Settings > Notifications: the Do Not Disturb row (1) has a switch (2), and the Turn off row under it says when it ends: When I turn it off, In one hour or Tomorrow morning. While it is on, a moon shows in the menu bar and the row says how long: "On until you turn it off", or the time it ends. Setting Default What it does Do Not Disturb Off Holds banners back; they wait in Notification Center. Turn off When I turn it off When Do Not Disturb ends by itself. Notification Center > Show Opens the list of notifications you missed.

title: Notifications: While a game or a film is full screen
text: When an app fills the whole screen, WolOS holds banners back by itself and shows them when you leave full screen. You do not have to turn anything on. See Playing full screen.

title: Notifications: Which apps may notify you
text: An app needs your permission to show notifications. You give it when the app asks, and you can take it back in System Settings > Privacy & Security, group Notifications: one switch per app. See Privacy and permissions.

title: Notifications: A worked example
text: Alice is giving a presentation from her laptop. Before she starts she presses Ctrl+Super+D: the moon appears in the menu bar and no chat message pops up on the projector. After the talk she clicks the clock: Notification Center shows the three messages she missed. She presses Ctrl+Super+D again, and new banners show as usual.

title: Notifications: If something goes wrong
text: What you see What to do No banners at all Do Not Disturb is on (a moon in the menu bar). Press Ctrl+Super+D or click Focus in Control Center. One app never shows banners It has no permission. Turn its switch on in System Settings > Privacy & Security > Notifications. Banners come back while you play The game is in a window, not full screen. Switch it to full screen, or turn on Do Not Disturb. A low-battery message shows despite Do Not Disturb That is on purpose: critical alerts always show. Plug the computer in. Notification Center is empty though you missed something The notification was cleared, or the app removed it when you opened it.

title: Sharing and devices: What it is
text: Everything that connects this computer to other devices and people near you: the name other devices see, Bluetooth headphones, keyboards and mice, sound played from a phone, your internet shared over Wi-Fi, files you send, and a second screen or projector. Most of it lives in System Settings > General > Sharing and System Settings > Bluetooth.

title: Sharing and devices: Why WolOS does it this way
text: Sharing means opening a door, so every door starts closed: nobody can log in to your computer from another one, it does not receive sound from phones, and it shares its internet with nobody, until you switch that on. The switches say in one line what they open, and the computer's name is the only thing other devices see by default.

title: Sharing and devices: How
Sharing and devices: Your computer's name
text: Open System Settings > General > Sharing. The Computer name field (1) is the name other computers on your network see, "and Bluetooth devices show it when pairing." Click it, type a new name and press Return. Use lowercase letters, digits and hyphens, up to 63 characters.

title: Sharing and devices: Settings on the Sharing page
text: Setting Default What it does Computer name (1) The name from the installer The name on the network and for Bluetooth pairing. Remote Login (2) Off Lets you log in to this computer from another one over the network, in a terminal. The line under it shows exactly what to type there. Turning it on asks for an administrator's password and opens port 22 in the firewall at once, with no restart. Leave it off unless you need it. AirPlay Receiver (3) Off "Play audio from iPhones, iPads and Macs on this computer." With it on, this computer appears in the phone's sound menu, and what you play there comes out of this computer's speakers. Turning it on opens the ports AirPlay needs in the firewall, for your local network only. Internet Sharing Off Turns this computer into a Wi-Fi hotspot: phones and other computers join it and use this computer's internet. See below. While you try WolOS from the USB stick, the Sharing page greys out the rows that need an administrator and says "Install WolOS to change these. The live system’s account has no password to allow them." Remote Login is not offered there at all. Internet Sharing works.

title: Sharing and devices: Share this computer's internet (a hotspot)
text: When the computer is online by cable, other devices can share that connection over its Wi-Fi. Open System Settings > General > Sharing and find Internet Sharing (4 in the picture above). The line under it reads "Share this computer’s internet with phones and other computers over Wi-Fi." Type a password in the Password field: 8 to 63 characters. The other devices need it to join. Turn on Internet Sharing. The line then reads "Other devices join “…” with the password you chose. They use this computer’s internet." The hotspot has your computer's name. On the phone, pick that name in its Wi-Fi list and type the password. Turn the switch off to end the hotspot. It never starts by itself, also not after a restart. No administrator's password is needed.

title: Sharing and devices: Bluetooth headphones, keyboards and mice
text: Put the device in pairing mode. Its own manual says how; often you hold a button until a light blinks. Open System Settings > Bluetooth. It says "This computer appears as “…”." and lists My Devices. Click Add Device… and wait a few seconds: Nearby Devices lists what is in pairing mode. Click yours. Answer the sheet if it asks. Some devices show a code on both sides: check that it matches and click Pair. Older keyboards want a PIN (try 0000 or 1234): type it and click Pair. A keyboard may instead ask you to type a code on it and press Return. When it says the device is paired, that is pairing: from now on it connects by itself when both are on. Next time, Control Center > Bluetooth lists it; click it to connect or disconnect. To remove a device, click Forget beside it in System Settings > Bluetooth, then confirm. Headphones play the computer's sound once connected; choose them in Control Center's Sound page if the sound stays on the speakers. See Sound.

title: Sharing and devices: Send a file to someone
text: By email: right-click the file in Files > Email…: a new message opens with the file attached. On a USB stick: copy it in Files; see Files and folders. In the Public folder: files you put in Public are the ones meant for other people on your network.

title: Sharing and devices: A second screen or a projector
text: Plug it in: WolOS uses it as more room for your windows, next to the laptop's screen. To show the same picture on both, open Control Center > Display (the arrow at the end of the Display slider) and click Screen Mirroring. System Settings > Displays has a card for each screen with its Resolution, Refresh Rate (how many pictures a second), Scale (the size of everything on it) and, for the second screen, Arrangement (where it stands next to the first).

title: Sharing and devices: An iPhone on a cable
text: Plug an iPhone into the computer with its cable: WolOS says "iPhone connected" once, so you know the computer sees it.

title: Sharing and devices: A worked example
text: Alice's new wireless headphones arrive. She holds their button until the light blinks blue, opens System Settings > Bluetooth, and clicks "Hatter Buds" when they appear: Connected. A video in the browser now plays in the headphones. In the evening her son wants to play music from his iPhone through the laptop's speakers; she turns on AirPlay Receiver in Sharing, and the laptop appears in his phone's sound menu as "wonderland".

title: Sharing and devices: If something goes wrong
text: What you see What to do "No Bluetooth Hardware" "This computer has no Bluetooth adapter. Plug in a USB adapter to use wireless devices." "No devices yet" Nothing was paired. "Put a device in pairing mode to connect it the first time." The device stays at "Connecting…" Turn the device off and on, keep it close to the computer, and click it again. The headphones are connected but the sound comes from the speakers Control Center > the arrow at the end of the Sound slider > tick the headphones. The computer name is refused Use lowercase letters, digits and hyphens only, up to 63 characters. A second screen stays black Check the cable and the screen's own input button, then System Settings > Displays: choose a lower Resolution for it. The phone does not show this computer for AirPlay Both must be on the same Wi-Fi network, and AirPlay Receiver must be on. "Use 8 to 63 characters for the hotspot password." The hotspot password is too short or too long. Type another one, then turn Internet Sharing on. "Internet Sharing needs a Wi-Fi device." This computer has no Wi-Fi, so it cannot make a hotspot. A small USB Wi-Fi adapter adds one. "The hotspot didn’t start. Check that Wi-Fi is on, then try again." Turn Wi-Fi on in Control Center and try again.

title: Sound: What it is
text: Everything about sound in one place: the volume, where sound comes out (speakers, headphones, a TV), which microphone listens, and a few helpers for calls. The quick controls are in Control Center; everything else is in System Settings > Sound.

title: Sound: Why WolOS does it this way
text: On many computers 100% does not mean the same thing on two devices, and a new microphone may arrive set so loud that it distorts. In WolOS, 100% is each device's own normal full level (0 dB), for speakers and microphones alike, so a new device starts sounding right. Going above it is possible, but only when you ask for it, because louder than normal can distort.

title: Sound: How
Sound: Set the volume
text: Drag the Sound slider in Control Center, or press the volume keys. A sign in the middle of the screen shows the new level. The mute key silences everything until you press it again.

title: Sound: Choose speakers, headphones and the microphone
text: Click the arrow at the end of the Sound slider in Control Center. Output lists where sound can go, Input lists the microphones, each with its own slider and mute button. Click a device to use it; the tick moves. Wireless headphones show their codec under their name.

title: Sound: System Settings > Sound
text: Press Super+, and choose Sound, or click Sound Settings… at the bottom of Control Center's Sound page. Setting Default What it does Output volume, Mute The same as the slider in Control Center. Output The device you used last Where sound comes out. Balance Middle Shifts sound to the left or right speaker. Allow louder Off "Lets volume sliders pass 100%." Use it for a quiet laptop speaker or a quiet microphone; above 100% sound can distort. Input and its level meter The built-in or last microphone Which microphone listens. The meter moves as you speak; red means too loud. Automatic input level Off Keeps your voice at an even level in calls. It adds an input called WolOS Microphone and makes it the default. Reduce background noise Off Filters out fans, keyboards and street noise from the microphone. Use the headset microphone automatically (with a Bluetooth headset) A headset switches to its call mode while an app records, so the microphone in the headset works. Pro Audio Automatic The sample rate and how much sound is prepared ahead (the buffer), for recording and music; see Low-latency sound. Troubleshooting Keep device awake for a device that clicks or cuts off the start of a sound; Ignore hardware volume for a device whose volume jumps or does nothing; Diagnostics with Copy for a report; Reset audio with Reset.

title: Sound: A worked example
text: Alice has a video call. Her colleagues say she sounds far away. She opens System Settings > Sound, watches the input meter while she speaks (it barely moves), turns on Automatic input level and Reduce background noise, and the call app now uses WolOS Microphone. Her voice comes through clearly, and the fan of her laptop no longer does.

title: Sound: If something goes wrong
text: What you see What to do No sound at all Check the mute key, then Control Center > Sound page: tick the device you want under Output. Sound comes from the speakers, not the headphones Tick the headphones under Output on the Sound page. "No microphone is connected" Nothing is plugged in or paired. Check the cable, or pair the headset in System Settings > Bluetooth. "Sound devices are coming back" The sound system restarted. Wait a few seconds. The microphone is too quiet Turn on Allow louder and raise the input slider while you watch the meter; red means it distorts. Or turn on Automatic input level. A Bluetooth headset sounds bad in calls That is its call mode, which every headset has. Turn Use the headset microphone automatically off if you only listen. Crackling or dropouts In Pro Audio, choose a larger buffer or Automatic. The volume jumps or does nothing on one device Turn on Ignore hardware volume in Troubleshooting. A switch flips back The change did not take; the line under the section says why. Try again. Nothing helps Reset next to Reset audio in Troubleshooting forgets stored volumes and devices and restarts sound. Copy next to Diagnostics puts a report on the clipboard to paste into a bug report.

title: Music and video formats: What it is
text: A format (or codec) is the way a song or a video is packed into a file. Most music, phone videos and films use a handful of them: MP3, AAC, H.264, HEVC and AC3 (Dolby Digital). WolOS adds all of them, plus the fonts most documents and web pages expect, in one step called Media Codecs. It is a Kit: a set of extras the Store adds together. You find it in two places: the installer's page Music and Video Formats, and the Store's Kits.

title: Music and video formats: Why
text: Some of these formats are patented in some countries, so whether to add them is your choice, not ours. WolOS never adds them on its own, and it never hides them behind a search either: one switch, a line for each format that says what it is for, and a sentence about the patents. Then your files just open.

title: Music and video formats: How
Music and video formats: While you install WolOS
text: On the page "Music and Video Formats", turn on Add Media Formats. You see what each format is for (MP3: Music files and podcasts, H.264: Most videos on the web and from cameras, and so on) and the sentence Some of these formats are patented in some countries. You choose whether to add them. Continue. The formats download while WolOS installs. Without the internet, the summary says they will be added "at first start with a network", and the Store's Kits page has them too.

title: Music and video formats: On a WolOS that is already installed
text: Open the Store and choose Kits in the sidebar. You see Media Codecs (Play and make MP3, AAC, H.264, HEVC and more) with a Get button, and what each format is for. Click Get. You see a password sheet: adding packages for every account needs an administrator. Type your password and click Allow. Wait for Added. You see the button change to Added. Files that did not open before now open in the music and video apps, the browser and the creative apps.

title: Music and video formats: What each part is for
text: Part You need it for MP3 Music files and podcasts AAC Music from stores, phone videos and streams H.264 Most videos on the web and from cameras HEVC (H.265) Videos from newer phones and 4K files AC3 (Dolby Digital) Sound on DVDs and many films Fonts Documents and web pages look as their authors meant

title: Music and video formats: A worked example
text: Alice's phone video opens with sound but no picture. She opens the Store, chooses Kits and clicks Get on Media Codecs. She types her password, clicks Allow and waits for the button to read Added. The same video now plays, and so do the MP3s her sister sent.

title: Music and video formats: If something goes wrong
text: What you see What to do A video opens with sound but no picture, or does not open The Kit is not added yet. Open the Store > Kits and check that Media Codecs says Added. Settings > Modules lists AAC, H.264, HEVC (H.265), AC3 (Dolby Digital) under Could Not Be Added You ticked the formats in the installer, but they could not be downloaded after several tries. Check that you're online and click Retry. Get does nothing offline The Kit downloads its parts. Connect to a network and try again. A file still will not play after the Kit is added Some files use rarer formats. Try another player from the Store's Play page, such as VLC or mpv.

title: Battery and sleep: What it is
text: WolOS decides how hard the computer works from whether it is plugged in: on battery it saves energy, on the charger it runs at full speed. System Settings > Battery (on a computer without a battery: Energy) shows the charge and the battery's health, and lets you choose differently.

title: Battery and sleep: Why WolOS does it this way
text: Most people never open power settings, and they should not have to. A laptop on battery should last, and the same laptop on the desk should be fast, without anyone choosing that twice a day. When you do want something else (a long train ride, a render that should finish quickly) one choice overrides the automatic one until you switch back.

title: Battery and sleep: How
text: Open System Settings > Battery. Setting Default What it does Battery level The charge, and the time left on battery. The time left appears once the battery reports how fast it is emptying, and never while it charges. Battery health How much the battery holds compared with new, and how many times it was charged. Energy Mode Automatic Automatic saves energy on battery and runs at full speed when plugged in. Low Power saves energy all the time (longer battery, a little slower). High Power runs at full speed all the time (faster, warmer, shorter battery). When the lid is closed Sleep What a laptop does when you close it. Memory Saver On Apps you have not used for a while give their memory back, so the app you work in has more. They come back exactly as they were when you click them. The app in front, apps playing sound or video, and games are never touched. App Nap Off Pauses an app that has been hidden and idle for 10 minutes, to save energy.

title: Battery and sleep: Sleep
text: Close the lid, choose Sleep in the WolOS menu (the logo at the left of the menu bar), click Sleep in the session panel (Super+Esc), or let the computer go to sleep by itself when you leave it. Restart… and Shut Down… are in the same menu; they ask first and act by themselves after 60 seconds. Every sleep locks the screen first, so the computer wakes to the lock screen. Press a key or open the lid to wake it. While you try WolOS from the USB stick there is no lock screen, because the trial account has no password, so the computer wakes straight to the desktop. On battery the screen turns off and the computer sleeps sooner than on the charger. Stay Awake in Control Center keeps it awake for a presentation or a long download.

title: Battery and sleep: Battery warnings
text: A notification comes at 20%, at 10% and at 5% left. At 3% you see "Your computer is going to sleep now. Connect to power to keep working." and it sleeps by itself, so nothing is lost when the battery runs out.

title: Battery and sleep: A worked example
text: Alice has a five-hour train ride and an old battery. She opens System Settings > Battery, sees "Battery health 81% of new" and chooses Low Power. Her laptop lasts the whole ride. At home, on the charger, she switches back to Automatic.

title: Battery and sleep: If something goes wrong
text: What you see What to do The battery runs down fast Choose Low Power, lower the brightness in Control Center, and check that Stay Awake is off. "Your computer is going to sleep now. Connect to power to keep working." The battery is at 3%. Plug the charger in. The computer does not sleep Stay Awake may be on (Control Center), or an app keeps it awake (System Settings > Privacy & Security, Keep Awake). Wi-Fi feels slow on battery Wi-Fi saves power on battery. Choose High Power while you need speed. The Energy Mode choice is missing This computer does not let WolOS change its speed. The automatic setting still saves energy on battery. "Your Disk Is Almost Full" Less than 5% of the disk is free. Empty the Trash and remove files you do not need.

title: Lock Screen and login window: What it is
text: The lock screen covers your desktop with the time, the date, your picture and a password field. Your apps keep running behind it. The login window is the same screen before anyone has signed in: it lists the accounts on this computer, and has Sleep, Restart and Shut Down at the bottom.

title: Lock Screen and login window: Why
text: A computer left open is an open account. Locking has to be quick enough that you do it, and automatic for the times you forget. The lock also has to hold: if the lock screen itself stops, the desktop stays covered and a new lock screen takes its place, so a crash never opens your session.

title: Lock Screen and login window: How
Lock Screen and login window: Lock now
text: Ctrl+Super+Q, or the WolOS menu (the logo at the top left) > Lock Screen, or type "lock" in Search (Super+Space) and press Return. While you try WolOS from the USB stick, nothing locks the screen. The trial account has no password, so nothing could unlock it: the WolOS menu and the session panel (Super+Esc) have no Lock Screen there, and the shortcut does nothing. To unlock, type your password and press Return (or the arrow button). The eye button shows what you typed. While Caps Lock is on, you see "⇪ Caps Lock is on" under the field. A wrong password says "Incorrect password", and you can type again.

title: Lock Screen and login window: Lock by itself: Settings > Lock Screen
text: Lock screen when inactive: after 1, 2, 5 (the default) or 10 minutes without input, or Never. Lock when the computer sleeps: on, the lock screen is up when the computer wakes. The display turns off one minute after the screen locks. With Never on battery, the display still turns off after 2 minutes without input, and the screen stays unlocked. Both settings are recorded like any other setting, so wol undo or Restore > Recent Changes takes a change back (Recovery).

title: Lock Screen and login window: The login window
text: Click your account. The password field opens under it; Back returns to the list. Type your password and press Return. After three wrong passwords (here and on the lock screen) the password hint of that account shows under the field (Setup asks for one; it is optional), as "Hint: …". With no hint, nothing is shown. Sleep, Restart and Shut Down work from the login window without signing in. Left alone for 10 minutes, the login window turns the display off; the first key or a move of the mouse turns it back on.

title: Lock Screen and login window: A worked example
text: Alice walks away from her desk for a coffee and presses Ctrl+Super+Q. The screen shows the clock and her picture, and her video call keeps running behind it. When she is back she types her password and presses Return. The desktop is exactly as she left it. For the days she forgets, Settings > Lock Screen locks it after 5 minutes.

title: Lock Screen and login window: If something goes wrong
text: What you see What to do "Incorrect password" Check Caps Lock and the keyboard layout, then type it again. After three tries the login window shows your hint. "Your password can’t be checked right now. Try again, or restart." The password check did not answer. Wait a moment and try again; if it keeps saying this, restart. "This computer can’t restart right now. If someone else is signed in, they need to sign out first." Restart from the lock screen does not end another person's session. Ask them to sign out, or unlock and restart from your account. "This computer can’t shut down right now. Try again." The request was not taken. Wait a moment and try again. "No Accounts" on the login window, with "No account on this computer can sign in here. Ask the person who looks after it for help." No account here can sign in at the login window. The person who looks after the computer can add one in Settings > Users & Groups. The screen locks too soon, or never Settings > Lock Screen > Lock screen when inactive.

title: Games: What it is
text: WolOS plays three kinds of games: Kind Where you get it How it runs Games made for WolOS and Linux The App Store's Play shelf, or Steam Like any other app. Windows games in your Steam library Steam, which is already on WolOS Steam runs them through its own compatibility tool, Proton, without anything to set up. Windows games from other shops A .exe file you download A double-click opens it with WolOS's Windows program runner.

title: Games: Why WolOS does it this way
text: You should not have to rebuy your games or learn a new launcher. Steam already knows how to run most Windows games, and it improves every week, so WolOS lets Steam do that and takes care of what usually goes wrong around it: the graphics pieces Steam needs, banners popping up during a game, and a clear sentence with a fix when something is missing.

title: Games: How
text: Open the App Store > Play for games you can get with one click, and for Steam itself. For your Steam library, open Steam from Search, sign in, install a game and press Play. Steam and your game library walks through the first start. Play full screen. While a game fills the screen, banners wait, and the screen shows each frame as soon as it is ready. Playing full screen explains what changes and how to get out of a game that froze. If a game will not start, one check finds the missing piece and says how to add it: When a game will not start.

title: Games: The Gaming module
text: System Settings > Modules > Gaming adds more for people who play a lot: the Windows program runner with its helpers for games outside Steam, a launcher for games from other shops, and an overlay that shows frames per second while you play. See Modules.

title: Games: Controllers
text: Plug a game controller in, or pair a wireless one in System Settings > Bluetooth. Steam sets up most controllers itself.

title: Games: A worked example
text: Bill had Steam on Windows with 60 games. On WolOS he opens Steam, signs in, and his library is there. He installs a Windows game he played last week and presses Play: it starts through the compatibility tool, full screen, with no banner interrupting him. One older game shows an error, so he follows When a game will not start, which tells him which piece to add.

title: Games: If something goes wrong
text: What you see What to do A game does not start Follow When a game will not start. A Windows game in Steam has no Install button In Steam's Settings > Compatibility, turn on running other titles with the compatibility tool. Banners appear during a game The game is in a window. Switch it to full screen in its own settings. A game froze Alt+Super+Esc opens Force Quit over the game. A game from another shop does not open Install the Gaming module, then double-click its .exe again.

title: Steam and your game library: What it is
text: Steam is already on WolOS. You open it like any other app, sign in with your Steam account, and your library is there: the games you bought on Windows are the same games here. Most of them were made for Windows. Steam runs those through its own compatibility tool (Proton): a translator that sits between a Windows game and WolOS, so the game believes it is on Windows. Think of it as a travel adapter for a plug: the game does not change, the socket does.

title: Steam and your game library: Why
text: Steam's compatibility tool is where the work to make Windows games run happens, every week, for thousands of titles. So WolOS does not add a second layer of its own on top. What WolOS adds is the part that usually goes wrong around Steam: before Steam starts, WolOS checks that the pieces Steam needs are in place (the 32-bit graphics files, the graphics driver, the matching NVIDIA files) and, when one is missing, tells you in one sentence what to do. You do not read a guide before you can play.

title: Steam and your game library: How
text: Open Steam. Press Super+Space for Search, type steam and press Return, or click Steam in the Store under Play. You see Steam in Search as an Application. In the Store it sits in the Play list with the line Thousands of games, one library. Wait for the first start. The first time, Steam downloads the rest of itself. You see a notification: Getting Steam ready. Steam downloads itself the first time you open it. It opens when it's ready. Keep the computer online; this happens once. Sign in with your Steam account, as you would on Windows. You see your library. Install a game from your library and press Play. A game made for Windows runs through the compatibility tool without anything to set. If a Windows game has no Install button, open Steam's Settings > Compatibility and turn on running other titles with the compatibility tool.

title: Steam and your game library: Games from outside Steam
text: A Windows program you downloaded yourself, such as a .exe installer from a game shop, opens with a double-click. WolOS gives each program its own folder of Windows settings, so one program cannot break another. For many such games at once, the Gaming module adds a games launcher and an on-screen frame-rate counter; see Modules.

title: Steam and your game library: On a screen with high resolution
text: On a sharp laptop screen Steam would look half size. When you start Steam from the Dock, Search or the Store, WolOS tells Steam how large your screen's scale is, so its text is readable.

title: Steam and your game library: A worked example
text: Alice installs Steam from the Store, opens it and waits for the "Getting Steam ready" notification to finish. She signs in with the account she has had for years, finds a game she bought on Windows, clicks Install and then Play. It runs, and she never changed a setting.

title: Steam and your game library: If something goes wrong
text: What you see What to do Steam couldn't download Steam could not fetch the rest of itself. Check that you're online, then open Steam again. Steam can't open yet. Your graphics driver isn't running. Restart the computer, then open Steam again. If it stays, see Hardware and drivers. Steam can't open yet. Part of Steam is missing. Run the game check-up: When a game will not start shows the one line to type, and the fix for each missing piece. Steam needs graphics files for your NVIDIA card. Run the game check-up on When a game will not start; the line marked FAIL has the fix. Steam looks tiny Start Steam from the Dock, Search or the Store, not from another launcher, so WolOS can pass the screen scale. A game with kernel anti-cheat will not start Some online games refuse every system except Windows, because their anti-cheat needs it. That is the game's rule, and its own page usually says so.

title: Playing full screen: What it is
text: When a game fills the whole screen, WolOS steps back. Notifications wait until you leave the game, each frame goes to the screen the moment the game finishes it, and a screen that can change its refresh rate (variable refresh rate, VRR for short) follows the game's pace. If the game freezes, Force Quit still opens on top of it. You set none of this up: it happens because the window is full screen.

title: Playing full screen: Why
text: A game that is interrupted, or that waits a few milliseconds for the screen, feels worse than a slower game that is never interrupted. So WolOS treats full screen as a promise: nothing of the desktop draws over the game, and nothing holds its frames back. Desktop widgets pause on that screen, Memory Saver never touches a game, and a banner that arrives while you play is kept for later rather than lost.

title: Playing full screen: How
text: Make the game full screen. Use the game's own video setting (Fullscreen, not Windowed), or press Ctrl+Super+F for any window. You see the game cover the menu bar and the Dock. Play. A notification that arrives now does not show. When you leave full screen, the banners you missed appear, and every one stays in Notification Center. Want silence outside games too? Open Control Center and choose Focus, then Do Not Disturb, For 1 hour or Until tomorrow morning. Ctrl+Super+D turns Do Not Disturb on or off. The same switch is in Settings > Notifications: "While Focus is on, banners stay quiet and wait in Notification Center. Critical alerts, such as a low battery, still show." If the game stops answering, press Alt+Super+Esc. You see Force Quit Applications over the game. Choose the game and click Force Quit. The rest of the desktop is not affected. Check the refresh rate in Settings > Displays if your screen supports more than 60 Hz. You see Refresh Rate next to Resolution and Scale. Choose the highest the screen offers; the variable refresh rate turns on only for full-screen windows, so the desktop stays steady.

title: Playing full screen: What changes while a game is full screen
text: What While you play Why Banners Wait, then show when you leave A banner drawn over the game would also slow its frames The volume sign Still shows for a moment You need to see the level you set Frames Go out at once, even if that means a slight tear Lower delay between your hand and the screen Variable refresh rate On, for full-screen windows only The screen follows the game's pace A game at a lower resolution Scaled sharp, not blurred Pixel art and text stay crisp Desktop widgets Paused on that screen They would spend power you want for the game Memory Saver Never touches the game Games are excluded by rule

title: Playing full screen: A worked example
text: Alice starts a game and presses Ctrl+Super+F to make it full screen. Halfway through a mail arrives and a calendar reminder fires, but nothing covers the game. When she quits, three banners appear at once and all three are waiting in Notification Center. The game was never interrupted.

title: Playing full screen: If something goes wrong
text: What you see What to do A banner showed over the game The game is in a window, not full screen. Switch it to Fullscreen in its video settings, or press Ctrl+Super+F. The picture tears on fast movement That is the price of sending frames at once. Turn on the game's own V-Sync, or use a screen with variable refresh rate. The game is frozen and the keys do nothing Press Alt+Super+Esc and Force Quit it. I missed a message while I played Open Notification Center (Settings > Notifications > Show): every notification you missed is there, newest first. The refresh rate stays at 60 Hz Pick it in Settings > Displays. The list shows only what the screen and cable report; some older cables carry 60 Hz only.
