title: When a game will not start: What it is
text: The check-up for games is one line, wol games doctor, that you type in the terminal. It looks at everything a game needs on this computer: Steam itself, the graphics driver, the 32-bit graphics files Steam still uses, the graphics driver games talk to (Vulkan, the modern way games reach the graphics card) and, on NVIDIA cards, files that must match the driver's version. Each check prints one line. A check that fails prints the line that fixes it right under it. Think of it as the warning lights on a car's dashboard, each with the name of the part.

title: When a game will not start: Why
text: When a game does not start on most computers, you get a black window or nothing, and then an evening of forum threads. Almost every one of those cases is a missing piece in the list above. Checking for them is cheap, so WolOS does it in one place and says the fix in a sentence. The same checks run when you open Steam: if one fails, a notification tells you instead of Steam crashing silently.

title: When a game will not start: How
text: Open Terminal. Press Super+Space, type te and press Return. Run the check. Type this and press Return: wol games doctor You see one line per check: ok, info, warn or FAIL, the check's name, and what it found. It ends with Ready: Steam and Windows games can run. or with the number of problems. A failed check looks like this (the names after fix: depend on your graphics card): FAIL lib32-gl 32-bit OpenGL or Vulkan missing (the Steam client is 32-bit) fix: sudo pacman -S --needed vulkan-icd-loader lib32-vulkan-icd-loader vulkan-radeon lib32-vulkan-radeon lib32-mesa Not ready: 1 problem(s). Run the fix lines above, then check again. Copy the fix line and run it. Select the text after fix: with the mouse, copy it, paste it into Terminal with Super+V and press Return. Terminal asks for your password, because the fix installs for every account. Nothing shows while you type, not even dots; press Return when done. Check again with the same line, then start the game. You see Ready: Steam and Windows games can run.

title: When a game will not start: What each check means
text: Check It looks at When it fails multilib The source of 32-bit software Steam and the 32-bit drivers come from there. The fix turns it on. steam Steam itself The fix line puts it back. drm A loaded graphics driver Nothing can draw. Open Settings > Hardware: a device that needs attention has a Fix button. lib32-gl 32-bit graphics files The Steam window itself is a 32-bit program and cannot start. vulkan-icd, vulkan A Vulkan driver for your card Windows games need one. If Vulkan sees only the processor, games would crawl. nvidia NVIDIA's 32-bit files, same version as the driver Steam cannot use the card. futex-waitv, ntsync Two features of the kernel that make Windows games smoother Only a warning: games still run, a little less smoothly. WolKernel has both. wine The runner for Windows programs outside Steam Only information: Steam games do not need it. The Gaming module adds it.

title: When a game will not start: A worked example
text: A game Alice just bought shows a black window and closes. She opens Terminal, types the check-up line and sees FAIL lib32-gl with a fix line under it. She copies the fix line, pastes it, types her password and waits. The second check-up ends with "Ready: Steam and Windows games can run." and the game starts.

title: When a game will not start: If something goes wrong
text: What you see What to do Every check says ok and the game still does not start Open the game's properties in Steam and choose another version of the compatibility tool, then try again. The game's page on community sites often names the version that works. drm fails after an update Restart once. If it stays, open Settings > Hardware and click Fix on the device that needs attention. The fix line says a package was not found The list of available software is out of date. Open Settings > Software Update, let it check for updates, then run the fix line again. A Windows program outside Steam does not open Install the Gaming module in Settings > Modules: it adds the runner for such programs. The game starts but stutters Check that the game runs full screen (Playing full screen), and that a laptop is plugged in: with Energy Mode on Automatic (Settings > Battery), WolOS saves energy on battery and runs at full speed when plugged in.

title: Creative apps in one step: What it is
text: The Creative module is a set of apps for making things, installed together in one step: Blender (3D and animation), GIMP (photo editing), Krita (painting), Inkscape (vector drawing), darktable (RAW photos), Kdenlive (video editing), OBS Studio (streaming and recording), Ardour (music production) and Audacity (sound editing). It also adds colour management and the pieces that let music apps use the smallest sound delay. A module is a bundle of apps WolOS keeps as one unit: you add it in one step, and you can remove it in one step (Modules).

title: Creative apps in one step: Why
text: Most people who make things need several of these tools, not one, and they should not pay a monthly fee for each of them. Installing nine apps one by one is a chore, and the sound pieces music apps need are easy to forget. So WolOS keeps them as one set. It is never ticked for you, because not everyone needs 1.3 GB of creative tools; you choose it when you want it.

title: Creative apps in one step: How
Creative apps in one step: While you install WolOS
text: On the page "Apps for What You Do", turn on Creative Apps. You see "Blender, GIMP, Krita, Inkscape, OBS, Kdenlive and more" under it, and the download size under the list. Finish the install. The apps download while WolOS installs. Without the internet, WolOS adds them at its first start with a network.

title: Creative apps in one step: On a WolOS that is already installed
text: Open Settings > Modules and click Install next to Creative. You see a password sheet: adding apps for every account needs an administrator. Type your password and click Allow. You see the module move to Installed when it is done. Open an app from Search: press Super+Space and type its name, for example krita.

title: Creative apps in one step: Only one or two apps?
text: You do not need the whole module. Open the Store, choose Create in the sidebar and click Get on the apps you want.

title: Creative apps in one step: Files from phones and cameras
text: Videos from phones and many cameras use formats some countries patent, so WolOS does not add them by itself. Add them in one click with the Media Codecs Kit: see Music and video formats.

title: Creative apps in one step: Sound with small delay
text: For recording through Ardour, or monitoring a microphone live, set a small buffer in Settings > Sound > Pro Audio: see Low-latency sound.

title: Creative apps in one step: A worked example
text: Alice ticks Creative Apps while she installs WolOS. When she first starts her computer a few minutes later, Krita and Blender are already in Search. She presses Super+Space, types "krita" and starts drawing. A month on she needs the space back and removes the module in Settings > Modules; her drawings are still in Pictures.

title: Creative apps in one step: If something goes wrong
text: What you see What to do The module is listed under Could Not Be Added It could not be downloaded after several tries. Check that you're online, then click Retry. "The list of modules couldn't be read" Try again in a minute. The Store's Create page still installs single apps. A phone video does not open in Kdenlive Add the Media Codecs Kit (Music and video formats). OBS does not hear the game See Sound for creators: the game can get its own track, apart from your microphone. Colours look different from another computer Every screen shows colours a little differently. Compare colours on the same screen, or use the colour management inside Krita, GIMP and darktable. You want the space back Settings > Modules, click the three dots next to Creative and remove it. Your files are not touched.

title: Dark Mode: What it is
text: Dark Mode turns the whole desktop and your apps dark: dark windows, dark menus, a dark terminal, light text. WolOS has three settings: Light, Dark, and Auto, which is light from 7:00 in the morning and dark from 19:00 in the evening.

title: Dark Mode: Why WolOS does it this way
text: A bright white screen in a dark room is tiring, and many people simply like dark better. One setting for everything means no app stays bright while the rest turns dark; Auto means you never have to think about it. Your accent colour follows along and is adjusted for each so it stays easy to read.

title: Dark Mode: How
Dark Mode: Switch it in one click
text: Open Control Center and click Dark Mode. It reads On or Off under its name. Click again to go back.

title: Dark Mode: Choose Light, Dark or Auto
text: Open System Settings > Appearance. Click Light, Dark or Auto in the row of three pictures at the top (1). The desktop and the apps that are open change at once. Setting What it does Light Light all day. Dark Dark all day. Auto Light from 7:00, dark from 19:00. The switch happens on its own at those times. The Dark Mode switch in Control Center changes between light and dark right away, whatever you chose here.

title: Dark Mode: With a theme
text: A theme from the gallery brings its own colours: some are light (Catppuccin Latte, Flexoki Light), most are dark. See Looks and themes.

title: Dark Mode: A worked example
text: Alice works late. She opens System Settings > Appearance and chooses Auto. At seven in the evening the desktop, her browser and her mail turn dark on their own; the next morning at seven they are light again. On a bright train one evening she wants it light, so she clicks Dark Mode in Control Center to turn it off; to have Auto back, she chooses it again in Appearance.

title: Dark Mode: If something goes wrong
text: What you see What to do One app stays light Some apps follow the setting only when they start. Quit it (Super+Q) and open it again. A few apps have their own light/dark choice in their settings. The accent colour does not change A theme from the gallery is chosen; themes bring their own accent. Choose Light, Dark or Auto to use the accent colours. Auto switches at the wrong time Check the time zone in System Settings > General > Date & Time. You want it back as before System Settings > Restore > Recent Changes > Undo next to Appearance.

title: Night Shift: What it is
text: Night Shift makes the colours of the screen warmer: whites turn a soft yellow-orange, as under a lamp, and the blue glow of the screen goes down. It changes the picture of every screen at once and nothing in your files or photos.

title: Night Shift: Why WolOS does it this way
text: A cold, blue-white screen late in the evening keeps many people awake and is hard on tired eyes. A warm screen is calmer. WolOS keeps it one switch, in all the places you would look for it, so turning it on is never more than one click or one key.

title: Night Shift: How
text: Turn it on or off in any of these places; they are the same switch: Control Center: click the Night Shift tile. A tile that is on is filled with the accent colour. The keyboard: Ctrl+Super+N. Control Center's Display page: click the arrow at the end of the Display slider; Night Shift is listed with On or Off. System Settings > Displays: the last row, Night Shift, "Warmer colours after dark", has a switch. Setting Default What it does Night Shift Off Warms the colours of every screen until you turn it off. Night Shift stays on until you turn it off; it does not switch by itself at a time of day. Left on, it is on again when you next sign in, also after a restart. Many people press Ctrl+Super+N in the evening and again in the morning. Tip Turn Night Shift off while you edit photos or choose colours: the warm tint changes how every colour looks on screen.

title: Night Shift: A worked example
text: Alice reads in bed on her laptop. She presses Ctrl+Super+N, and the white pages turn warm. In the morning she presses it again before she looks at the photos from her holiday, so their colours look right.

title: Night Shift: If something goes wrong
text: What you see What to do The screen looks yellow and you do not know why Night Shift is on. Press Ctrl+Super+N, or click the Night Shift tile in Control Center. The switch flips back Night Shift could not be turned on. Try again; if it keeps happening, restart the computer. The shortcut does nothing It may have been changed. System Settings > Keyboard > Keyboard Shortcuts shows it as Turn Night Shift on or off.

title: Wallpapers: What it is
text: The wallpaper is the picture on the desktop, behind your windows. WolOS comes with its own pictures, including Dynamic, which changes with the time of day, and you can use any photo of yours.

title: Wallpapers: Why WolOS does it this way
text: The desktop is the one part of the screen that is only for you. A picture that follows the day (bright in the morning, dusk in the evening, night after dark) makes the computer feel calmer without asking you to do anything. And because colours matter, WolOS can make a whole theme from your picture in one click.

title: Wallpapers: How
text: Open System Settings > Wallpaper, or Choose… on the Wallpaper row of System Settings > Appearance. Dynamic (1): "Dynamic shows the day picture in daytime, dusk in the evening and night after dark." It changes by itself. One of WolOS's pictures (2): Wonderland Day, Wonderland Dusk or Wonderland Night. Click one; the chosen picture has a coloured frame and its name in bold. Your own photo (3): click Add Photo… and choose any picture on the computer. It fills the screen. The desktop changes as soon as you click. Like every look, the change can be undone in System Settings > Restore > Recent Changes.

title: Wallpapers: A theme from your picture
text: In System Settings > Appearance, the row Theme from your wallpaper has Make Theme. It takes the colours of your desktop picture and makes a theme from them, checked so that text stays readable, and applies it at once. It is called From Your Wallpaper. See Looks and themes.

title: Wallpapers: A worked example
text: Alice wants her cat on the desktop. She opens System Settings > Wallpaper, clicks Add Photo…, chooses Dinah.jpg in Pictures and clicks Open: Dinah fills the screen. In Appearance she clicks Make Theme, and the menus and buttons take on the ginger and cream of the photo.

title: Wallpapers: If something goes wrong
text: What you see What to do "The desktop picture couldn’t be read. Choose another in Wallpaper." Make Theme could not read the picture. Choose another picture, then Make Theme again. Your photo looks blurry It is smaller than the screen. Use a photo with at least as many pixels as the screen (System Settings > Displays shows the resolution). The wallpaper changes by itself Dynamic is chosen; it follows the time of day. Choose another picture to keep one. You want the old picture back System Settings > Restore > Recent Changes > Undo next to Wallpaper.

title: The Dock and the menu bar: What it is
text: The Dock is the row of app icons at the bottom of the screen; the menu bar is the strip at the top. System Settings > Desktop & Dock decides how both look and behave, and how windows are placed.

title: The Dock and the menu bar: Why WolOS does it this way
text: The Dock and the menu bar are on screen all day, so they should suit you: big icons for tired eyes or a touch screen, small ones for a small laptop, a Dock that hides when every pixel counts. Every option takes effect as you change it, so you see the result while you decide.

title: The Dock and the menu bar: How
text: Open System Settings > Desktop & Dock. Setting Default What it does Magnification (1) On Icons grow under the pointer as it moves along the Dock, so the one you aim at is easy to hit. Automatically hide and show the Dock (2) Off The Dock slides away and comes back when the pointer reaches the bottom edge of the screen. Windows get the whole height. Size (3) 56 points, between Small (32) and Large (96) How big the icons are. Delay before the Dock shows (4) None With hiding on: how long the pointer waits at the edge before the Dock comes, from None up to Long (5 seconds). A delay stops it from popping up when you only meant to reach the bottom of a window. Show battery percentage (5) Off The number next to the battery icon in the menu bar. Show date (5) On The date next to the time in the menu bar. Tile windows (6) Off Places windows side by side to fill the screen; see below.

title: The Dock and the menu bar: Tiling: windows side by side
text: With Tile windows on, a new window takes a share of the screen instead of floating on top, and the windows together fill the screen without overlapping. The rows under it set how: Arrangement: Split the focused window (each new window halves the one you are in) or Main window and stack (one big window on one side, the others stacked beside it). Space between windows: from Narrow to Wide. Tiling shortcuts > Show… lists the keys that move and resize tiled windows. Keep Floating: apps that should always float above the others, like a calculator. Add App… adds one; Remove takes it off the list. Turn Tile windows off again and every window floats as before.

title: The Dock and the menu bar: What the menu bar shows
text: Besides the date and the battery here, System Settings > Control Center chooses which status icons and switches appear. See Control Center.

title: The Dock and the menu bar: A worked example
text: Alice has a small laptop screen. She turns on Automatically hide and show the Dock, so her documents get the whole height, and sets the Delay a little above None, so the Dock does not jump up whenever she scrolls to the bottom of a page. She turns on Show battery percentage to see exactly how much charge is left on the train.

title: The Dock and the menu bar: If something goes wrong
text: What you see What to do The Dock is gone Hiding is on. Move the pointer to the bottom edge and wait, or turn Automatically hide and show the Dock off. The Dock shows up whenever the pointer is near the bottom Raise Delay before the Dock shows. Icons jump in size as you move along the Dock That is Magnification. Turn it off for a calm Dock. A switch flips back The change could not be saved; the switch shows what is set. Try again. Windows suddenly fill the screen side by side Tile windows is on. Turn it off to let windows float.

title: The keyboard: What it is
text: System Settings > Keyboard sets how your keyboard behaves: how quickly a held key repeats, which layouts you type in (for example English and German, or a layout with accents), and every keyboard shortcut of WolOS.

title: The keyboard: Why WolOS does it this way
text: Shortcuts are only quick if they are the keys your fingers already know. So WolOS uses Super (the Windows key) as its command key, the way Command works on a Mac: Super with a letter always goes to the app in front, Ctrl keeps the meaning each app gives it, and every shortcut can be changed and set back.

title: The keyboard: How
The keyboard: Key repeat
text: Setting Default What it does Key repeat rate (1) 25 a second, between Slow and Fast How quickly a held key types the letter again. Delay until repeat (2) 0.4 seconds, between Long and Short How long you hold a key before it starts repeating. Make it longer if letters come out twice when you type slowly. Type in Try it (5), "Type here to test", to feel the change before you leave the pane.

title: The keyboard: Keyboard layouts (input sources)
text: An input source is a keyboard layout: which letter each key types. The one you chose while installing is listed under Input Sources (4) as Default. Click Add Input Source… and choose a language and layout. To switch while you type, press Ctrl+Space: "Press ⌃Space to switch to the next input source." To remove one, click Remove on its row.

title: The keyboard: Change a keyboard shortcut
text: Click Keyboard Shortcuts (3), "Change or add shortcuts for WolOS". The page starts with what the symbols mean: ⌘ is "Command: the Windows or Super key", ⌥ is "Option: Alt", ⌃ is "Control: Ctrl" and ⇧ is "Shift". Then every shortcut, grouped: Search, Overview, Windows, Apps, Screenshots and the rest. Click a shortcut and press the new keys. If another shortcut already has them, WolOS asks whether to swap the two. The reset arrow on a row brings back that shortcut's key; Restore Defaults at the bottom brings back all of them. To add your own, a custom shortcut opens an app or runs a command; it needs a name and what to run. Press Shift+Super+/ anywhere for a sheet of every shortcut. The complete list, with every key in words, is in the Reference.

title: The keyboard: The shortcuts worth learning first
text: Keys What they do Super+Space Search Super+Tab Switch apps Super+, System Settings Super+Return A terminal Super+C, Super+V Copy, paste Shift+Super+V Clipboard history Shift+Super+3, 4, 5 Screenshot of the screen, an area, or the toolbar Ctrl+Super+Q Lock the screen Ctrl+Super+N, D, I Night Shift, Do Not Disturb, Stay Awake Ctrl+Alt+Left, Right The desktop to the left or right

title: The keyboard: A worked example
text: Alice writes in English and in German. She clicks Add Input Source…, chooses German, and from then on presses Ctrl+Space to switch between the two whenever she changes language. She uses Super+Return for the terminal so rarely that she gives it Shift+Super+T instead: she clicks the shortcut, presses the new keys, and it is changed.

title: The keyboard: If something goes wrong
text: What you see What to do The wrong letters appear The other input source is on. Press Ctrl+Space, or check Input Sources. Letters come out twice Make Delay until repeat longer. A shortcut does nothing It may have been changed or given to another action. Restore Defaults in Keyboard Shortcuts brings back WolOS's keys. An app's own shortcut no longer works A WolOS shortcut has the same keys. Give the WolOS shortcut other keys, and the app gets them back. The volume or brightness keys do nothing Some keyboards send them only with the Fn key held.

title: Looks and themes: What it is
text: How WolOS looks is three choices, from small to large: Light, Dark or Auto (Auto is light from 7:00 and dark from 19:00) and an accent colour, in System Settings > Appearance. A theme: a complete set of colours for the desktop, window borders, the lock screen, the terminal and your apps. WolOS ships 21 of them; plugins can add more. A theme from your wallpaper, made from the colours of your desktop picture in one click. The theme picker (Ctrl+Super+T) shows every theme as a small preview card, so you can switch without opening Settings.

title: Looks and themes: Why WolOS does it this way
text: People change a look far more often than they change anything else, so it has to be safe and quick: one click, the whole system at once, and an undo. A theme that only restyled the desktop's own apps would leave every other window looking out of place, so one choice restyles every kind of app, the terminal included. And every theme, including the one made from your picture, is checked so text stays readable on its background.

title: Looks and themes: How
Looks and themes: Pick a theme
text: Press Ctrl+Super+T, or open System Settings > Appearance. Choose Light, Dark or Auto (1), and click an accent colour (2): Violet (the default), Lake, Orchid, Rose, Tangerine, Marigold, Jade or Slate. Or click a theme in the gallery (3). The desktop and your apps change at once. Themes that plugins bring are listed after WolOS's own, under "From plugins" in the picker (with the plugin's name after each) and "From Plugins" in System Settings. Escape closes the picker. The accent colours apply to the WolOS Light and Dark looks; a theme brings its own. In Settings the footnote says it: "A theme restyles the whole desktop and your apps at once. Accent colors apply to the WolOS Light and Dark looks." Switch between light and dark from anywhere with Dark Mode in Control Center; see Dark Mode.

title: Looks and themes: A theme from your wallpaper
text: Choose a desktop picture (Settings > Wallpaper, or Choose… on the Wallpaper row of Appearance). Press Make Theme on the row Theme from your wallpaper ("Colors taken from the desktop picture, readable everywhere."). The new theme, called From Your Wallpaper, is applied at once. The colours are picked so every text and background pair stays readable, so a dark or busy picture still gives a theme you can read.

title: Looks and themes: Make your own
text: Make a theme > Open Studio in System Settings > Appearance opens Theme Studio, where you build one from scratch and share it as a plugin (The Maker).

title: Looks and themes: Take it back
text: Every change of look is recorded: System Settings > Restore > Recent Changes > Undo takes it back (Backups and undo).

title: Looks and themes: Blur, corners and animations
text: System Settings > Effects & Looks sets how glassy and soft the desktop is: blur and transparency behind panels, rounded corners, window borders and shadows, and animations, with presets that set all of them at once. System Settings > Accessibility > Reduce motion turns most animations off.

title: Looks and themes: A worked example
text: Alice likes the look of her beach photo. She opens Settings > Appearance, chooses Dark, picks a blue accent, then clicks the theme made from her wallpaper. The windows, the Dock, the terminal and the lock screen all take the colours of the photo. She dislikes it next week and picks another theme from the picker with Ctrl+Super+T.

title: Looks and themes: If something goes wrong
text: What you see What to do "The desktop picture couldn’t be read. Choose another in Wallpaper." Make Theme could not decode the picture. Pick another picture, then press Make Theme again. An app kept its old colours Most apps change at once; some only when they start again. Quit the app (Super+Q) and open it. The accent colour does nothing A theme from the gallery is active, and themes bring their own accent. Pick Light, Dark or Auto to use the accent colours. A plugin's themes are missing The plugin is off. Turn it on in the App Store, Plugins.

title: Arranging widgets: What it is
text: Edit Widgets is the mode in which you arrange the cards on your desktop: the clock, the calendar, the weather, music, batteries, system load, a world clock, a timer, a note, and widgets from plugins. In this mode a gallery opens next to the cards, every card gets a minus button, and you can drag cards around. Outside it, the cards stay where you put them and cannot be moved by accident.

title: Arranging widgets: Why
text: A desktop you look at all day should hold what you glance at, where you glance. A separate editing mode keeps that simple: you see exactly what you will get, sources never run in the gallery (it previews with sample data), and nothing moves when you only meant to click a card. How each widget works, and how to build your own, is on Desktop widgets.

title: Arranging widgets: How
text: Start editing. Right-click an empty spot of the desktop and choose Edit Widgets…. Or open Settings > Widgets and press Edit Widgets… on Arrange widgets. Pick a widget in the gallery's list. Its preview shows on the right. Choose a size: Small, Medium or Large. Press Add Widget (or click the preview). The card goes to the first free spot that fits. Drag cards to move them; they snap to a grid. Take one off with the minus button at its corner (Remove Widget). Leave with Done, Esc, or the desktop menu's Done Editing. For the weather, the gallery asks for a city first: type it in Search for a city and pick one. Only what you type is sent to look it up.

title: Arranging widgets: Without the editing mode
text: Right-click a card for its own settings: its size, the clock's face (Analog or Digital), the weather's city (Choose City…) and units (Celsius or Fahrenheit), and Remove Widget. Settings > Widgets adds a built-in widget at the first free spot, removes one, and has Arrange widgets for the rest. From a terminal: wol widgets add <kind> [size], wol widgets remove <id> (the id wol widgets list shows).

title: Arranging widgets: A worked example
text: Alice wants a clock and the weather on her desktop. She right-clicks the desktop and chooses Edit Widgets, clicks Clock and then Add Widget, picks Medium for the weather and clicks Add Widget again. She drags the two cards to the right side of the screen and clicks Done. They stay exactly there until she opens Edit Widgets again.

title: Arranging widgets: If something goes wrong
text: What you see What to do "No room. Remove a widget or pick a smaller size." The desktop has no free spot of that size. Remove a card, or choose Small. "The desktop is full. Remove a widget first." Settings found no free spot. Remove a card first. "Pick a city before adding, or choose one on the widget." Search for a city in the gallery, or add the weather card and use Choose City… on it. "No city by that name." Try the city's name in another spelling, or a larger city nearby. "This widget has problems. Fix its widget.json and reload." A widget package of yours has an error; the gallery shows it. Fix the file and run wol widgets reload (Desktop widgets). Cards will not move Cards move only in Edit Widgets. Right-click the desktop and choose Edit Widgets….

title: What a terminal is: What it is
text: A terminal is a window where you tell the computer what to do by typing a sentence instead of clicking a button. You type a command, press Return, and the answer appears as text right under it. Then the terminal waits for the next one. Inside the terminal window a program called the shell reads what you type and runs it. WolOS uses a shell called zsh unless you choose another; zsh basics is the next page. You never need the terminal for everyday things on WolOS: every page above this one works with windows and buttons. The terminal is for when you want to do something many times, or exactly the same way every time, or something no button offers.

title: What a terminal is: Why you might want one
text: A button does one thing. A command can be combined with others, repeated, saved in a file and run again tomorrow. "Rename these 300 photos by date", "make a copy of my Documents folder every Friday" or "show me what is using the disk" are one line each in a terminal. And when someone helps you on a forum, a command is easier to send and to follow than ten screenshots. WolOS's own command, wol, can change most of what System Settings changes, so whatever you learn here also works in a script later. A setting it changes can be undone like one changed in Settings, and anything that affects the whole computer still asks for your password on screen.

title: What a terminal is: How
What a terminal is: Open a terminal
text: Press Super+Return, or click Terminal in the Dock (the dark icon with >_), or press Super+Space, type "terminal" and press Return. The numbers in the picture: Terminal in the menu bar. Like any app, it has its name and its menus at the top while its window is in front. The prompt, ~ ❯. This is where the shell waits for you. The part before the arrow says which folder you are in: ~ (a tilde) is the short name of your home folder. The arrow turns red after a command that failed, so you notice. A command: ls, short for list. It lists what is in the folder you are in. The answer. The terminal prints it under the command. Folders are shown in colour, files in plain text. An argument. ls Documents lists the Documents folder instead. Words after the command are its arguments: they tell it what to work on. The cursor. The block shows where the next letter you type will go. Terminal in the Dock, with a dot because it is running.

title: What a terminal is: The parts of a command line
text: A command line is read from left to right, separated by spaces: ls -l Documents ls is the command. -l is an option: an argument that starts with a dash and changes how the command works (here: one line per file, with its size and date). Documents is an argument: what to list. Most commands follow this pattern: the command, then options, then what to work on. Capitals matter: ls works and LS does not, and documents is a different name from Documents.

title: What a terminal is: Paths: the address of a file
text: Every file has an address called a path: the folders you go through to reach it, separated by /. Your notes file has the path /home/aliceliddell/Documents/notes.txt (with your own account name instead of aliceliddell). Because the home folder is used so often, ~ stands for it: ~/Documents/notes.txt is the same file. A path that starts with / or ~ is complete. A path without them starts from the folder you are in. Two special names help: .. is the folder one level up, and . is the folder you are in. cd Documents/Recipes (change directory) moves you into the Recipes folder inside Documents. It prints nothing; silence means it worked. The prompt now reads ~/Documents/Recipes ❯, so you always know where you are. pwd (print working directory) says the same in full. cat ../notes.txt shows the file notes.txt from one folder up: .. is Documents. cd with nothing after it takes you home from anywhere. pwd prints /home/aliceliddell, the full path of the home folder.

title: What a terminal is: Tab finishes names for you
text: Type the start of a name and press Tab: the shell completes it. That saves typing and, more important, spelling mistakes. After cd Doc and Tab, the line reads cd Documents/ (1): the only name starting with Doc is filled in. The grey text after it (2) is a suggestion from the commands you typed before. Press the Right arrow key to take it, or keep typing to ignore it. When several names fit, Tab shows them all; press Tab again to move through them and Return to pick one.

title: What a terminal is: Stop a command: Ctrl+C
text: Some commands run until you stop them. ping localhost checks that the computer answers itself, once a second, for ever. Ctrl+C stops whatever is running and gives you the prompt back. In a terminal, Ctrl+C means stop, not copy. That is why copying uses Super:

title: What a terminal is: Copy and paste in a terminal
text: To Press Copy what you selected Super+C (or Ctrl+Shift+C) Paste Super+V (or Ctrl+Shift+V) Stop the running command Ctrl+C Clear the window Ctrl+L Bring back an earlier command Up arrow (then Return to run it again, or edit it first) Close the window Super+W Select text with the mouse as anywhere else: drag over it, or double-click a word. Careful Read a command before you paste it from a website, and never paste one that starts with sudo unless you know what it does: sudo runs it with the power to change the whole system. WolOS asks for your password on screen for anything that affects the whole computer, so a command you did not expect to need a password is a reason to stop.

title: What a terminal is: Your first five commands
text: Type What it does ls Lists the files and folders where you are. cd Documents Goes into the Documents folder. cd .. goes up one, cd alone goes home. pwd Prints the full path of the folder you are in. cat notes.txt Shows what is in a text file. wol help Lists what WolOS's own command can do; see The terminal and the wol command.

title: What a terminal is: A worked example
text: Alice wants to know how many photos she has from her holiday. She opens a terminal with Super+Return, types cd Pic, presses Tab (the line becomes cd Pictures/), types Hol, presses Tab again (cd Pictures/Holiday/) and presses Return. The prompt now reads ~/Pictures/Holiday ❯. She types ls and sees every photo. To count them she types ls | wc -l: the bar | hands the list to wc -l, which counts lines, and the terminal prints 214. She presses Up twice to get back ls, and Super+W to close the window.

title: What a terminal is: If something goes wrong
text: The shell tells you in one line what it did not understand, and the arrow of the next prompt turns red. What you see What it means and what to do zsh: command not found: lss (1) No command has that name. Check the spelling; ls was meant. If the spelling is right, the program is not installed. cd: no such file or directory: Documnets (2) No folder has that name where you are. Press Tab after the first letters instead of typing the whole name. cat: notes.txt: No such file or directory (3) The file is not in the folder you are in. Give its path, as in (4), or cd to its folder first. Nothing happens and there is no prompt A command is still running or waiting for you to type. Press Ctrl+C. > or quote> at the start of the line The shell thinks a sentence is not finished, usually because of an unpaired quote mark. Press Ctrl+C and type the line again. Permission denied The file belongs to the system or to another account. Your own files are in your home folder. A command asks for a password and nothing appears as you type That is on purpose: password letters are not shown. Type it and press Return. The window is full of text Ctrl+L clears it. Nothing is lost; scroll up to see it again.

title: zsh basics: What it is
text: zsh is the shell that reads what you type in a WolOS terminal. What a terminal is taught the parts of a command line; this page teaches what zsh adds on top so that typing commands is quick and forgiving: it remembers what you typed, finishes names, suggests whole commands, colours mistakes before you press Return, and lets you join small commands into bigger ones.

title: zsh basics: Why WolOS does it this way
text: zsh runs the same commands as the shells of most servers and tutorials, so what you read elsewhere works here. WolOS sets it up for you: the history is large and shared between your terminal windows, Tab completion ignores capitals, the prompt shows where you are and whether the last command worked, and none of it needs a configuration file of your own. Your own settings go in one file that WolOS never touches, so an update never undoes them.

title: zsh basics: How
zsh basics: The prompt tells you three things
text: ~/Documents/Recipes main ❯ The folder you are in (long paths are shortened to the last three folders), the branch name when the folder is a project kept in git, and the arrow. The arrow is in the accent colour when the last command worked and red when it failed.

title: zsh basics: History: every command you typed
text: Up arrow brings back the command before; press it again to go further back. If you typed the start of a command first, Up shows only earlier commands that start the same way: type cd and press Up to step through your earlier cd commands. History is shared: a command typed in one terminal window is in the history of the others too. The same command twice in a row is kept once. The last 50,000 commands are kept. A command that starts with a space is not kept at all. Use that for a line with a password in it. Tip When you press Return on a command brought back with !! (the last command) or similar shortcuts, zsh first shows the full command and waits for a second Return, so you see what will run.

title: zsh basics: Tab: finish names, list choices
text: Press Tab after the first letters of a command, a file or a folder. With one match, zsh fills it in. With several, the first Tab lists them and the second walks through the list with highlighted entries; Return picks one and Escape keeps what you typed. Shift+Tab walks back. Tab is forgiving: capitals do not matter (doc finds Documents), and you can give the start of each part of a name (D/R finds Documents/Recipes). Tab also completes the options of many commands: type ls -- and press Tab.

title: zsh basics: Suggestions in grey
text: While you type, zsh shows in grey the rest of a command you typed before. Press Right arrow or End to take it, or just keep typing to ignore it.

title: zsh basics: Colours before you press Return
text: As you type, the command turns green when zsh knows it and red when it does not, so lss is red before you run it. A file or folder that exists is underlined.

title: zsh basics: Moving around a line
text: Keys What they do Home, End Start or end of the line Ctrl+Left, Ctrl+Right (or Alt) One word left or right Ctrl+Backspace Delete the word before the cursor Ctrl+A, Ctrl+E Start or end of the line (the same as Home and End) Ctrl+U Delete the whole line Ctrl+C Give up on this line (or stop the running command) Ctrl+L Clear the window

title: zsh basics: Go to a folder by its name
text: Type just the name of a folder and press Return: zsh goes there, as if you had typed cd in front. Documents takes you to Documents, .. one folder up.

title: zsh basics: Short forms WolOS adds
text: Type Means ll ls -lh: one line per file, with sizes in KB, MB and GB la The same, with {{tip:hidden-file

title: zsh basics: Wildcards: many files at once
text: * stands for any letters, ? for exactly one. zsh replaces the pattern with every matching name before the command runs. Type Means ls *.jpg Every file whose name ends in .jpg ls IMG_20?.jpg IMG_200.jpg to IMG_209.jpg cp *.pdf ~/Documents Copy every PDF here into Documents Careful A wildcard makes a command act on many files at once. Run ls with the same pattern first to see which files it means, especially before rm (remove), which deletes without the Trash.

title: zsh basics: Joining commands
text: You write What happens ls ~/Pictures | wc -l The bar | (a pipe) hands the output of the first command to the second: wc -l counts the lines, so this counts your pictures. ls ~/Documents > list.txt > saves the output to a file instead of showing it (and replaces the file if it exists). >> adds to the end instead. cd Documents && ls && runs the second command only if the first worked. # a note Anything after # is a comment and is not run.

title: zsh basics: Quotes for names with spaces
text: A space separates arguments, so a name with a space needs quotes: cd "Holiday photos" or cd 'Holiday photos'. Tab adds the right marks for you. Single quotes keep everything as typed; inside double quotes $HOME and friends are replaced by their value.

title: zsh basics: Your own settings
text: Your settings go in the file .zshrc in your home folder (a hidden file). WolOS's own settings are read first and yours afterwards, so a line of yours wins. Updates never touch your file. Open it with a text editor, add for example alias photos='cd ~/Pictures' save it, and open a new terminal: typing photos now takes you to your pictures.

title: zsh basics: More in the Console module
text: System Settings > Modules > Console adds tools many people like: a richer prompt in the colours of your theme, a searchable history on Ctrl+R, a file picker on Ctrl+T, z to jump to folders you visit often, and a colourful ls. Each one turns itself on once it is installed.

title: zsh basics: Another shell for new terminal windows
text: System Settings > General > Shell in the terminal chooses the shell new terminal windows open in: bash, fish, nu or PowerShell, when installed. Your account itself keeps zsh, because the desktop and other programs expect it. See PowerShell basics.

title: zsh basics: A worked example
text: Alice has 40 photos named IMG_…jpg in Downloads and wants them in a new folder. She types cd Dow, Tab, Return (zsh completes Downloads/). ls *.jpg | wc -l prints 40. mkdir ~/Pictures/Garden makes the new folder, and mv *.jpg ~/Pictures/Garden moves them all. ls ~/Pictures/Garden | wc -l prints 40 again. Pressing Up three times brings back the ls line in case she needs it once more.

title: zsh basics: If something goes wrong
text: What you see What to do zsh: no matches found: *.jpg No file matches the pattern where you are. Check the folder with pwd and ls. zsh: command not found: … Check the spelling (the red colour warned you). If it is right, the program is not installed. A line starting with quote> or dquote> An opening quote mark has no closing one. Type it and press Return, or Ctrl+C to start again. Your alias does nothing Open a new terminal window: .zshrc is read when a terminal starts. The terminal behaves strangely after editing .zshrc Rename the file (in Files, show hidden files with Ctrl+H), open a new terminal: WolOS's own settings are back.

title: Your first shell script: What it is
text: A script is a text file with commands in it, one under the other. You write the commands once. From then on, one short word runs all of them, in order, the same way every time. A shell script is written in the language you already type in the terminal. Everything What a terminal is and zsh basics taught works inside one: ls, cd, echo, paths, quotes. This page writes the scripts in bash, the shell language of most scripts you will find on the web; it reads almost the same as zsh. You need nothing you do not already have: Text Editor to write the file, and a terminal to run it.

title: Your first shell script: Why it is worth it
text: Anything you type more than twice is worth a script. A script does not forget a step, does not mistype a folder name at the end of a long day, and does the job the same way next month. It is also easy to share: send the file, and someone else does exactly what you did. WolOS treats a script with care. It runs as you, with your permissions, never as the system's own account. Before you run a script you can ask WolOS to read it and point out mistakes, without running a single line.

title: Your first shell script: How
Your first shell script: 1. Make a file
text: Open Text Editor (press Super+Space and type "text"), and type these four lines exactly: #!/usr/bin/env bash # My first script: says hello. echo "Hello!" echo "Today is $(date +%A)." Save it in your home folder with the name hello. A script needs no ending on its name; the first line says what it is. What each line does: Line Means #!/usr/bin/env bash The first line, called the shebang. It says: "read this file with bash". It must be the very first line, with nothing before #!. # My first script: says hello. A comment. Every line that starts with # is for people; the computer skips it. Say what the script does, so you still know in a year. echo "Hello!" Prints Hello! in the terminal. echo "Today is $(date +%A)." $(…) runs a command and puts its answer into the text. date +%A answers with the name of the day.

title: Your first shell script: 2. Make it run
text: Open a terminal (Super+Return). Your home folder is where the terminal starts, so the file is right there. Type: chmod +x hello and press Return. chmod +x gives the file permission to run, the way a program has it. It prints nothing; silence means it worked. You do this once per script. Why this step: a text file you download or write is never allowed to run on its own. You decide which files are programs. That keeps a file that only looks like a document from starting anything.

title: Your first shell script: 3. Run it
text: ./hello You see: Hello! Today is Wednesday. ./ means "in the folder I am in". The terminal runs only programs it knows by name, so a script of your own needs that short path in front of it. You can also run it with WolOS's own command: wol script run hello That works even before chmod +x. And to have the script read for mistakes without running any of it: wol script check hello When everything is right you see one line, hello: bash script, parses. Parses means every line made sense. With the Developer module installed, the line also says that a style checker found nothing to improve.

title: Your first shell script: 4. A variable
text: A variable is a name that holds a value. Make a new file, greet: #!/usr/bin/env bash # Says hello to someone. name="Alice" echo "Hello, $name!" name="Alice" puts the word Alice in the variable name. $name takes it out again. Run chmod +x greet, then ./greet, and you see Hello, Alice!. Careful No spaces around =. name = "Alice" is read as a command called name, and you see name: command not found. A script becomes more useful when you tell it the value when you run it. Change the third line to: name="$1" $1 is the first argument you give the script. Now: ./greet Alice ./greet "Alice Liddell" print Hello, Alice! and Hello, Alice Liddell!. The quote marks around Alice Liddell make the two words one argument. Tip Always write a variable inside double quotes, as "$name" and "$1". Without them, a value with a space in it, such as Summer Trip.jpg, falls apart into two words, and the command looks for two files that do not exist.

title: Your first shell script: 5. A loop
text: A loop runs the same lines once for each item in a list. This script lists the photos in a folder of Pictures and counts them. Save it as photos: #!/usr/bin/env bash # Lists the photos in a folder of Pictures and counts them. # How: ./photos Holiday folder="$HOME/Pictures/$1" if [ ! -d "$folder" ]; then echo "There is no folder called $1 in Pictures." exit 1 fi count=0 for photo in "$folder"/*; do echo "Found: $(basename "$photo")" count=$((count + 1)) done echo "$count photos in $1." Run chmod +x photos, then ./photos Holiday: Found: Summer Trip.jpg Found: beach.jpg Found: cake.JPG 3 photos in Holiday. Read it from the top: Lines Mean folder="$HOME/Pictures/$1" $HOME is your home folder. With Holiday, the variable holds the path of Pictures/Holiday. if [ ! -d "$folder" ]; then … fi If there is no such folder (! is not, -d is is a folder), say so and stop. fi closes the if. exit 1 Stops the script and reports that it failed (below). count=0 A variable to count with. for photo in "$folder"/*; do … done The loop. * stands for every file in the folder; for each one, photo holds its path and the lines between do and done run. basename "$photo" The name of the file without the folders in front of it. count=$((count + 1)) $((…)) does arithmetic: one more than before. The name Summer Trip.jpg has a space and still comes through whole, because every variable is in double quotes.

title: Your first shell script: 6. Did it work? The exit status
text: Every command ends with an exit status: a number, 0 when it worked, anything else when it did not. The prompt arrow turns red after a command that did not end with 0, and echo $? prints the number of the last one: ./photos Holidya There is no folder called Holidya in Pictures. echo $? 1 exit 1 in the script is how photos says "this did not work". Use 1 for a failure and let the script end normally when everything went well; the end of a script is a 0. By itself, bash carries on after a command fails. To make a script stop at the first command that fails, put this line right under the first one: set -e

title: Your first shell script: A worked example
text: Alice wants a copy of her Documents folder every Friday, kept in a folder named after the day. She writes backup: #!/usr/bin/env bash # Copies Documents into a folder in Backups named after today. # How: ./backup set -e today=$(date +%Y-%m-%d) mkdir -p "$HOME/Backups/$today" cp -r "$HOME/Documents" "$HOME/Backups/$today/" echo "Saved a copy in Backups/$today." date +%Y-%m-%d answers with the date as 2026-11-04. mkdir -p makes the folder, and the folders above it if they are missing. cp -r copies a folder with everything in it. set -e makes sure the last line is printed only when the copy really happened. She runs wol script check backup (it says backup: bash script, parses), then chmod +x backup and ./backup, and sees Saved a copy in Backups/2026-11-04. In Files, Backups now holds a folder for today with Documents inside. Every Friday she presses Super+Return, types ./backup and presses Return.

title: Your first shell script: If something goes wrong
text: The terminal tells you in one line what it did not like. The line often starts with the script's name and the number of the line in the file. What you see What it means and what to do zsh: permission denied: ./hello The file may not run yet. Type chmod +x hello once, then run it again. zsh: command not found: hello You left out ./ in front of the name. Type ./hello. zsh: no such file or directory: ./hello No file has that name in the folder you are in. ls shows what is there; capitals matter. line 2: name: command not found Spaces around =. Write name="Alice", with no spaces. line 3: ech: command not found A mistyped command on that line. Fix the spelling, save, and run it again. Without set -e the script carries on after this. unexpected EOF while looking for matching and a quote mark A quote mark is opened and never closed. The line number bash prints just before it, above wol script check's own sentence, is the line where the quote opens; count the quote marks on it. Hello, ! The script needs an argument and got none. Add it after the name: ./greet Alice. Found: * and 1 photos The folder is empty or its name is wrong, so * matched nothing. The check at the top of photos catches a wrong name. /usr/bin/env: 'bash\r': No such file or directory The file was saved on Windows, with line endings bash does not read. Open it in Text Editor and save it again. The script runs for ever Press Ctrl+C to stop it, then look at the loop: something in it never ends. The next step is Your first Ruby script: the same ladder, with a language that keeps a name with a space in it whole without any quote marks. Scripts and shells shows how to run a script on another computer.

title: PowerShell basics: What it is
text: PowerShell is a shell that many people know from Windows. Its commands have names made of a verb and a noun (Get-ChildItem, Set-Location), and instead of plain text it hands objects from one command to the next: a list of files is a list of files with names, sizes and dates, not lines of text you have to cut apart. On WolOS PowerShell is one choice next to zsh. It comes with the Console module and, once installed, you can open it inside any terminal or make it the shell every new terminal window opens in.

title: PowerShell basics: Why WolOS does it this way
text: If you have years of PowerShell in your fingers, you should not have to relearn them to use a terminal on WolOS. So PowerShell gets the same treatment as zsh: the same prompt (folder, project branch, an arrow that turns red after a failure), the same keys, a history of 50,000 lines without duplicates, grey suggestions from your history, and the colours of your theme. What WolOS does not change is the shell your account logs in with, which stays zsh: the desktop and many programs hand it short commands written for zsh, and PowerShell reads those differently.

title: PowerShell basics: How
PowerShell basics: Add PowerShell
text: Open System Settings > Modules. Find Console and click Install. It asks for an administrator's password, because it adds programs for the whole computer; PowerShell itself goes into your account only. Wait until Console shows Ready. See Modules.

title: PowerShell basics: Open it
text: For one session: in any terminal, type pwsh and press Return. The prompt changes to PowerShell's. Type exit to go back to zsh. For every new terminal window: System Settings > General > Shell in the terminal, choose pwsh. You see under the menu "New terminal windows open in it. You still log in with zsh." Windows that are already open keep their shell.

title: PowerShell basics: The commands are Verb-Noun
text: PowerShell Short form What it does Get-ChildItem dir, gci Lists the files and folders where you are Set-Location Documents cd Documents Goes into a folder Get-Location pwd Shows where you are Get-Content notes.txt type, gc Shows a text file Copy-Item a.txt b.txt copy Copies a file Move-Item a.txt Documents move Moves a file Remove-Item old.txt del Deletes a file (without the Trash) New-Item -ItemType Directory Garden mkdir Garden Makes a folder Get-Help Get-ChildItem help gci Explains a command ls, cat, cp, mv, rm and sort work too, but in PowerShell on WolOS they are the same programs as in zsh, not short forms of the commands above: ls lists in colour like in zsh, and what they print is plain text. Use dir or gci when you want to pass the list on to another PowerShell command, and Sort-Object (not sort) to sort it. The verbs are few and always mean the same: Get reads, Set changes, New makes, Remove deletes. Once you know them you can often guess a command: Get-Date, Get-Process, Get-Command *Item* (every command with "Item" in its name). Capitals do not matter.

title: PowerShell basics: Options start with a dash and can be shortened
text: Get-ChildItem -Recurse -Filter *.jpg lists every JPEG here and in all folders below. You may shorten an option as long as it stays clear (-Rec), and Tab completes it: type Get-ChildItem - and press Tab to walk through every option.

title: PowerShell basics: Objects in the pipeline
text: The bar | hands the result of one command to the next, as in zsh, but what travels is objects. That makes sorting, filtering and choosing columns one word each: Get-ChildItem ~/Pictures -Recurse -Filter *.jpg | Sort-Object Length -Descending | Select-Object -First 5 Name, Length This lists your five biggest photos with their names and sizes. Sort-Object Length sorts by size because every file object has a Length; nothing had to be cut out of text. Where-Object filters: Get-ChildItem | Where-Object Length -gt 1MB keeps files over one megabyte.

title: PowerShell basics: Variables
text: A name with $ in front holds a value: $folder = "~/Documents", then Get-ChildItem $folder. $HOME is your home folder, and $PROFILE is the path of your own settings file.

title: PowerShell basics: Keys
text: They are the same as in zsh, so switching between the two is painless: Keys What they do Tab, Shift+Tab A menu of completions you can walk through, forward and back Up, Down Earlier commands; with some letters typed, only the ones that start the same way Right arrow or End Take the grey suggestion from your history Ctrl+Left, Ctrl+Right One word left or right Ctrl+C Stop the running command, or give up on this line Ctrl+L Clear the window A line that starts with a space is not kept in the history.

title: PowerShell basics: Your own settings
text: Type $PROFILE to see where your settings file is. Open it with code $PROFILE (if you have the Developer module) or any text editor, add your own functions or aliases, and open a new window. WolOS's own settings are read first and yours afterwards, and updates never touch your file.

title: PowerShell basics: A worked example
text: Bill moved to WolOS from Windows. He installs the Console module, chooses pwsh in System Settings > General > Shell in the terminal, and opens a terminal. To find what fills his Downloads folder he types gci ~/Downloads | Sort-Object Length -Descending | select -First 3 Name, Length and sees his three biggest downloads. He removes an old installer with Remove-Item ~/Downloads/setup.exe. Later, a tutorial gives him a zsh command; he types zsh, pastes it, and exit brings him back to PowerShell.

title: PowerShell basics: If something goes wrong
text: What you see What to do zsh: command not found: pwsh PowerShell is not installed. Install the Console module (System Settings > Modules). PowerShell is not in the Shell in the terminal menu The menu lists only shells that are installed. Install the Console module, then open System Settings again. "The shell couldn’t be changed. Try again in a moment." The choice was not saved, and the menu shows the shell that is still set. Choose again. A terminal says the chosen shell is not installed, so it uses zsh PowerShell was removed. Install Console again, or choose another shell in System Settings > General. A command from a website does not work in PowerShell It was written for zsh or bash. Type zsh, run it there, and exit to come back. The term '…' is not recognized No command has that name. Check the spelling, or find it with Get-Command *word*.

title: Your first Ruby script: What it is
text: rsh is Ruby with terminal commands in it. A script in rsh is a Ruby program, and any line that starts with a word Ruby does not know is run as a command, exactly as you would type it in the terminal. So one file holds both: Ruby to count, decide and repeat, and commands such as ls, mkdir and cp to do the work. rsh comes with WolOS. Its scripts end in .rsh. If you have read Your first shell script, this page climbs the same ladder: a file, the first line, making it run, running it, then values, a loop and what to do when something fails.

title: Your first Ruby script: Why WolOS does it this way
text: A shell script is quick to write and easy to get wrong. Every value is text that the shell splits again at each space, so a file called Summer Trip.jpg turns into two files that do not exist unless you remember the quote marks every time. A command that fails is easy to miss, and the script carries on. Ruby has none of those traps, but in plain Ruby running a command takes a whole line of code. rsh keeps both: you write commands the way you type them, and they get Ruby's care. A value you put into a command is always exactly one argument, whatever it holds. A command that fails stops the script and says where, unless you catch it and decide what to do.

title: Your first Ruby script: How
Your first Ruby script: 1. Make a file
text: Open Text Editor (press Super+Space and type "text"), and type: #!/usr/bin/env rsh # My first rsh script: Ruby and commands together. name = ENV.fetch("USER") puts "Hello, #{name}!" ls ~/Pictures/Holiday Save it in your home folder as hello.rsh. What each line does: Line Means #!/usr/bin/env rsh The first line, the shebang: "read this file with rsh". # My first rsh … A comment, for people. name = ENV.fetch("USER") Ruby: puts your account name in the variable name. puts "Hello, #{name}!" Ruby: prints a line. #{…} puts a value into the text. ls ~/Pictures/Holiday A command: Ruby has nothing called ls, so rsh runs it as in the terminal. How rsh tells them apart is the first word of the line. Something Ruby knows (name, puts, if, end, a name starting with a capital) makes the line Ruby. A word Ruby does not know makes it a command.

title: Your first Ruby script: 2. Make it run and run it
text: Open a terminal (Super+Return) and type, once: chmod +x hello.rsh Then run it: ./hello.rsh You see: Hello, aliceliddell! Summer Trip.jpg beach.jpg cake.JPG The first line came from Ruby, the rest from ls. WolOS's own command runs it too, with no chmod needed, and can read it for mistakes first without running anything: wol script check hello.rsh wol script run hello.rsh The check answers hello.rsh: rsh script, parses and rsh is clean: every line made sense, and rsh found nothing risky in it.

title: Your first Ruby script: 3. Ruby uses what a command says
text: Put a command between back-quotes, `, and Ruby gets its answer as text. Save this as count.rsh: #!/usr/bin/env rsh # Counts the photos in a folder of Pictures. # How: ./count.rsh Holiday folder = ARGV.fetch(0) photos = `ls ~/Pictures/#{folder}`.lines.size puts "#{folder} holds #{photos} photos." ARGV.fetch(0) is the first argument you give the script. .lines.size counts the lines of what ls printed. Run chmod +x count.rsh, then ./count.rsh Holiday, and you see Holiday holds 3 photos.

title: Your first Ruby script: 4. A loop, with one argument per value
text: This script moves the photos of a folder into a new folder, Sorted, and writes the ending .JPG in small letters on the way. Save it as sort.rsh: #!/usr/bin/env rsh # Moves the photos of a folder into Sorted, with .jpg in small letters. # How: ./sort.rsh Holiday folder = File.join(ENV.fetch("HOME"), "Pictures", ARGV.fetch(0)) mkdir -p #{folder}/Sorted count = 0 Dir.glob("#{folder}/*.{jpg,JPG}").each do |photo| name = File.basename(photo).sub(/\.JPG\z/, ".jpg") mv #{photo} #{folder}/Sorted/#{name} count += 1 end puts "Moved #{count} photos into Sorted." Run chmod +x sort.rsh, then ./sort.rsh Holiday. You see Moved 3 photos into Sorted., and in Files, Pictures/Holiday/Sorted holds Summer Trip.jpg, beach.jpg and cake.jpg. Lines Mean folder = File.join(…) Ruby builds the path of the folder from its parts. mkdir -p #{folder}/Sorted A command, with a Ruby value inside: #{…} in a command line puts the value in. Dir.glob(…).each do |photo| … end A loop: for every file ending in .jpg or .JPG, photo holds its path and the lines up to end run. name = File.basename(photo).sub(…) Ruby: the file name, with .JPG at the end changed to .jpg. mv #{photo} #{folder}/Sorted/#{name} A command: moves the file. Summer Trip.jpg moved as one file, with no quote marks anywhere. That is the rule that keeps you safe: a value in a command is always exactly one argument. It is never split at a space, never read as a pattern, and never read as another command. Try it: #!/usr/bin/env rsh name = "Summer Trip; rm -rf ~" echo #{name} This prints Summer Trip; rm -rf ~ and does nothing else. In a careless shell script the ; would end one command and start the next, and the next one would delete your home folder. A file name from the web, from a download or from someone else's folder can hold anything; in rsh it stays a name. Tip A list gives one argument per item: with photos = Dir.glob("*.jpg"), the line ls -l #{photos} lists each photo, each one whole.

title: Your first Ruby script: 5. When a command fails
text: Every command ends with an exit status, 0 when it worked. When a command in an rsh script ends with anything else, the script stops there and tells you the file, the line and the number. Here is copy.rsh, run when there is no folder called Backup: #!/usr/bin/env rsh cp ~/Documents/notes.txt ~/Backup/ puts "Notes copied." cp: cannot create regular file '/home/aliceliddell/Backup/': Not a directory rsh: ./copy.rsh:2: cp exited 1 The first line is what cp said; the second is rsh telling you that line 2 failed, so Notes copied. was never printed. A script never carries on as if a step had worked. To decide yourself what happens, put the command between begin and rescue. Ruby calls this rescuing a failure: begin cp -r ~/Documents ~/Backups puts "Saved a copy." rescue => e puts "The copy did not work: #{e.stderr.strip}" exit 1 end If cp works, you see Saved a copy. If it fails, the lines after rescue run: e holds what went wrong, and e.stderr is what the command said about it. exit 1 ends the script and reports the failure. A command used as a question, after if or unless, never stops the script; it is just yes or no: if grep -q milk ~/Documents/notes.txt puts "Milk is on the list." end

title: Your first Ruby script: 6. Files without commands: Sh
text: Many small jobs are about files: find the old ones, move them, check that a program is there. For those rsh has Sh, a set of helpers you call from Ruby. They work on the files themselves, start no program, and give back a Ruby value: a list of paths, a piece of text, or yes or no. Nothing needs to be loaded first. Save this as tidy.rsh: #!/usr/bin/env rsh # Moves downloads older than 30 days into Downloads/Old. # How: ./tidy.rsh downloads = File.join(ENV.fetch("HOME"), "Downloads") old = Sh.find(downloads, type: :file, older: 30 * 86400, maxdepth: 1) if old.empty? puts "Nothing to tidy." exit end Sh.mkdir_p("#{downloads}/Old") old.each { |file| Sh.mv(file, "#{downloads}/Old") } puts "Moved #{old.size} downloads into Old." Helper What it gives Sh.find(folder, name: "*.pdf", type: :file, older: seconds) The paths below the folder that match, sorted. maxdepth: 1 looks only at the folder's own files. Sh.grep("milk", file) The lines of the file that hold the text. Sh.which("rsync") Where the program is, or nil when it is not installed. Sh.read(file), Sh.write(file, text) A file's text, read or written. Sh.mkdir_p, Sh.cp, Sh.cp_r, Sh.mv, Sh.rm, Sh.rm_rf The same as the commands of those names. Sh.tmpdir { |dir| … } A new folder only you can read, removed again when the block ends. Sh.rm_rf refuses an empty name, /, . and .., and any path that leads to / or to the folder you are in: it raises an error and removes nothing. A list from Sh.find also goes straight into a command, one argument per path: ls -l #{old}.

title: Your first Ruby script: A worked example
text: Alice wants a copy of Documents in a folder named after today, and a clear sentence when something stops it. She writes backup.rsh: #!/usr/bin/env rsh # Copies Documents into a folder in Backups named after today. # How: ./backup.rsh today = Time.now.strftime("%Y-%m-%d") target = File.join(ENV.fetch("HOME"), "Backups", today) mkdir -p #{target} begin cp -r ~/Documents #{target} puts "Saved a copy in Backups/#{today}." rescue => e puts "The copy did not work: #{e.stderr.strip}" exit 1 end Time.now.strftime("%Y-%m-%d") is Ruby for today's date, as 2026-11-04. She runs wol script check backup.rsh, which answers backup.rsh: rsh script, parses and rsh is clean, then wol script run backup.rsh, and sees Saved a copy in Backups/2026-11-04. On a computer without a Documents folder the same script says The copy did not work: cp: cannot stat '/home/aliceliddell/Documents': No such file or directory and ends with exit status 1.

title: Your first Ruby script: If something goes wrong
text: What you see What it means and what to do zsh: permission denied: ./hello.rsh The file may not run yet. Type chmod +x hello.rsh once, or use wol script run hello.rsh. rsh: ./copy.rsh:2: cp exited 1 The command on line 2 failed and the script stopped. The line above it is what the command said. Fix the cause, or rescue it (step 5). rsh: lss: command not found A command name is misspelled, or the program is not installed. index 0 outside of array bounds with IndexError The script needs an argument and got none. Add it after the name: ./count.rsh Holiday. a value in a command is nil A variable you put in a command holds nothing (Ruby calls that nil). rsh stops instead of running the command with a missing word. Check where the variable is set. A line you meant as a command ran as Ruby Its first word is also a variable or method in your script, such as date after date = …. Put $ in front to force a command: $ date +%A. undefined method with NoMethodError A Ruby word is misspelled, or it is not in the Ruby that comes with rsh. For your home folder, write ENV.fetch("HOME"). bad.rsh:3:0: syntax error, unexpected end of file rsh stopped understanding the file at line 3: usually an end or a closing quote mark is missing above it. wol script check shows this without running anything; fix the line, save, check again. Tip A file ending in .rb mixes Ruby and commands the same way when rsh reads it, so start it with #!/usr/bin/env rsh. To keep a file as plain Ruby, with no line ever run as a command, make # rsh: ruby the line right after the shebang.

title: Your first Ruby script: Where to learn more
text: The rsh page shows more of what rsh does, with each job written both as a shell script and in rsh. Scripts that change settings shows what WolOS asks before a script changes a setting, and Scripts and shells how to run a script on another computer.

title: Scripts that change settings: What it is
text: A script is a text file with commands in it. You write it once, and from then on one command runs all of them, in order, every time the same way. WolOS runs scripts written for the shell and scripts written in Ruby, a programming language that reads almost like English. Ruby is part of every WolOS, so there is nothing to install. Two commands do everything on this page: wol script check reads a script and tells you about mistakes without running any of it; wol script run runs it.

title: Scripts that change settings: Why WolOS does it this way
text: A script runs with your permissions, and scripts are often copied from somewhere. So WolOS runs every script the same careful way. It never runs one as root. It hands your arguments to the script exactly as you typed them. It leaves the passwords and keys your terminal may hold out of the script's reach. And when a script asks WolOS to change something (a setting, an app, Do Not Disturb), you see a sheet on screen first and decide, just as for any helper. Every run is written down in System Settings > Assistants & Automation, so you can see later what ran and when.

title: Scripts that change settings: How
Scripts that change settings: 1. Write the script
text: Open Text Editor (Search: "text"), and type: #!/usr/bin/env ruby # Greets you and says how many files are in a folder. # How: wol script run hello.rb Documents # frozen_string_literal: true folder = ARGV.fetch(0, 'Documents') path = File.join(Dir.home, folder) count = Dir.children(path).length puts "Hello, #{ENV.fetch('USER')}!" puts "#{folder} holds #{count} files and folders." Save it in your home folder as hello.rb. What each line does: Line Means #!/usr/bin/env ruby The first line says which language the file is in. WolOS also knows a Ruby script by the .rb at the end of its name. # … A comment, for people. The first comments say what the script does and how to start it. # frozen_string_literal: true A habit of careful Ruby: the texts in the script cannot be changed by accident. folder = ARGV.fetch(0, 'Documents') The first argument you give the script, or Documents when you give none. path = File.join(Dir.home, folder) Builds the path of that folder inside your home folder. count = Dir.children(path).length Counts what is in it. puts "…" Prints a line. #{…} inside the quotes puts a value into the text.

title: Scripts that change settings: 2. Check it
text: Open a terminal (Super+Return) and type: wol script check hello.rb When everything is right you see one line: hello.rb: ruby script, parses and rubocop is clean Parses means Ruby understood every line. Rubocop is clean means the style checker found nothing to improve; it comes with the Developer module, and without it the check reads the script only. Nothing in the script ran. If something is wrong, you see one sentence per problem, with the line and the column of the file above it. Fix the line in Text Editor, save, and check again.

title: Scripts that change settings: 3. Run it
text: wol script run hello.rb Pictures You see: Hello, aliceliddell! Pictures holds 12 files and folders. Pictures was handed to the script as its first argument. Without it, the script counts Documents.

title: Scripts that change settings: 4. Let it change something, with your say-so
text: Scripts become useful when they act. Add these lines at the end of hello.rb: system('wol', 'focus', 'on', exception: true) puts 'Do Not Disturb is on.' Run it again. Because the script now asks WolOS to turn on Do Not Disturb, a sheet appears and names the script (“hello”, its file name without the ending) and what it wants to do. Click Allow Once, and the script continues. Deny stops that change, and the script stops with an error. Always Allow lets this script do this kind of change from now on without asking; you can take that back in System Settings > Assistants & Automation, where Ask Again next to script:hello under Always Allowed makes it ask next time, or in Terminal with wol helpers forget script:hello. Tip Write the words of a command separately, as system('wol', 'focus', 'on') does, never as one text. Then a folder name with a space or a quote mark in it can never be mistaken for another command.

title: Scripts that change settings: 5. See what ran
text: System Settings > Assistants & Automation lists every script run: which script, when, and how it ended. The arguments are not listed, because they may hold private words.

title: Scripts that change settings: What a script may and may not do
text: A script Runs as you Yes. sudo wol script run is refused. Reads and writes your files Yes, like any program you start. Be as careful with a script from somewhere else as with any program. Changes settings or apps through wol Only after you allow it on the sheet. Changes that affect everyone also ask for an administrator's password. Reads the system through wol (battery, disks, settings) Yes, without asking. Sees passwords and keys stored in your terminal No. It gets your name, your home folder, your language and the desktop, and nothing else from your terminal.

title: Scripts that change settings: A worked example
text: Alice wants a quiet hour while she backs up her photos. She writes backup.rb: #!/usr/bin/env ruby # Turns Do Not Disturb on while it makes a copy of a folder. # How: wol script run backup.rb Pictures # frozen_string_literal: true folder = ARGV.fetch(0) system('wol', 'focus', 'on', exception: true) system('tar', 'czf', "#{folder}.tar.gz", '-C', Dir.home, folder, exception: true) puts "Saved #{folder}.tar.gz" wol script check backup.rb says it parses. wol script run backup.rb Pictures shows the sheet for Do Not Disturb; she clicks Always Allow, and the copy Pictures.tar.gz appears in the folder she ran it from. Next Sunday she runs the same line again, and this time no sheet appears.

title: Scripts that change settings: If something goes wrong
text: What you see What to do wol: hello.rb: no such script (or it is not text) The file is not where you are, or the name is different. Check with ls, or give its path: wol script run ~/hello.rb. wol: tidy.py is a python script; wol script runs sh, bash, ruby and rsh. Only shell, Ruby and rsh scripts run through wol script. A message about line 7, column 12 Ruby or the style checker found a mistake there. Open the file, go to that line, fix it, save, check again. `fetch': index 0 outside of array bounds | The script needs an argument and got none. Add it after the file name. No such file or directory @ dir_initialize The folder you gave does not exist in your home folder. Check the spelling (capitals matter). The script stops after you clicked Deny That is the point of the sheet. Run it again and allow, or change the script. A program the script uses is not found Scripts get a fixed list of places to look for programs. Use programs that come with WolOS, or give the full path. The Scripts and shells page goes further: shell scripts, running a script on another computer, and choosing the shell of your terminal.

title: The terminal and the wol command: What it is
text: Terminal is the app where you type commands instead of clicking. You never need it for everyday things in WolOS, but it is often the fastest way. wol is WolOS's own command: one word in front of everything the system can do, from the theme and the volume to updates, modules, games and Secure Boot. Think of it as a remote control with a button for every setting: Settings, scripts and AI helpers all press the same buttons, so what works in one works in the others.

title: The terminal and the wol command: Why
text: One command for the whole system means one place to find help, one set of words to learn, and one gate. A command that only reads never asks for anything. A command that changes your own settings just does it, and you can undo it. A command that changes the system for every account asks for an administrator's password, and a helper program can never answer that question for you.

title: The terminal and the wol command: How
text: Open Terminal. Press Super+Space, type te and press Return. Or press Super+Enter. You see a Terminal window with a prompt (~ ❯): the place to type. Ask for help. Type wol --help and press Return. You see every command with one line on what it does; the list is long, so scroll up for the start. Add --help to any command to see what it does without running it: wol update --help. Read something. Try: wol settings wol battery wol network You see your desktop settings, the battery's charge and health, and whether you are online. Reading never asks for anything. Change something of yours.
