Try: wol appearance set dark You see the menu bar and the window title bars turn dark, as if you had chosen Dark in Settings > Appearance, and the look that is now in use: its theme, whether it is dark, and its accent colour. Undo it. wol undo You see the change reversed, and which change was undone with the command that would redo it. wol history lists your recent changes, and Settings > Restore shows the same list with an Undo button on each. Change the system. Commands that install for every account, or change how the computer starts, ask for an administrator's password. When the request comes from a program, the sheet names it:

title: The terminal and the wol command: Ten commands worth knowing
text: Command Does wol --help Every group of commands wol settings Your desktop settings wol appearance set light, dark or auto Light, dark, or following the time of day wol audio volume 50 The volume, in percent wol toggle nightlight Warmer colours after dark, on or off wol undo Undo the last change (wol history lists them) wol update status What the daily check found: fixes, security fixes, a new release wol modules list The optional modules and their state wol games doctor What games need on this computer, with the fix wol audio doctor A sound check, with the fix For example, wol modules list prints each optional module with its state and size: Add --json to a reading command to get data a script can use. The complete list has every command and says which ones helper programs may call.

title: The terminal and the wol command: A worked example
text: Alice wants a dark desktop in the evening. She opens Terminal, types wol appearance set dark and presses Return: the menu bar and the windows turn dark at once. The next morning she types wol undo and the light look is back. No password was asked, because both changes were hers alone.

title: The terminal and the wol command: If something goes wrong
text: What you see What to do wol: unknown command 'lss'; did you mean 'list'? A word of the command is misspelt. Use the word it suggests, or see every command with wol --help. Commands are lowercase. zsh: command not found The first word is misspelt: the command is wol, in lowercase. A command asks for a password and you are not an administrator Ask the person who owns the computer; Settings > Users & Groups shows who is an administrator. Nothing shows while you type a password That is on purpose. Type it and press Return. A change made from Terminal went wrong wol undo, or Settings > Restore > Recent Changes > Undo. A helper program wants to change something It shows a sheet with its name. Deny stops it; Allow Once lets it this time only. See Assistants and automation.

title: The terminal and the wol command: Related
text: The wol command (complete list) · Keyboard shortcuts · Assistants and automation · Recovery

title: Scripts and shells: What it is
text: Two things for people who use the terminal: scripts, and the shell a terminal window opens in. A script is a text file of commands that you edit and run: tidy a folder, back something up, turn on Do Not Disturb while a long job runs. WolOS runs four kinds the same way: sh, bash, Ruby and rsh. The first line names the interpreter (#!/bin/sh, #!/usr/bin/env bash, #!/usr/bin/env ruby, #!/usr/bin/env rsh), or, without that line, the name ends in .sh, .bash, .rb or .rsh. wol script is the one command for all of them: check reads a script without running it, run runs it here, on runs it on another computer. The shell is the program that reads what you type in a terminal window. Every account logs in with zsh; Settings > General > Shell in the terminal chooses another one for new terminal windows: bash, fish, nu or pwsh (PowerShell), when installed. The full reference for scripts, with every rule, is Scripts: sh, bash and Ruby.

title: Scripts and shells: Why
text: A script should run the moment you save it, with nothing to compile and nothing to install: sh, bash and ruby are part of every WolOS. But a script also runs with your permissions, often copied from somewhere, so wol script run takes away the easy ways to go wrong: it never runs as root, it hands your arguments to the script as they are (never through a shell that could reinterpret them), it leaves the tokens and keys in your terminal's environment out, and every change it makes through wol appears on screen first. Every run is recorded, so you can see later what ran. The shell is a matter of habit: someone who works in PowerShell all day should not have to retrain their fingers. But the login shell is what the desktop session and remote logins hand plain POSIX commands to, and PowerShell, fish or nu would not run them. So the choice applies to terminal windows only, and the login shell stays zsh.

title: Scripts and shells: How: scripts
Scripts and shells: Check a script
text: $ wol script check backup.rb backup.rb: ruby script, parses and rubocop is clean wol script check <file> reads the file without running any of it, then runs that language's linter when one is installed (the Developer module brings the Ruby one; rsh checks its own scripts). Each problem is one sentence, with the line and column above it. wol script alone prints the four kinds and how each is checked.

title: Scripts and shells: Run it
text: wol script run backup.rb ~/Documents As you, never as root. sudo wol script run is refused. Your arguments as they are. Put -- before arguments that start with -- (wol script run tidy.rb -- --dry-run). A clean environment. The script keeps who you are and where (your home, user name, language, the terminal and the desktop session) and gets a fixed search path. Everything else from your shell is left out. Changes ask. The script runs as a helper named after its file without the ending (script:backup; the sheet says “backup”). When it calls wol to change something (a setting, an app, a module), the approval sheet appears; an administrator change asks for the password. Reads run without asking. Your choices for helpers apply (Assistants and automation). One record per run, in Settings > Assistants & Automation: which script, when, and how it ended. Its arguments are not recorded, since they may hold secrets. The script's exit code is passed on as it is.

title: Scripts and shells: Run it on another computer
text: wol script on studio.local backup.rb ~/Documents The file is sent over ssh and run there the same way, with that computer's interpreter. Nothing is copied to its disk. ssh uses your keys and never asks for a password here. The other computer needs remote login turned on (Settings > General > Sharing). On another WolOS a change through wol is refused there, because nobody is at that screen to approve it; reads work.

title: Scripts and shells: Elsewhere
text: The same file works wherever WolOS runs a program: as a widget's data source, as a plugin command or hotkey, as a .wol bundle's entry. Each place keeps its own permission (plugins need the run permission, for example).

title: Scripts and shells: A first Ruby script
text: #!/usr/bin/env ruby # Turns Do Not Disturb on while a backup runs. # How: wol script run backup.rb <folder> # frozen_string_literal: true folder = ARGV.fetch(0) system('wol', 'focus', 'on', exception: true) system('tar', 'czf', "#{folder}.tar.gz", folder, exception: true) Two habits keep scripts safe: give commands their words separately (system('tar', 'czf', out, dir), never one string), and read data with JSON.parse, never with loaders that can run code. Only the interpreter's own libraries are there; no extra packages are needed.

title: Scripts and shells: What it does not do
text: wol script run is not a jail. A script can read and write what you can, like any program you start.

title: Scripts and shells: How: the shell in the terminal
text: Open Settings > General. The last row is Shell in the terminal. Pick a shell from its menu. It lists only the shells installed on this computer, by program name: zsh, bash, fish, nu, pwsh. Open a new terminal window. It starts in that shell. Windows already open keep theirs. The choice is recorded like any setting, so wol undo takes it back. The account's login shell stays zsh.

title: Scripts and shells: PowerShell, fish and nu
text: They come with the Console module (Settings > Modules > Console, which asks for an administrator's password). PowerShell installs into your account only (~/.local/bin/pwsh), the others system-wide. Each gets the same prompt, keys and history size as zsh, in the theme's colours. In PowerShell that means the folder and git branch in the prompt, an arrow in the theme's OK or error colour, 50,000 lines of history without duplicates, and Ctrl+R to search it (Modules).

title: Scripts and shells: A worked example
text: Alice writes a six-line script that copies her Documents folder to a USB stick. She checks it first with wol script check, which reads the script without running it and says whether it is in order. Then she runs it with wol script run, and WolOS asks her on screen to approve the change it makes. Every run is recorded, so next month she can see exactly what happened.

title: Scripts and shells: If something goes wrong
text: What wol script says in the terminal: It says What to do wol: notes.txt: no such script (or it is not text) Check the file name and folder. wol: tidy.py is a python script; wol script runs sh, bash, ruby and rsh. Only these four kinds run through wol script. Run other programs directly. wol: 'my box' is not a host name, an address or user@host Use the name or address from your ssh setup. Problem What to do An approval sheet appears while the script runs That is the gate: the script asked wol to change something. Allow it, or deny it if you did not expect it. The script cannot find a program it used in your terminal It gets a fixed search path. Call the program by its full path, or install it system-wide. A token or key your script needs is missing Your shell's environment is left out on purpose. Read the secret from a file in your home instead. wol script on changes are refused Nobody is at the other computer's screen to approve them. Run the script there in person, or only read. A terminal window says the shell chosen in Settings is not installed, so it uses zsh The shell was removed or the Console module is not installed. Install it, or pick another shell in Settings > General. The shell couldn’t be changed. Try again in a moment. under the menu The choice was not saved, and the menu shows the saved shell again. Try once more. PowerShell is not in the menu Install the Console module first; the menu lists installed shells only.

title: Modules: tools for what you do: What it is
text: A module is a bundle of tools for one kind of work, kept together as one unit: add it with one click, remove it with one click, and everything it brought goes with it. WolOS has nine: Module What it brings Download Developer Git, a code editor, containers, every programming language one project at a time, and Crystal with Cryswol (Set up for development) about 350 MB AI Assistants A coding assistant in the terminal that can act on WolOS only through approval sheets about 300 MB Local AI Open AI models that run on this computer, using your graphics card when it can up to 3.5 GB Sessions Terminal windows reopen where they were (Sessions) about 20 MB Creative Blender, GIMP, Krita, Inkscape, OBS Studio, darktable, Kdenlive, Ardour and Audacity (Creative apps in one step) about 1.3 GB Gaming Tools for Windows games that do not come from Steam (Steam and your game library) about 260 MB Console A themed prompt and handy terminal tools, the same keys and colours in every shell about 180 MB Input methods Typing Japanese, Chinese and Korean in every app about 210 MB Scanners Network and USB scanners without drivers, and an app to scan documents about 20 MB None of them is switched on for you.

title: Modules: tools for what you do: Why WolOS does it this way
text: Most people never write code or edit video, and a base system that carried every tool would be huge for them. So WolOS stays small and quick to install, and a person who needs a tool set gets it in one approval instead of a day of setting up. Removing a module takes away what it added, so trying one costs nothing.

title: Modules: tools for what you do: How
Modules: tools for what you do: While you install WolOS
text: On the page "Apps for What You Do", turn on the modules you want. The installer offers five of them: Developer Tools, AI Assistants, Local AI, Creative Apps and Gaming. The size to download is under the list. Finish the install. The modules download while WolOS installs. Without internet, WolOS remembers what you ticked and adds it at the first start with a network.

title: Modules: tools for what you do: Later, in Settings
text: Open System Settings > Modules. Press Super+, and choose Modules. You see Installed modules above and Available ones below, each with its size. Click Install next to a module. You see a password sheet: adding tools for every account needs an administrator. Type your password and click Allow. Watch the row move to Installed. It reads Ready when it is done. If it reads Finish Setup instead, click the button: this runs the part that belongs to your own account, and takes a few seconds. To remove a module, click the three dots next to it and choose Remove. What it added goes with it. Your own files are not touched.

title: Modules: tools for what you do: A worked example
text: Alice wants to edit a video her friend sent. She opens System Settings > Modules, clicks Install next to Creative, types her password and clicks Allow. A few minutes later the row says Ready. She presses Super+Space, types "kdenlive" and opens the editor. When the project is finished she removes the module, and the 1.3 GB comes back.

title: Modules: tools for what you do: If something goes wrong
text: What you see What to do "Installs when this computer next starts online." You ticked it in the installer but there was no network. It installs by itself when the network comes up, on Wi-Fi too. A module under Could Not Be Added It could not be downloaded after several tries. Check that you are online, then click Retry. "No modules are available", or a message that the list could not be read Try again in a minute. The Store's Create page still installs single apps. Finish Setup stays Click it again while you are online; the page says in one sentence what stopped. Local AI is slow It uses your graphics card when one fits; in a virtual machine or on a computer without a supported card it uses the processor, which is slower. An AI assistant asks you to approve a change That is the rule: it can look at things freely, but every change goes through an approval sheet that you answer (Privacy and permissions).

title: Plugins: add to the desktop itself: What it is
text: A plugin adds something to the desktop itself, not a new window: an item in the menu bar, a card on the desktop, a tile in Control Center, an icon in the Dock or results in Search. Plugins install for you only and update on their own, apart from WolOS updates. Every plugin in the Store was checked and signed by the WolOS plugin index.

title: Plugins: add to the desktop itself: Why WolOS does it this way
text: A plugin sits very close to your desktop, so it must say what it wants before it gets it. Each plugin lists what it asks for in plain words ("Asks to: show notifications"), and gets only that. A plugin that asks for nothing can do nothing but draw. If a plugin fails three times in a row, WolOS turns it off by itself, so one broken plugin cannot spoil your desktop.

title: Plugins: add to the desktop itself: How
text: Open the App Store and choose Plugins in the sidebar. You see Your Plugins (the ones you have) and Available (the ones you can get). Read what it asks for. Under every name is one line: what the plugin does and what it asks for ("Asks for nothing", "Asks to: read data from the web"). Click Get on a plugin you want. It installs for you and does not need an administrator. Click Turn On. Its parts appear where they belong: the weather in the menu bar, the clock card on the desktop. Turn it off or remove it from the same row (Turn Off, Remove). When a new version is out, the row says Update, with the version. A tile, a Dock item or a shortcut from a plugin that runs a program can do so only when its row says "Asks to: run commands as you": Turn On is your yes, for everything the row lists. When an update of a plugin you use asks for more, the row says what is new and its button reads Allow; until you click it, the plugin keeps what it had. Turn Off takes every permission back. Changes a plugin makes through WolOS itself still show the approval sheet (Privacy and permissions).

title: Plugins: add to the desktop itself: Make your own
text: Create Plugin… at the top of the Plugins page opens Plugin Maker, an app with an editor that checks your work as you type and a preview of the menu bar, Dock and desktop that cannot change your real desktop. When it is ready, Create Package writes one file you can share. Share… shows the steps to send it to the plugin index. The same app has Theme Studio, for making a theme with sliders and contrast checks (Looks and themes). The full description of a plugin file is in the Reference (Plugin API reference).

title: Plugins: add to the desktop itself: A worked example
text: Alice wants to know the time in Lisbon without opening anything. In the App Store she opens Plugins, reads "World Clock: Times in other cities. Asks for nothing.", clicks Get and then Turn On. A card with the times appears on her desktop. Later she finds she does not use it, so she opens the same row and clicks Turn Off. The card disappears; the plugin stays installed in case she wants it back.

title: Plugins: add to the desktop itself: If something goes wrong
text: What you see What to do A plugin says it needs a newer WolOS Update WolOS in System Settings > Software Update, then try again. A plugin turned itself off It failed three times in a row. Turn it on again; if it stops again, remove it and tell its author. A tile or a Dock item from a plugin does nothing The plugin may not run programs. If its row in the Store says Allow, a new version asks for more: read what, then click Allow. A plugin's web request fails A plugin may only talk to the sites it named, and cannot be sent to another one. Too many notifications from a plugin Plugin notifications are limited in number. To stop them, turn the plugin off in the Store (Turn Off on its row); Do Not Disturb holds them back for a while (Notifications). Create Plugin will not use a name The first part of the name, org.wolos, is kept for the plugins WolOS ships. Choose another.

title: Secure Boot: What it is
text: Secure Boot is the check, made by the computer's firmware, that lets only signed programs start. WolOS signs its boot images with keys made on your computer, at install. No image carries a shared WolOS key, and no two computers share one. In the installer it is a page you choose: Use Secure Boot is off unless you turn it on, and you can turn it on later in Settings > Privacy & Security > Startup Security. Think of it as a seal on a jar: at every start the computer checks that the seal is unbroken, which means nobody changed WolOS while the computer was off. The seal is made with a key that only your computer has.

title: Secure Boot: Why
text: A vendor key that signs every copy of a system is one secret that, once leaked, unlocks every copy. A key per computer has no such single point (the decision: Signed boot with this computer's keys). The price is that the computer signs its own updates, so its key lives on it, encrypted to the TPM chip when there is one. The other price is the blue key screen: your firmware has never seen this computer's key, so it asks you once.

title: Secure Boot: How
Secure Boot: Which path your computer takes
text: The installer picks the simplest path your firmware allows (wol boot detect shows which) and the Secure Boot page says what On and Off mean for it: Your firmware What happens when Secure Boot is on In Setup Mode WolOS puts its own keys next to Microsoft's. "Nothing to click". Microsoft's third-party certificate present (most PCs), Secure Boot on or off A signed, unmodified first stage starts WolOS's loader. "One blue screen after the restart" asks you to confirm the key once. If Secure Boot is already on in the firmware you cannot leave it off here (WolOS would only start after a trip to the startup settings), so the page just says one blue screen will come. Secure Boot on and the firmware trusts only Windows A firmware setting has to change first. The installer's sheet "Change One Startup Setting First" says: after installing, open the startup settings (often F2, F10, F12 or Delete) and allow third-party certificates (sometimes called Microsoft UEFI CA or Other OS). Then the blue screen asks once. None of the above WolOS starts without signatures and Settings says so. On a computer that trusts WolOS only through its firmware keys, Secure Boot switches itself to the stronger setup after the key has been enrolled.

title: Secure Boot: The key screen on the installed system, step by step
text: After the restart a blue screen appears: the key screen. It comes from your computer's firmware, not from WolOS, and it waits for you. It looks like an old computer screen: blue, white letters, a short menu. The mouse does not work there: use the arrow keys and Enter. Press a key. You see a short menu that includes Enroll MOK. Choose Enroll MOK, then Continue, then Yes. You see a prompt for a password. Type boot. Nothing shows while you type. Press Enter. Choose Reboot. WolOS starts. You will not see this screen again. The word comes from wol boot password. The blog post The blue screen at first start tells the story of this screen.

title: Secure Boot: The live USB stick with Secure Boot on
text: The live stick boots with Secure Boot on. Its first-stage loader, boot loader and kernel image are signed with the WolOS live-image key. The first start from the stick asks once to enrol that key. The certificate is on the stick as ENROL_THIS_KEY_FOR_WOLOS.cer (also EFI/wolos/), with a README.txt that says the same as these steps: If a screen says "Verification failed", press Enter. At "Press any key", press a key within 10 seconds. You see the same kind of blue menu. Choose Enroll key from disk, then the volume that holds ENROL_THIS_KEY_FOR_WOLOS.cer (your USB stick, often the last one in the list; if you see EFI\Microsoft, press Esc and pick the next one), then the file. Choose Continue, then Yes. Choose Reboot. WolOS starts and the blue screen does not come back. Missed the 10 seconds? Start from the stick again: the screen comes back. This key starts the WolOS stick only. An installed WolOS uses its own key, and the installer says what to expect before its restart. With Secure Boot off in the firmware, none of this is read and the stick starts straight away. When the install put WolOS's own keys into the firmware (Setup Mode), the stick is not signed with those keys and will no longer start on that computer. Remove it when the screen goes dark.

title: Secure Boot: Checking and repeating it
text: Command or place Does wol boot status Prints how well this computer is protected at start: the Secure Boot level, the security chip, kernel lockdown and the state of the system seal. Settings reads the same facts. Settings > Privacy & Security > Startup Security Shows how this computer starts. If a key is waiting it says "This computer's key is queued: a blue screen asks once at the next restart", and Finish Secure Boot setup finishes it (it runs once, then the page reads the facts again). wol boot enroll (administrator) Queues this computer's key for the key screen again. Restart.

title: Secure Boot: What signing protects
text: When WolOS starts signed, the kernel runs locked down and accepts only signed drivers. The seal on the system files and a version number are part of what is signed, so an older, retired copy of the system cannot be started again. The key that opens your disk follows signed kernels: updates keep unlocking the disk, while a kernel that someone changed does not. The boot menu can no longer be edited at start. What it costs: a locked-down kernel does not hibernate, and extra drivers from outside WolOS, such as NVIDIA's, need the same key screen once.

title: Secure Boot: A worked example
text: Alice installs WolOS with Use Secure Boot on. Her computer trusts the usual third-party certificate, so the installer says "One blue screen after the restart". After the first restart a blue screen appears. She presses a key, uses the arrow keys to choose Enroll MOK, then Continue, then Yes, types boot (nothing shows while she types) and presses Enter, then chooses Reboot. WolOS starts, and the blue screen never comes back. Total time: under a minute.

title: Secure Boot: If something goes wrong
text: What you see What to do I missed the blue screen, or the computer started without asking WolOS starts without the key and asks again at the next start (wolos-mok-enroll.service repeats it until the key is enrolled). Or run wol boot enroll and restart. The password boot seems wrong Nothing shows while you type, so type it and press Enter. If the screen refuses it, run wol boot enroll, restart and try again. wol boot password prints the word. The blue screen comes back at every start The key was not enrolled: you chose a different option or did not finish. Repeat the steps, ending with Reboot. Windows asks for its {{tip:bitlocker BitLocker}} recovery key after the Secure Boot step The disk asks for a password (or the recovery key) after a Secure Boot or firmware change The security chip refused because the measured state changed. Type your account password; the next start is automatic again because the chip is sealed again (wol encrypt reseal runs on its own). See Recovery. The stick says "Verification failed" and nothing else Follow the live-stick steps above, or turn Secure Boot off in the firmware for the first start. WolOS will not start at all with Secure Boot on Open the firmware's startup menu and pick the other slot, or turn Secure Boot off. Settings > Privacy & Security > Startup Security says what the installed system expects. Settings says the computer starts without signatures The firmware was neither in Setup Mode nor trusting Microsoft's third-party certificate when you installed, so WolOS started unsigned and said so. If you change that setting later, Startup Security is where you finish the setup. A {{tip:virtual-machine virtual machine}} such as VirtualBox

title: Startup Security: What it is
text: Startup Security is a page in Settings, under Privacy & Security. It reads how this computer started and says it in one row per fact. When a Secure Boot setup is still waiting, it also has the button that finishes it. It changes nothing on its own.

title: Startup Security: Why
text: What protects a computer before anything is on screen is invisible: the firmware, its keys, the first program it starts. If something there is off, you would not notice until it matters. This page puts those facts where you can check them in a few seconds, in words, and offers the fix right there instead of in a terminal. How Secure Boot is set up in the first place is on Secure Boot.

title: Startup Security: How
text: Open Settings > Privacy & Security > Startup Security, or type "startup" in the Settings search.

title: Startup Security: Reading the rows
text: Row What it says What it means Secure Boot On, with this computer's own keys / On, with this computer's enrolled key / On / Off in the firmware settings / Off Whether the firmware checks the signature of what it starts, and with which keys. "Off in the firmware settings" means WolOS is set up for it but the firmware's switch is off. Keys This computer's own keys / This computer's enrolled key / The firmware's keys / None Whose keys WolOS is signed for. Own keys: the installer put WolOS's keys into the firmware. Enrolled key: a key you confirmed once on the blue key screen. The firmware's keys: the keys the computer came with. Kernel lockdown On / On, strict / Off Whether the running system refuses changes to itself while it runs (unsigned drivers, writing to its memory). It is on whenever WolOS started signed. Security chip TPM 2.0 / None The chip that can open an encrypted disk by itself when the computer starts unchanged. Measured startup On / Off Whether each step of the start was recorded in the chip, so a changed step is noticed. Sealed system On / Off Whether the system files are checked against a signed list at every start (Recovery). Release a number The release this system belongs to. An older, retired copy with a lower number is not started again. If the facts cannot be read, the page shows Secure Boot: Unknown.

title: Startup Security: Finish Secure Boot setup
text: When the key still has to reach the firmware, the page has a row Finish Secure Boot setup with a Finish Setup button. Press Finish Setup. If Settings asks for an administrator’s password, enter it. The page then says "This computer’s key is queued: a blue screen asks once at the next restart." and lists the steps of that screen. Restart and follow the blue screen: press a key, choose Enroll MOK, then Continue, then Yes, type the password the page names, and choose Reboot. The full walk-through, with what to do if you miss it, is on Secure Boot. After the restart the row is gone: there is nothing left to finish.

title: Startup Security: A worked example
text: Alice installed WolOS with Secure Boot on and wonders whether it worked. She opens Settings > Privacy & Security > Startup Security and reads: Secure Boot On, Keys: this computer's enrolled key, Kernel lockdown On, Security chip TPM 2.0, Sealed system On. Everything is as it should be, so she closes the page; nothing was changed by looking.

title: Startup Security: If something goes wrong
text: What you see What to do "This computer’s key is queued: a blue screen asks once at the next restart." Restart and confirm the key on the blue screen. It stays queued until you do. Secure Boot says Off in the firmware settings Turn Secure Boot on in the firmware's setup (often F2 or Del while the computer starts). WolOS is ready for it. Keys says None and Secure Boot is Off WolOS started without signatures, as it said at install. If you turn Secure Boot on later, come back here to finish the setup. Security chip says None The computer has no chip, or it is off in the firmware. Disk encryption then asks for your password at every start. Finish Setup did not work The page says why, in one sentence at the bottom. Try again, or run wol boot enroll in a terminal and restart.

title: Sessions: reopen last time's windows: What it is
text: A session here is the set of terminal and coding-agent windows you had open: which desktop each was on, which folder it was in, and what it was running. With the Sessions module installed, WolOS saves that set while you work and, at your next login, asks once whether to open those windows again. Only terminals and agents are saved. Other apps reopen as they always do (Settings > General > Login Items).

title: Sessions: reopen last time's windows: Why
text: Work in a terminal is mostly place: the project folder, the desktop it lives on, the agent conversation you were in. A restart, a crash or a power cut throws that away, and rebuilding it by hand takes longer than the restart did. No program survives a reboot, but the place does, so WolOS keeps the place and starts the programs again. It asks instead of doing it on its own, because some days you want a clean desk.

title: Sessions: reopen last time's windows: How
text: Install the module. Settings > Modules > Sessions (it asks for an administrator's password), or wol modules install ai-sessions in a terminal. See Modules. Work as usual. Every minute WolOS saves the terminal and agent windows of this session, so a crash or a power cut loses at most a minute. Log Out, Restart and Shut Down save the set once more before any window is asked to close, so an ordinary end of the day loses nothing. That last save waits at most 10 seconds, so it never holds up the logout. Log in again. A notification asks: You see "Reopen 3 windows from last time?" with "Your terminals and coding agents open again on their desktops, in their folders." and a Reopen button. Click Reopen. Each window opens again on its desktop, in its folder: a plain terminal as a terminal, a named terminal multiplexer session reattached, a coding agent continuing its last conversation (claude --continue). Or dismiss the notification. Nothing reopens. WolOS starts saving this new session instead, so the old set is replaced about a minute later. The offer comes once per login, and only for a set saved in the last 30 days. Up to 64 windows are kept. From a terminal: Command Does wol sessions list Shows the saved windows (--json for scripts). wol sessions save Saves the current set now. wol sessions restore Reopens the saved set now. A helper or assistant may read the list; saving and reopening always show an approval sheet, every time (Assistants and automation).

title: Sessions: reopen last time's windows: What is saved, and what never runs
text: The file is ~/.local/state/wolos/sessions.json, in your account. For each window it keeps the desktop number, the folder, the kind (terminal or agent), a title and one of a few known commands. On restore the command is matched against that fixed list and rebuilt from it, never run as text, and a folder must be a plain absolute path. A window whose entry does not pass is skipped. A file someone edited by hand can therefore move a window, but cannot make WolOS run a program of its choosing.

title: Sessions: reopen last time's windows: A worked example
text: Alice has a terminal in her project folder on desktop two and another running a build on desktop three. The power goes out. At login a notification asks whether to reopen her windows; she clicks yes, and both terminals are back on their desktops in their folders, ready for her to run the build again.

title: Sessions: reopen last time's windows: If something goes wrong
text: What you see What to do No offer at login The module is not installed, nothing was saved in the last 30 days, or this login already asked. wol sessions list shows what is saved. Apps other than terminals did not come back Sessions keeps terminals and agents only. Add other apps to Settings > General > Login Items. An assistant's wol sessions restore asks you That is the gate: reopening windows always asks.

title: Low-latency sound: What it is
text: Latency is the delay between a sound happening and you hearing it through the computer. While you watch a film it does not matter. While you sing into a microphone and listen to yourself in headphones, or play a keyboard into a music app, a delay of a few hundredths of a second already sounds like an echo. The delay comes from the buffer: the small batch of sound the computer prepares before it plays it. A small buffer means less delay, but the computer must keep up; if it does not, you hear a click (a dropout). Settings > Sound > Pro Audio sets that buffer for the whole computer.

title: Low-latency sound: Why
text: There is no buffer that is right for everything. Monitoring through a music app wants the smallest; a stream wants a middle size; video and Bluetooth want a large one, and a laptop on battery saves power with a large one. So WolOS leaves the buffer on Automatic for everyday use, lets music apps and games ask for small buffers on their own, and gives you one place to fix the size for a session. A web browser cannot drag the whole computer down to a tiny buffer: ordinary apps have a floor, while music apps and games may go to the smallest.

title: Low-latency sound: How
text: Check the sound first. Open Terminal (Super+Space, type te, Return) and run: wol audio doctor You see each check (the sound services, inputs above their normal level, forced buffers, dropouts, the streaming pieces), each with the exact fix. Open Settings > Sound. Press Super+, and choose Sound, or type "buffer" in the Settings search field. You see the outputs and inputs at the top. Pro Audio is further down the page. Choose a Buffer size in Pro Audio for the job: Job Buffer size Live monitoring through a music app (Ardour, for example) 64 samples (1.3 ms) Streaming and recording a voice 256 samples Everything else, and Bluetooth Automatic The change applies at once, survives a restart, and stays until you change it back. Leave Sample rate on Automatic unless a session needs one rate throughout. Automatic follows 44.1, 88.2 and 96 kHz material instead of converting it. Watch Dropouts. The Pro Audio card counts them: "None", or how many since sound started. If the number grows while you record, choose the next larger buffer.

title: Low-latency sound: Music apps and audio interfaces
text: Music apps such as Ardour see WolOS's sound server as their own audio engine, with the buffer you chose, so there is nothing else to start. The Creative module adds Ardour and the piece they need; see Creative apps in one step. A USB audio interface keeps its own knobs for microphone gain. To give a music app every channel of an interface raw, switch the card's profile to Pro Audio in a terminal: pactl list short cards names the card, then pactl set-card-profile <card> pro-audio.

title: Low-latency sound: A worked example
text: Alice plays a keyboard into Ardour and hears her notes a hair too late. She opens Settings > Sound, finds Pro Audio and chooses 64 samples. The delay is gone, but after a minute she hears small clicks and the Dropouts count starts to grow, so she chooses 128 samples instead. Clicks stop, and the notes still feel instant. When the session is over she sets the buffer back to Automatic.

title: Low-latency sound: If something goes wrong
text: What you see What to do Clicks or crackles while recording The buffer is too small for this computer right now. Choose the next larger size, close other apps, or plug the laptop in. Try another USB port or a powered hub for an interface. Your voice comes back late in the headphones The buffer is large. Choose 64 or 128 samples in Pro Audio. The music app says it cannot start its audio engine Run wol audio doctor and follow the line marked as a problem. In a virtual machine the buffer stays large That is on purpose: virtual sound cards cannot keep small buffers, so WolOS raises them. Measure on real hardware. You want everything back as it was wol audio reset shows what a reset would do; wol audio reset --yes removes the Pro Audio choice, forgets stored volumes and restarts sound. Apps reconnect by themselves.

title: Recovery: when something does not start: What it is
text: A page of ways back, in the order to try them. WolOS keeps two slots (copies of the system), asks for a recovery key if the disk cannot open, keeps a list of recent settings changes you can undo, and has checks that name what is wrong. Think of it as the emergency card in a car: the first line is the thing most people need, and every line after it is rarer.

title: Recovery: when something does not start: Why
text: When something does not start you have the least patience and the least information. Each tool here answers one question: which slot am I on, can I open my disk, what did I change, which file differs, which device lacks a driver.

title: Recovery: when something does not start: How
text: Find your symptom, then follow the numbered steps.

title: Recovery: when something does not start: The system will not start after an update
text: Nothing to do. If the new slot fails to start three times in a row, the computer starts the other slot by itself. Wait for the second start. The computer restarts by itself up to three times. You see the old system, with your files and apps as they were. Check which slot runs. Open a terminal and run wol update status. You see which slot is running and what the last check found. Try again later. The failed slot sorts last in the boot menu. An older slot cannot be started again once it is retired; this is deliberate (Secure Boot). To go back on purpose: wol update rollback (asks for the administrator password) chooses the previous restore point for the next start. Settings > Restore lists the earlier system states. Programs you installed since that restore point are still there after you go back.

title: Recovery: when something does not start: An update was cut off
text: The power went, or the computer was switched off, while an update was being built. Start the computer as usual. You see the system you had before the update, with your restore point still there. Nothing of the cut-off update is used. Check what happened: wol update status. It answers The last update was interrupted before it finished; nothing of it is used. Update again to finish it. Update again. Click Update Now in Settings > General > Software Update. The update starts from the beginning and finishes.

title: Recovery: when something does not start: The disk asks for a password
text: At start the computer tries the security chip (TPM), then your account password, then the recovery key. One prompt takes both the password and the recovery key. A wrong entry simply asks again, as often as you need: there is no limit of three tries that would stop the start. Type your account password. This is the usual case after a Secure Boot or firmware change: the chip refuses because the measured state changed. You see WolOS start. The next start is automatic again, because the chip is sealed again to the state measured now. If you forgot the password, type the recovery key. It was shown once at the end of the install. If you chose Save to USB, it is a file on that stick. If you changed your password with passwd in a terminal, the disk still wants the previous one; the chip and the recovery key still work. Change your password in Settings > Users & Groups instead, which keeps the disk password in step. Accented letters cannot be typed before WolOS starts. That is why the installer asks for letters, digits and common symbols for a disk password. With no password, no chip and no recovery key, the data cannot be read. That is what encryption means.

title: Recovery: when something does not start: A setting broke the desktop
text: Open Settings > Restore. You see Recent Changes: what changed, when, and who made it (System Settings, Control Center, Terminal, a script or an assistant). Click Undo on the change. From a terminal: wol history lists changes, wol undo undoes the last one. If the desktop itself misbehaves, run wol shell reload. The desktop reconnects to the window manager by itself after it restarts, and the lock screen comes back if it crashes. If a theme or plugin is the cause: wol theme list then wol theme set wol-dark (or any listed id) sets a theme again; wol plugin disable <id> turns a plugin off. A plugin that keeps failing is turned off on its own.

title: Recovery: when something does not start: An app stopped answering
text: Press Alt+Super+Esc. You see Force Quit Applications: "If an app doesn't respond for a while, choose it and click Force Quit." Choose the app and click Force Quit. The other apps and the desktop keep running. It works over a full-screen game too.

title: Recovery: when something does not start: A system file or a device is wrong
text: Check the system files: wol base verify. You see every base file that differs from the signed list, or nothing. The same check runs at every start. Check devices: wol hw status. You see devices that need a driver or firmware, each with the fix. wol hw fix loads missing drivers (administrator password); wol hw fix --yes also installs packages. Check sound: wol audio doctor. wol audio reset --yes forgets stored sound defaults and restarts the sound server. Check games: wol games doctor prints the command that fixes each failed check. Deliberate changes: on a sealed system, wol seal off makes it writable until the next update (developer mode).

title: Recovery: when something does not start: A black screen after the install
text: VirtualBox: check the virtual machine's display settings on Download. Real hardware: if you can reach a terminal, wol hw status names devices that need a driver and prints the fix.

title: Recovery: when something does not start: Starting over
text: Try WolOS from the stick changes nothing on the disk. The installer can install again over an earlier WolOS. Next to Windows, the other system is kept (Installing next to Windows). If an install fails, the Failed page names the step. The log stays on the installed system at /var/log/wolos-install.log. See Installing WolOS.

title: Recovery: when something does not start: What to include in a report
text: wol about, wol update status, wol boot status (Secure Boot, TPM and seal state), and for sound the diagnostics that Copy diagnostics in Settings > Sound > Troubleshooting puts on the clipboard. Report on GitHub.

title: Recovery: when something does not start: A worked example
text: After an update Alice's computer does not reach the desktop. She restarts it twice more; on the third failed start WolOS switches to the other copy of the system by itself and her desktop appears. She opens Settings > Restore, looks at the list of recent changes and clicks Undo on the one she made last. Her files were never touched.

title: Recovery: when something does not start: If something goes wrong
text: What you see What to do WolOS does not appear at start Open the firmware's startup menu (often F12, F9 or Esc) and pick the WolOS entry. The boot loader update failed on a shared startup partition The other system's loader is put back; start it from the firmware menu. You cannot unlock the disk Use the recovery key (section "The disk asks for a password"). Nothing here helps Collect the items under "What to include in a report" and open an issue.

title: Network settings: addresses, VPN, proxy, encrypted DNS and airplane mode: What it is
text: Most networks need nothing from you: plug in the cable or join the Wi-Fi and the router hands your computer an address. Some places ask for more. A printer room may need a fixed address, work may give you a VPN file, a school may send the web through a proxy server, and on a plane every radio has to be off. All of it lives in System Settings > Network, and each part has a wol command for scripts.

title: Network settings: addresses, VPN, proxy, encrypted DNS and airplane mode: Why WolOS does it this way
text: A wrong network setting can cut you off, and then you cannot even look up how to fix it. So WolOS checks what you type before it saves anything (an address with the router of another network is refused with a sentence that says why), and a typed address gets 15 seconds to prove it works: if the computer loses the network with it, the connection goes back to automatic by itself. Keys stay out of sight: the key in a VPN file moves into your login keyring and is handed over only when you connect.

title: Network settings: addresses, VPN, proxy, encrypted DNS and airplane mode: How
Network settings: addresses, VPN, proxy, encrypted DNS and airplane mode: Give a connection a fixed address
text: Open System Settings > Network. Under the connection (Ethernet or Wi-Fi) click Configure… next to IP settings. Next to Configure IPv4, choose Manual. Type the Address with its prefix (for example 192.168.1.20/24), the Router (192.168.1.1) and, if you like, the DNS servers, separated by commas. Click Apply. The page tells you it is trying the new address. Within 15 seconds it either says the settings are saved, or that the new address did not reach the network and the connection went back to Automatic. To go back to the router's address at any time, choose Automatic and click Apply. Only IPv4 is typed in; IPv6 always comes from the network.

title: Network settings: addresses, VPN, proxy, encrypted DNS and airplane mode: Add and use a VPN
text: In System Settings > Network, find VPN and click Import… next to Add VPN. Pick the file you were given: a WireGuard file (it ends in .conf) or an OpenVPN file (.ovpn). The VPN appears in the list with its kind and Not connected. Click Connect; the row then says connected, and a VPN section with its own address and DNS servers appears above. Click Disconnect to stop it, or the … button and Forget VPN to delete it and its saved key. An OpenVPN connection may ask for its password: a VPN password field appears; type it and click Connect again. It is remembered in your keyring once it worked.

title: Network settings: addresses, VPN, proxy, encrypted DNS and airplane mode: Send the web through a proxy
text: In System Settings > Network, click Proxy. Choose Automatic and type the Configuration address (the PAC file your network gave you), or choose Manual and type the servers, each as a name and a port: Web proxy (HTTP), Secure web proxy (HTTPS), SOCKS proxy. In Don’t use the proxy for, list the names and networks to reach directly, separated by commas (for example .example.com, 10.0.0.0/8). Your own computer is always reached directly. Click Apply and type an administrator's password. The proxy applies to every account. Apps opened from then on use it; an app that was already open may need to be opened again.

title: Network settings: addresses, VPN, proxy, encrypted DNS and airplane mode: Encrypt the names your computer looks up
text: Every web address starts with a name lookup, which normally travels unencrypted, so the network can read and change it. DNS over TLS encrypts it. In System Settings > Network, click DNS over TLS. Choose When available (encrypted when the server can, plain otherwise) or Always (encrypted or no answer at all). In DNS servers, type servers that speak DNS over TLS, each with the name of its certificate after #, for example 9.9.9.9#dns.quad9.net. Always needs at least one: the router at home cannot encrypt, and every lookup would fail. Click Apply and type an administrator's password. It applies to every app at once.

title: Network settings: addresses, VPN, proxy, encrypted DNS and airplane mode: Airplane mode
text: Turn on Airplane Mode at the top of System Settings > Network, or click its tile in Control Center: Wi-Fi, Bluetooth and mobile data switch off, and the menu bar shows a plane. Turning it off brings back only the radios that were on before. A network cable keeps working in airplane mode.

title: Network settings: addresses, VPN, proxy, encrypted DNS and airplane mode: The same from the terminal
text: wol network ip enp0s1 wol network ip enp0s1 manual 192.168.1.20/24 192.168.1.1 1.1.1.1 9.9.9.9 wol network ip enp0s1 auto wol vpn import ~/Downloads/office.conf wol vpn connect office wol vpn disconnect office wol proxy manual http=proxy.example.com:3128 https=proxy.example.com:3128 no-proxy=.example.com wol proxy off wol dns tls opportunistic 9.9.9.9#dns.quad9.net wol airplane on wol network ip exits with an error when the new address had to be undone. wol proxy and wol dns tls read the administrator's password on their input. Every command prints the new state; add --json for scripts.

title: Network settings: addresses, VPN, proxy, encrypted DNS and airplane mode: When something goes wrong
text: What you see What it means and what to do The address is refused because of the router The router's numbers have to fall inside the address's prefix: 192.168.1.1 fits 192.168.1.20/24, 10.0.0.1 does not. The connection went back to Automatic The typed address did not reach the network within 15 seconds. Check the numbers with whoever runs the network. A VPN file is refused It is not a WireGuard or OpenVPN configuration this computer can read. Ask the people who run the VPN for the file again. The VPN connects but no site opens The file's DNS server or routes may be wrong: ask the people who run the VPN. No site opens after DNS over TLS With Always, a server that cannot encrypt gives no answer: choose When available or another server.

title: Set up for development: What it is
text: The Developer module turns WolOS into a workstation for writing software, in one step. It adds Git and the GitHub command line, a code editor (Code - OSS), mise (one tool that installs any version of Node, Python, Go, Rust and other languages, per project), containers that run without administrator rights (podman), terminal tools (lazygit, btop, zellij, jq) and a programmer's font. It also adds Crystal, the language WolOS apps are written in, with Cryswol, the library that lets a Crystal program use everything WolOS offers. A module is a bundle WolOS keeps as one unit: added in one step, removed in one step.

title: Set up for development: Why
text: Setting up a new computer for programming usually costs a day of installing, configuring and finding out what is missing. A module makes that one tick. The base system stays small for everyone else, because the module is never ticked for you. And because Crystal and Cryswol come with it, the first app you write is a real WolOS app, not a web page in a window.

title: Set up for development: How
Set up for development: While you install WolOS
text: On the page "Apps for What You Do", turn on Developer Tools. You see "Code editor, Git, containers and programming languages" under it, and the download size under the list. Finish the install. The module downloads while WolOS installs; without the internet it is added at the first start with a network.

title: Set up for development: On a WolOS that is already installed
text: Open Settings > Modules (or type "modules" in the Settings search field) and click Install next to Developer. You see a password sheet: adding packages for every account needs an administrator. Type your password and click Allow. Let it finish. Right after the packages, Settings runs the part that belongs to your own account: it makes the folder ~/Work for your projects and turns on the container service for you. You see Ready next to Developer. If you see Finish Setup instead (for example when the module was added from a terminal), click it once. It changes nothing when run again. Open Terminal (Super+Space, type te, Return) and check: crystal --version git --version You see both answer with a version number. In a terminal the same two steps are: wol modules install dev wol modules enable dev

title: Set up for development: More tools from the Store
text: The Store's Develop page has editors, IDEs, database tools and a game engine, each one click.

title: Set up for development: Languages with mise
text: mise installs a language per project without touching the system. In a project folder: mise use node@22 mise use python@3.13 The version is written to the project, so the next person who opens it gets the same one.

title: Set up for development: A worked example
text: Alice wants to try a small web project. She opens System Settings > Modules, clicks Install next to Developer and types her password. When the row says Ready, she opens Terminal, types crystal --version and git --version and sees both answer with a version number. Her projects go in the new Work folder, and she opens them in the code editor. Her laptop was ready for programming in the time it took to make tea.

title: Set up for development: If something goes wrong
text: What you see What to do The password sheet says "Incorrect password. Try again." Type the password again: Caps Lock or another keyboard layout changes letters, and the eye button in the field shows what you typed. In 0.12.0 a right password could be refused here; that is fixed since 0.13. If the sheet still refuses it, run sudo /usr/lib/wolos/modules-install dev in Terminal (it asks for the same password), then click Finish Setup in Settings > Modules. crystal: command not found The module is not installed yet. Settings > Modules > Developer > Install, or wol modules install dev. Developer is under Could Not Be Added It could not be downloaded after several tries. Check that you're online and click Retry. Finish Setup stays The user step stopped. Run wol modules enable dev in Terminal: it says which step failed. A container tool says it cannot reach the Docker socket Run wol modules enable dev again; it turns on the container service for your account. You want the space back Settings > Modules, click … next to Developer and remove it, or wol modules remove dev. ~/Work and your files stay.

title: Your first app in Crystal: What it is
text: A WolOS app can be one file. This page walks through a twelve-line program in Crystal, the language WolOS apps are written in. It reads like a script and builds into a normal program. The program uses Cryswol, the Crystal library that speaks to WolOS for you: it opens a connection to the system, asks what the system is called and whether it is light or dark, and tries to post a notification. Think of Cryswol as the app's phone line to WolOS: the app asks, WolOS answers, and WolOS decides what the app may do.

title: Your first app in Crystal: Why
text: WolOS gives apps one way in: a stable system library, and Cryswol on top of it for Crystal. An app never needs administrator rights to talk to the system, and it never reaches around the rules: before it does something personal, such as showing notifications, the person using it decides. For you as a developer that means no memory handling and no error codes: you get Crystal objects, and a refusal arrives as an error that carries WolOS's own sentence, ready to show to a person.

title: Your first app in Crystal: How
text: Before you start: add the Developer module, which brings Crystal and Cryswol. See Set up for development. Make a folder for the project in Terminal: mkdir -p ~/Work/hello && cd ~/Work/hello Write the program. Open the editor (code hello.cr, or any editor) and save this as hello.cr: require "cryswol" Wol::Context.open("org.example.hello") do |ctx| info = Wol::System.info(ctx) puts "Hello from #{info.os_name}, in #{info.appearance} mode" begin Wol::Notification.post(ctx, "Hello", "My first WolOS app") puts "Notification sent" rescue e : Wol::PermissionDenied puts e.message end end Wol::Context.open connects to WolOS under an app id, a name that is yours alone (here org.example.hello), and closes the connection when the block ends. Build it. Crystal needs to know where the system's Crystal libraries live: CRYSTAL_PATH="/usr/lib/wolos/crystal:$(crystal env CRYSTAL_PATH)" crystal build hello.cr You see no output and a new program called hello in the folder. The first build takes a little while; later ones are quicker. Run it: ./hello You see Hello from WolOS, in Light mode (or Dark), printed by your program, and then WolOS's own sentence: Notifications are off for hello. Turn them on in System Settings > Privacy & Security. A new app may not show notifications until the person allows it, and the rescue turns that refusal into a line of text instead of a crash. Look at Privacy & Security. Open Settings > Privacy & Security. You see hello under Notifications, with its switch off: the pane lists every app that holds a permission, and also every app that was refused one, so the person can let it. Turn the switch on and run ./hello again; this time the notification appears. The program above shows the part every app needs anyway: a refusal arrives as an error with a sentence you can show to the person.

title: Your first app in Crystal: What you just used
text: Line Does require "cryswol" Loads Cryswol. Everything is under the name Wol. Wol::Context.open(...) do |ctx| One connection to WolOS for this app, closed for you at the end. Wol::System.info(ctx) What the system is: its name, the kernel, light or dark, the accent colour. Wol::Notification.post(ctx, title, body) A notification, if the person allowed it. rescue e : Wol::PermissionDenied What to do when the person has not allowed it: here, print WolOS's sentence. Cryswol covers much more: windows, menus, the clipboard, saved preferences, open and save panels, power, network, sound, Search, messages between apps and background services. The Cryswol reference lists every one with the permission it needs.

title: Your first app in Crystal: Next: a window
text: For an app with a window, buttons and lists, follow Your first Wolkit app. Wolkit is the WolOS kit for app windows; it is in preview.

title: Your first app in Crystal: Share it on WolOS Hub
text: WolOS Hub lists apps, plugins and extensions made by anyone. Your files stay in your own public repository on GitHub; the Hub checks every version, signs it and lists it. Publishing takes five steps the first time, all on one page, https://hub.wolos.org/publish. Its rail on the left shows the five steps and folds each finished one into one line. Sign in. Click Sign in with GitHub. The Hub asks only for your public profile and the organisations you belong to. Accept the agreements. Read the Contributor Agreement and the Publisher Agreement, tick the box under each, and click Accept and continue. You accept them once; when one changes, the Hub asks again before your next release. Install WolOS Hub on GitHub. Click Install on GitHub, choose the repositories you publish from, and install. Back on the Hub, click I have installed it if the page has not noticed by itself. The repository must be public, because people download your files from its releases. Connect a repository. Pick it in the list and say what it is: App, Plugin or Extension. The Hub fills in the rest from GitHub and shows it, for example "It will be listed as alice.notes" and the name your release file needs: an app ends in .wol, a plugin in .wolplug, an extension in .wolext. Change the details edits the id, name, one sentence, licence and file name. Click Connect. Push a tag. The page shows three lines with your names filled in, and a Copy button. Run them in your project folder: git tag v1.0.0 && git push origin v1.0.0 && gh release create v1.0.0 alice.notes-1.0.0.wol The page shows "Waiting for your tag. This page notices it.", then See where it stands. Each version has a status page with four stages: Received, Checked, Signed and Published. It refreshes by itself, and a version is usually listed within about an hour. After the first time, every release is the last step only: push a new tag and publish its release with the file attached. A version that was checked is never replaced, so a fix goes out as a new version with a new tag.

title: Your first app in Crystal: A worked example
text: Alice builds the twelve-line program and runs it. It prints the name of her system and whether it is light or dark, then tries to post a notification. Her app is new, so WolOS refuses, and the program prints the sentence WolOS gave with the refusal and carries on without crashing, which is exactly how every app is meant to behave. In System Settings > Privacy & Security she finds hello under Notifications with its switch off, turns it on and runs the program again: this time the notification appears.

title: Your first app in Crystal: If something goes wrong
text: What you see What to do crystal: command not found Add the Developer module: wol modules install dev. can't find file 'cryswol' The build line is missing CRYSTAL_PATH. Copy step 3 as it is. Unhandled exception: Notifications are off for hello. The program has no rescue for Wol::PermissionDenied. Add it as in step 2, and show the sentence to the person using your app. Wol::Unavailable The WolOS system service is not answering, for example in a plain console without a desktop session. Run the program from Terminal on the desktop. Wol::UsageError The program used something after its connection was closed, or outside the block it belongs to. This is a bug to fix in the code; it is never shown to a person. The Hub's status page says "No file found in the release" The release has no file with the name step 4 showed. Attach it on GitHub, then click Check again. "The tag is not a version" A version is a number such as v1.2.3 or 1.2.3. Tag the release again with one. "Turn on two-factor sign-in on your GitHub account first." The Publisher Agreement asks for it. Turn it on in GitHub's settings, then connect again. "Your GitHub account is younger than 90 days." The Hub lists a first app once the GitHub account is 90 days old. The app starts here but not on another computer It was built against a newer system library. When you package it, say which version it needs (depends=(libwol>=1.N)).

title: Cryswol and Wolkit: apps made for WolOS: What it is
text: WolOS apps are written in Crystal, a language that reads like a script and builds into a normal program. Two libraries make it a WolOS app: Cryswol is the phone line between your program and the system. Through it a program opens windows, posts notifications, uses the clipboard, saves preferences, opens file panels, shares, plays sound and asks for the things a person may allow or refuse. Wolkit is the kit for programs that draw their own window: a description of the window, state that updates only the parts that change, and the parts the interface guidelines name (toolbar, sidebar, sheet, menu, tabs). Your program never needs administrator rights to talk to the system, and it never reaches around the rules: before it does something personal, such as showing notifications, the person using it decides. A refusal arrives in your program as an error that carries WolOS's own sentence, ready to show.

title: Cryswol and Wolkit: apps made for WolOS: Why WolOS does it this way
text: Writing an app should not mean managing memory by hand or decoding error numbers. Cryswol does that once, in one place, so a program of twelve lines is a real app. Splitting the work keeps both halves good: the fast, safe things (layout, text, painting, input, accessibility) live in the engine under Wolkit, and the pleasant things (the language you write in, components, tools) live in the Crystal part.

title: Cryswol and Wolkit: apps made for WolOS: How
text: Install the Developer Tools. Tick Developer Tools in the installer, or open System Settings > Modules and click Install next to Developer (Set up for development). Write and run a first program. Your first app in Crystal walks through twelve lines that read the system, ask to post a notification and handle a refusal. Draw a window. The Wolkit tutorial in the Reference builds a small to-do app in about fifteen minutes: a signal, a text field, a list, a style sheet, a test and a package (Your first Wolkit app). Look things up. The Reference has every object of Cryswol (Cryswol), every element of Wolkit (Wolkit), its style language (Wolkit style), the engine (libWolkit) and the interface guidelines (Interface guidelines). The Cryswol page shows what it looks like.

title: Cryswol and Wolkit: apps made for WolOS: A worked example
text: Alice writes a small program that asks the system whether it is in light or dark mode and tries to post a notification. The first time, WolOS asks her to allow notifications for the program. She says no, and the program prints the sentence WolOS gave it: it says where in System Settings she could allow it later. Her program is finished, small, and behaves the way people expect an app to behave.

title: Cryswol and Wolkit: apps made for WolOS: If something goes wrong
text: What you see What to do crystal: command not found The Developer module is not installed. Install it in System Settings > Modules (the row Developer). A permission error with a sentence The person has not allowed it. Show the sentence; it says where in System Settings to allow it. A window freezes while a file panel is open Call the panel in the background, so the window keeps drawing. The Reference shows how. An app refuses to start on another computer It was built for a newer system library than that computer has. Update that computer, then try again.
